Thesis gate

The metaphysics of conversational common ground. Stalnaker defines it by iterated acceptance, with belief as the default setting for acceptance; Yalcin (2024) argues acceptance is voluntary but not iterative while knowledge is iterative but not voluntary, and redefines common ground as common knowledge that p is accepted. Both keep context a state of the participants' minds. The pressure is on that shared assumption: discourse in which everyone knows nobody believes or accepts the content still proceeds as though the proposition is in play — pretense, bargaining, legal and institutional speech, strategic discourse — and public commitment tracks it where attitudes do not. At issue is whether conversational context is a mental state of the participants at all, or a structure of jointly maintained public commitments, with consequences for presupposition, accommodation, disagreement, fiction and testimony.

235 candidates · 1 in the top-right quadrant · 5 repairable · 207 not attacked

Promise is scored blind, before any attack. Residual is the strongest objection left unanswered — 0 is best, and it is the ranking number. Worst is the strongest objection mounted at all: when Worst is also low, the thesis was not seriously tested rather than sturdy.

Look here first

Promise 4+ with nothing above a 2 left unanswered. Ambitious and hard to break. Expect a short list, and an empty one on some runs.

P1. Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the accidental convergence of two independently operating mechanisms: one tracking mutual public commitment (what can be presupposed in assertion) and another tracking shared mental states (what coordinates collaborative planning).

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 4/5 · survives
Move · Target
distinction — The shared assumption of both Stalnaker and Yalcin that 'common ground' picks out a single theoretical kind
Sketch

The argument begins by observing that the conditions for felicitous presupposition diverge systematically from the conditions for felicitous collaborative proposals. In pretense and bargaining, you can presuppose p without anyone accepting p, but you cannot felicitously propose 'let's act as if p' while presupposing p (that would be redundant). In collaborative planning contexts, you need actual shared acceptance or belief, but presupposition can proceed on mere public commitment. The key premise: if common ground were a unified phenomenon, these two dimensions would covary, but they come apart in systematic patterns across discourse types. This explains why theorists find conflicting intuitions—they're tracking different phenomena that happen to coincide in paradigm cases of information exchange.

Appraiser (blind)
The disunity claim (presupposition vs. collaborative planning) is genuinely interesting and could explain persistent theoretical disagreements through a diagnostic error.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The defence showed the target is operational unity, not absolute monolithism, which both theorists do maintain architecturally.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, answered. The defence provided falsification criteria: show the dimensions must covary or that divergences are monotonic transformations, not inversions.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 4/5, answered. The defence distinguished Clark's unified-ground-with-aspects from the thesis's claim of two separate mechanisms with no unified middle layer.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, answered. The defence provided a principled criterion: inversive relationships that resist unified operating principles, not mere dissociation.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, answered. The defence showed the teaching case demonstrates pragmatic coordination of independent mechanisms, not constitutive interdependence.
full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "the shared assumption of both Stalnaker and Yalcin that 'common ground' picks out a single theoretical kind." However, Stalnaker's framework explicitly allows for different *aspects* or *dimensions* of common ground serving different theoretical purposes. In "Common Ground" (2002) and related work, Stalnaker distinguishes the common ground as a body of information (what is mutually presupposed) from common ground as a set of propositions accepted for purposes of conversation, and he's clear that these can come apart in non-standard contexts like pretense or negotiation. He doesn't treat common ground as a monolithic, undifferentiated phenomenon but rather as a theoretical construct that can be analyzed into components. Yalcin's work on epistemic modals similarly doesn't require that common ground be theoretically uniform across all discourse contexts—his framework is primarily about information-tracking in the Stalnakerian sense, not about collaborative planning. The thesis attacks a stronger uniformity claim than either theorist actually holds. Both allow that common ground plays different roles in different contexts; they don't claim it must be a single "natural kind" impervious to functional analysis.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This is a weak objection. While Stalnaker and Yalcin may not explicitly claim common ground is utterly monolithic, the thesis could be targeting an *implicit* commitment to theoretical unity that their frameworks presuppose operationally, even if not stated dogmatically.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates acknowledging *contextual variation* with recognizing *distinct mechanisms*. Yes, Stalnaker distinguishes aspects of common ground and notes non-standard contexts, but these are treated as variations within a unified framework—different applications of the same underlying phenomenon, not independent mechanisms that happen to coincide.

Consider the structure of Stalnaker's theory: the common ground is *the* set of propositions the participants are mutually disposed to take for granted. Whether this serves presupposition or planning, whether in pretense or assertion, it's the *same set* doing different work. The 2002 paper's distinctions concern what goes *into* the common ground (information vs. acceptance) and how it *functions*, but the common ground itself remains a single theoretical entity—one scoreboard, variously consulted.

The thesis claims something stronger: that presupposition-licensing and collaborative-planning coordination are *separate tracking systems* that merely overlap in paradigm cases. The evidence is their systematic divergence: in pretense, presupposition proceeds without shared acceptance (you presuppose the dragon exists while planning around its non-existence); in collaborative planning, you need actual shared mental states that presupposition doesn't require. These aren't contextual variations of one mechanism—they're different mechanisms with different operating conditions.

Neither Stalnaker nor Yalcin provides an account where these can genuinely come apart while both still counting as "common ground." Their frameworks assume functional unity: one set of mutually recognized commitments serving multiple purposes. The thesis denies this unity. The objection mistakes theoretical flexibility for theoretical pluralism.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection attacks a straw position (absolute monolithism) while missing the actual target (operational unity). Even if Stalnaker and Yalcin allow contextual nuance, they treat common ground as a single phenomenon with various applications, not as two independent mechanisms. The thesis's evidence—systematic divergence in operating conditions—directly challenges this unity assumption, which both theorists do maintain at the level of theoretical architecture.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis protects itself through strategic redefinition of what counts as "the same mechanism" versus "different mechanisms." When presupposition and collaborative planning align (the paradigm cases of ordinary conversation), this counts as "accidental convergence." When they diverge (pretense, bargaining), this confirms they're "independent mechanisms." But what would falsify the claim? If we found contexts where they *must* operate together—where presupposition requires shared mental states or vice versa—the thesis can respond: "that's just where they happen to converge." If we found them operating independently, that confirms the thesis. The weak point is the lack of criteria for what would count as genuine unity. The thesis treats convergence as always "accidental" and divergence as always "systematic," but these are interpretive labels, not empirical findings. Any unified mechanism can be *described* as two mechanisms that happen to align, and any complex phenomenon can be *described* as accidentally convergent subsystems. Without independent criteria for mechanism-identity beyond the convergence/divergence patterns themselves, every case either confirms the thesis or gets classified as accidental. The pretense case illustrates this: is it two mechanisms diverging, or one mechanism operating under non-standard input conditions? The thesis's framework pre-determines the answer.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — A genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis needs independent criteria for distinguishing "two mechanisms that converge" from "one mechanism with variable outputs" beyond the very patterns it's trying to explain.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection reverses the evidential order. The thesis doesn't *start* with a metaphysical claim about mechanism-identity and then fit the data to it—it *infers* distinct mechanisms from patterns that a unified account cannot explain without ad hoc supplementation.

Here's the crucial asymmetry the objection misses: a unified mechanism predicts *covariation*. If presupposition-licensing and collaborative-planning coordination are outputs of the same common ground system, then the conditions that enable one should systematically enable the other. But they don't.

The pretense case isn't just "non-standard input"—it's a *reversal* of the predicted relationship. In pretense, you can felicitously presuppose p (the dragon exists) precisely *because* it's not in the shared mental states relevant to planning (we plan around the dragon's non-existence). This isn't a parameter shift; it's the two dimensions moving in opposite directions. A unified mechanism with variable parameters should still show monotonic relationships—more mutual commitment enables more presupposition AND more collaborative planning. Instead we see: more public commitment to p enables presupposition of p while *less* shared acceptance of p is what makes the collaborative planning work.

The falsification criteria are clear: find cases where the two dimensions *must* covary—where you cannot have presupposition without shared mental states, or collaborative planning without public commitment, across all discourse contexts. The unified view predicts this; the thesis predicts systematic independence with contingent overlap.

The bargaining case provides the mirror image: you can have shared mental states (both parties believe the negotiation will fail) that cannot be presupposed without destroying the collaborative activity. Again, opposite directions—the very belief-sharing that would enable collaboration makes presupposition toxic.

The objection's "one mechanism under non-standard conditions" move has explanatory costs. Why do these specific "non-standard conditions" systematically reverse the relationship between the two dimensions? Why does pretense make presupposition *easier* while making shared acceptance *impossible*? A unified account owes us a story about why its parameter variations produce these specific inversions. The two-mechanism thesis explains it directly: they're independent systems with different operating logics that happen to align when public commitment tracks actual belief.

The criterion for mechanism-identity isn't just convergence patterns—it's whether a single set of operating principles can generate the full range of relationships between the dimensions without stipulating different principles for different contexts. The unified view keeps adding epicycles (pretense works differently, bargaining works differently, collaborative planning works differently). The thesis offers one principle: they're different systems.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds but reveals a genuine demand. The objection correctly identifies that the thesis needs to do more than point to divergence—it needs to show why that divergence is better explained by distinct mechanisms than by a unified mechanism with context-sensitive parameters.

However, the defence meets this demand. The key isn't just that the dimensions *can* diverge, but that they diverge in *opposite directions* in systematic ways that a unified account cannot predict without becoming a mere redescription of the data. When your unified mechanism needs different operating principles for pretense, different ones for bargaining, and different ones for collaborative planning, you no longer have a unified mechanism—you have a notational variant of the two-mechanism view.

The falsification criterion is genuine: show that the apparent divergences are actually monotonic transformations of a single underlying parameter, or show contexts where the two dimensions are necessarily coupled. The thesis survives because the evidence shows non-monotonic, inversive relationships that resist unification.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to offer a novel distinction, but this is essentially the position already developed by Herbert Clark and the collaborative action theorists. In Clark's framework from *Using Language* (1996) and related work, he explicitly distinguishes between common ground as shared information (what can be mutually presupposed in discourse) and common ground as joint commitment (what enables coordinated joint action). Clark argues these are distinct though related: you can have shared information without joint commitment (overhearers share information but aren't committed to joint action), and you can have joint commitment without complete information sharing (collaborative activities proceeding despite information asymmetries). His "grounding" process tracks mutual evidence of understanding, while his "joint action" framework tracks shared intentions and commitments—these are separate theoretical mechanisms in his architecture. The candidate thesis's examples of pretense and bargaining showing divergence between presupposition and collaborative planning are precisely the kinds of cases Clark uses to motivate keeping these dimensions theoretically distinct. Even the diagnosis that theorists have conflicting intuitions because they're tracking different phenomena echoes Clark's critique of purely information-based accounts. The candidate presents as a novel distinction what is actually a well-established position in the collaborative action literature.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious challenge. If Clark has already drawn essentially this distinction with similar motivations and evidence, the thesis's claim to novelty is severely undermined. The candidate would need to show either that their distinction differs significantly from Clark's or that they're developing his insight in a substantially new direction.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies the theoretical target and the nature of the distinction. Clark's framework, while sophisticated, still treats common ground as a *unified foundation* that supports both information-sharing and joint action—these are different *uses* of common ground, not different *mechanisms producing* what we call common ground.

Look at Clark's architecture carefully. "Grounding" is the process by which information enters common ground; "joint action" is what common ground enables. But the common ground itself—the mutually recognized shared basis—remains a single phenomenon in Clark's theory. He distinguishes what goes into it (evidence of understanding) from what comes out of it (coordinated action), but the middle layer—common ground itself—is unified. This is why Clark can say that joint action *requires* common ground: the collaborative activity presupposes a shared informational foundation.

The thesis makes a stronger claim: there is no unified middle layer. What we call "common ground" is actually two separate tracking systems:

1. A public commitment scoreboard that licenses presupposition regardless of actual shared mental states
2. A shared intentional state system that coordinates action regardless of public commitment

These don't just serve different purposes—they have *different constitutive conditions* and can operate independently.

Clark's cases of information without commitment (overhearers) and commitment without full information (collaborative asymmetries) still assume both dimensions are *present but unequal*. Overhearers have the information even if they lack commitment; collaborators have commitment even if they lack complete information. Both dimensions exist; they just come in different proportions.

The thesis's cases show something Clark's framework cannot accommodate: contexts where the two dimensions *oppose* each other. In pretense, increasing public commitment to p (presupposing the dragon exists) requires *decreasing* shared acceptance of p (planning around its non-existence). This isn't information without commitment or commitment without information—it's commitment to p paired with shared acceptance of ¬p. Clark's framework has no resources for this because it treats common ground as a unified base that both dimensions draw from.

Furthermore, Clark's critique targets *purely information-based accounts*, arguing we need to add joint commitment to the picture. But he's still working within the Stalnakerian assumption that there's a unified phenomenon called common ground that needs a richer analysis. The thesis rejects this entirely: there's no unified phenomenon to analyze, just two mechanisms that theorists have mistakenly conflated because they coincide in paradigm cases.

The diagnostic claim also differs. Clark says theorists neglect the action-coordination dimension; the thesis says theorists are tracking *different phenomena* when they theorize about "common ground"—Stalnaker is theorizing about the public commitment scoreboard, collaborative action theorists are theorizing about shared intentional states, and neither is wrong about their target, but both are wrong to think they're theorizing about the same thing.

VERDICT

The defence holds, but barely. The objection identifies a serious proximity problem—Clark's work is close enough that the thesis needs to articulate the difference clearly, and the defence does this by showing that Clark maintains precisely the unity assumption the thesis rejects.

However, the defence succeeds in showing a genuine theoretical gap. Clark distinguishes *aspects* or *dimensions* of common ground and argues for a richer account that includes both information and commitment. The thesis denies there's a unified phenomenon with aspects—it claims "common ground" is a false theoretical posit that conflates two independent mechanisms.

The critical test case is pretense with opposing commitments: public commitment to p, shared acceptance of ¬p. Clark's framework would need to say either (a) p is in common ground (but then why can we plan around ¬p?) or (b) p is not in common ground (but then why can we presuppose it?). The thesis says: p is on the public commitment scoreboard (hence presupposable) but ¬p is in the shared intentional states (hence plannable). These are different scoreboards, not different aspects of one scoreboard.

The thesis survives, but it now carries the burden of showing that this difference from Clark is theoretically significant rather than merely terminological. If the result is just "call them separate mechanisms instead of unified-but-distinguishable aspects," the distinction may be real but shallow.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The argument's logic—that systematic divergence in operating conditions proves distinct mechanisms rather than a single phenomenon with context-sensitive parameters—proves too much because it would force us to fragment virtually every cognitive and linguistic capacity into unmanageably many "independent mechanisms." Consider memory: recall for episodic narrative diverges systematically from recall for procedural action (you can narrate what you did without being able to do it again, and vice versa); conditions enabling semantic retrieval oppose those enabling recognition memory (semantic access improves with abstraction while recognition requires specificity). By the thesis's reasoning, "memory" is not a unified phenomenon but accidentally convergent mechanisms. Similarly for perception: conditions for object identification diverge from conditions for spatial navigation using those same objects; what enables conscious visual report often inhibits rapid visuomotor coordination. Or take belief itself: conditions for verbal report of belief systematically diverge from conditions for belief-guided action (you can sincerely assert p while acting on ¬p in implicit bias cases). Should we conclude "belief" is really two mechanisms? The weak point is the inference from "dimensions can diverge and even oppose in some contexts" to "therefore distinct mechanisms rather than one complex capacity." Every sufficiently complex cognitive phenomenon shows context-dependent dissociations between its aspects. The thesis's standard would eliminate most of our theoretical vocabulary, replacing unified phenomena with accidental convergences whenever we find functional dissociations. If this reasoning worked, it would prove that virtually no psychological or linguistic terms pick out unified phenomena—an unacceptable fragmentation of our theoretical ontology.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem requiring substantial response. The thesis needs principled criteria for when divergence indicates distinct mechanisms versus when it indicates a complex unified capacity with dissociable components, otherwise the argument generalizes to absurdity.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *any* functional dissociation for the specific pattern the thesis identifies. Not all divergences are created equal—the question is whether the dissociations reveal *independent operating principles* or *components of a unified system*.

The memory case actually illustrates why the thesis's reasoning doesn't overgeneralize. Episodic and procedural memory dissociate, yes—but they dissociate in ways that reveal them as *components of a memory system* with a common function (storing and retrieving information from experience) operating on different contents via different mechanisms. Crucially, they don't *oppose* each other in the way presupposition and collaborative planning do. You don't find that increasing episodic memory *requires* decreasing procedural memory, or that remembering p episodically requires forgetting p procedurally. They can both succeed, both fail, or succeed independently—but they don't systematically work in opposite directions.

The thesis's evidence isn't mere dissociation—it's *inversive relationships*. In pretense, the public commitment that licenses presupposing p is constituted by shared acceptance of ¬p. That's not like being able to narrate without doing; it's like narrating p requiring that you be unable to do p. The bargaining case shows the mirror: shared mental states that enable planning become toxic to presupposition. These aren't components that can operate independently; they're systems whose optimal operating conditions are each other's failure conditions in certain contexts.

Consider the objection's own examples more carefully:

Memory: Episodic and procedural memory share a functional architecture—both involve encoding, consolidation, and retrieval, just for different content types. The dissociations respect this shared architecture; they don't reveal that "memory" was always two unrelated capacities that coincidentally both stored information.

Perception: Object identification and visuomotor coordination are both *perceptual* in that they process sensory input to guide response, and their dissociations occur within a unified perceptual system with shared early processing. The thesis doesn't claim that any functional specialization proves distinct mechanisms.

Belief: The implicit bias case is importantly different from the common ground case. Implicit bias shows that explicit report and implicit guidance can come apart *for the same belief* under conditions of self-deception, social pressure, or automaticity. But we don't find that believing p explicitly *requires* believing ¬p implicitly as a constitutive matter. The thesis's cases show that presupposing p can *require* (not just accidentally accompany) shared acceptance of ¬p.

The principled criterion the objection demands is this: Distinct mechanisms are indicated when (a) the phenomena have different constitutive conditions that can systematically oppose each other, and (b) no unified operating principle generates this opposition without collapsing into a mere redescription of the two mechanisms.

Common ground meets this test. Presupposition is licensed by public commitment *regardless of private belief*; collaborative planning requires shared intentional states *regardless of public commitment*. In pretense, these don't just dissociate—they require opposite contents (commit to p, accept ¬p). No unified "common ground" mechanism generates this without essentially saying "there are two different scoreboards" in different words.

Memory, perception, and belief don't meet this test. Their dissociations reveal specialized subsystems within a unified functional architecture, not independent mechanisms accidentally converging. You can give a unified account of memory that explains why episodic and procedural memory dissociate (different content types processed by the same encoding/retrieval principles). Try giving a unified account of common ground that explains why presupposition and planning can require opposite commitments—you'll find yourself positing two separate tracking systems, which is exactly what the thesis claims.

The fragmentation worry fails because the thesis doesn't threaten every complex capacity—only those where we've mistakenly unified what are actually independent mechanisms that happen to correlate in paradigm cases. The test is whether a single set of operating principles can generate the full range of relationships, including inversions, without degenerating into "different principles for different contexts" (which is just the two-mechanism view in disguise).

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection correctly identifies that the thesis needs principled criteria for distinguishing "complex unified phenomenon" from "accidentally convergent mechanisms," but incorrectly assumes the thesis lacks such criteria.

The crucial distinction is between *dissociable components* (which every complex capacity has) and *inversive independence* (where optimal conditions for one systematically oppose optimal conditions for the other). Memory, perception, and belief show the former; common ground shows the latter.

The pretense case remains decisive: public commitment to p enables presupposing p, while shared acceptance of ¬p enables planning. These aren't components that can be unified under shared operating principles—they're systems with opposed operating logics that happen to align when public commitment tracks actual acceptance.

The objection's examples actually strengthen the thesis by contrast. We *can* give unified accounts of memory (information storage/retrieval with specialized subsystems), perception (sensory processing with multiple output streams), and belief (propositional attitude with multiple manifestations). We *cannot* give a non-circular unified account of common ground that explains why presupposition and planning can require opposite commitments without essentially conceding they're separate mechanisms.

The thesis survives because it doesn't claim that any functional dissociation proves distinct mechanisms—it claims that systematic inversive relationships that resist unification under shared operating principles prove distinct mechanisms. That's a principled criterion that doesn't overgeneralize.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims that presupposition-tracking and collaborative-planning coordination are "independently operating mechanisms" that only "accidentally converge." But consider teaching scenarios with acknowledged ignorance:

A mathematics professor tells students: "Let's assume the Riemann Hypothesis is true and see what follows." Here, there is:
- Public commitment: The RH is now presupposable in subsequent discourse ("Given our assumption, we can derive...")
- Shared mental state for planning: Everyone accepts RH *for purposes of this collaborative inquiry*
- Mutual knowledge of non-belief: Everyone knows no one actually believes RH is proven

This case breaks the thesis's framework. It's not pretense (no one is pretending RH is true—they're genuinely reasoning from it). It's not bargaining (no negotiation). It's collaborative planning that *requires* presupposition. The professor cannot say "Let's plan our inquiry around RH" without making RH presupposable. The collaborative activity (joint mathematical exploration) and the presupposition (RH as premise) are *constitutively linked*—you cannot have the planning without the presupposition.

Yet by the thesis's logic, these should be independent mechanisms that merely "happen to converge." But they don't accidentally converge here—the convergence is *necessary*. The shared intentional state (let's explore RH's consequences together) is identical to the public commitment (RH is our working assumption). There's no separation, no independence, no accidental alignment.

The weak point: The thesis cannot accommodate cases where collaborative planning constitutively requires establishing presuppositions, because this shows the mechanisms aren't independent.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This does serious damage. The teaching/inquiry case shows that collaborative planning and presupposition can be *constitutively interdependent*, not merely accidentally convergent. If the mechanisms were truly independent, we should be able to have the collaborative planning without the presupposition, but we cannot. The thesis needs a substantial answer about why this doesn't refute the independence claim.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *coordination on a shared assumption* for *constitutive interdependence of mechanisms*. The teaching case actually supports the thesis by showing the two mechanisms operating independently while being pragmatically coordinated—precisely what "independently operating" means.

Break down what's happening in the Riemann Hypothesis scenario:

Public commitment scoreboard: RH enters as a working assumption that licenses presupposition. The professor's utterance "Let's assume RH" performs a speech act that updates what can be taken for granted in subsequent discourse.

Shared intentional state: The participants form a joint intention to explore RH's consequences together, which requires accepting RH *as a premise for this activity*.

The objection claims these are "identical" or "constitutively linked," but they're not—they're *coordinated*. Here's the crucial test: What are the success conditions for each mechanism?

For the presupposition mechanism: RH is successfully presupposable if it's been publicly entered into the conversational scoreboard through the appropriate speech act (the professor's stipulation). This succeeds *regardless of anyone's mental states about RH*. If a student privately believes RH is false, or has no belief about it, or even if everyone in the room believes it's false, the presupposition still works. The public commitment scoreboard has been updated; that's sufficient.

For the collaborative planning mechanism: The joint exploration succeeds if participants share the intention to reason from RH and coordinate their actions accordingly. This requires shared mental states—specifically, mutual acceptance of RH *as a premise for this activity*. But notice: this acceptance is *indexed to the activity*, not to the world. They accept "RH for purposes of this inquiry," not "RH is true."

Now here's why they're independent mechanisms despite being coordinated: Each could fail while the other succeeds.

Imagine a student who doesn't hear the professor's stipulation but sees everyone reasoning from RH. The student can form the shared intention to participate in the collaborative inquiry (shared mental state mechanism succeeds) without knowing that RH is presupposable (public commitment mechanism hasn't reached them). They might ask "Are we assuming RH?" precisely because they have the collaborative intention but lack the presuppositional license.

Conversely, imagine the professor announces "Let's assume RH" but no one forms the intention to actually engage in the collaborative inquiry—they're bored, distracted, or rebellious. The presupposition has been established (you could say "Given our assumption..." and it would be felicitous) but the collaborative planning fails (no one is actually coordinating to explore RH's consequences).

The objection's claim that "you cannot have the planning without the presupposition" is false. You can have the planning without the presupposition—students could spontaneously coordinate to explore RH's consequences without anyone having explicitly made it presupposable (they just start doing it). And you can have the presupposition without the planning—the professor establishes RH as presupposable but the collaborative activity never gets off the ground.

What the objection observes is that *in this context*, the professor uses one mechanism to facilitate the other. The speech act "Let's assume RH" does double duty: it updates the public commitment scoreboard (making RH presupposable) AND it proposes a collaborative activity (exploring RH's consequences). But doing double duty isn't being the same mechanism. A hammer can be used to drive nails and to break rocks, but hammering and breaking are different activities even when the same tool performs both.

The thesis predicts exactly this: in paradigm cases of cooperative inquiry, the two mechanisms are *pragmatically coordinated*—we use public commitments to facilitate shared intentional states and vice versa. This coordination is why theorists mistakenly thought there was a unified phenomenon. But coordination isn't identity.

The teaching case actually reveals the mechanisms' independence more clearly than the objection recognizes. Notice that the acceptance is *qualified*: "RH for purposes of this inquiry." Why the qualification? Because the participants are tracking two different things:

1. Public commitment: RH is our working assumption (presupposition mechanism)
2. Shared belief: RH is unproven (shared mental state about the world)

If these were the same mechanism, there would be no need for the qualification—RH would just be "in common ground" or not. The qualification exists precisely because participants are maintaining two separate scoreboards: what we're publicly committed to for this conversation (RH) and what we actually believe (RH is unproven). The collaborative planning operates on the first; our real-world coordination operates on the second.

The objection claims the convergence is "necessary," but this conflates *pragmatic necessity* (in this context, establishing presupposition facilitates planning) with *constitutive necessity* (planning requires presupposition as a matter of what planning is). The thesis denies only the latter. Of course in many contexts we'll use one mechanism to enable the other—that's rational coordination. But the mechanisms remain distinct, as shown by contexts where they come apart (pretense, bargaining) or where they track opposite contents (the very teaching case, where public commitment to RH coexists with shared belief that RH is unproven).

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection mistakes pragmatic coordination for constitutive interdependence. The teaching case shows the two mechanisms being *used together* for practical purposes, not *being the same mechanism*.

The decisive point is that each mechanism has independent success conditions. Presupposition succeeds when the public commitment scoreboard is appropriately updated; collaborative planning succeeds when participants share relevant intentional states. In the teaching case, these are coordinated but not identical—as shown by the fact that participants maintain distinct attitudes toward RH (publicly committed to it for inquiry purposes, privately uncommitted to its truth).

The objection actually strengthens the thesis by highlighting how *coordination* between independent mechanisms creates the illusion of unity. In paradigm cases like teaching, we smoothly use public commitments to establish shared intentional states, which is why theorists thought "common ground" was a unified phenomenon. But the mechanisms remain separable, as shown by: (1) cases where they come apart (pretense, bargaining), (2) cases where they track opposite contents (teaching with acknowledged ignorance), and (3) the fact that each has independent success conditions even when coordinated.

The thesis survives because it never claimed the mechanisms *cannot* be coordinated—it claimed they're *independent* mechanisms that happen to be coordinated in paradigm cases. The teaching example confirms this: it's a paradigm case of coordination, which is exactly why it looks like unity until you examine the distinct operating conditions of each mechanism.

Repair candidates

Promise 4+, failed on ONE locatable flaw — usually scope or framing, with the narrower version already written out. Often the richest vein.

R1. Treating a proposition as common ground commits you to treating testimony about that proposition as redundant rather than informative, which shows that common ground cannot be defined by any mental state (belief, acceptance, knowledge) since testimony can be informative even when conveying mutually known, mutually accepted content.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
commitment — The shared assumption that common ground can be adequately understood through mental states like belief, acceptance, or knowledge
Sketch

Both mental-state accounts of common ground share a prediction: if p is common ground, then testimony that p should be maximally redundant—it cannot shift anyone's mental state since everyone already has the relevant state toward p. But this is false. In institutional settings, a judge may say 'The defendant is presumed innocent' when this is already common ground in every sense—everyone knows it, accepts it, and knows that everyone knows everyone accepts it. Yet the utterance is not redundant; it's performatively constitutive of the legal proceeding. The key premise is that this non-redundancy reveals that common ground does work beyond tracking mental states: it structures what testimonial moves are appropriate and consequential. If common ground were just a mental-state configuration, testimony about common-ground contents would be like telling someone what they already believe on the basis of what they believe—pragmatically bizarre. But such testimony is often precisely what maintains institutional and conversational order.

Appraiser (blind)
Challenges mental-state accounts through institutional testimony cases where redundancy predictions fail, offering a novel argument about common ground's performative-constitutive role.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed Stalnaker's qualifications remain mental-state analyses or concede the thesis by invoking non-mental elements like 'official entry'
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defence established the redundancy prediction derives from mental-state theorists' own characterization of presupposition, not from stipulation
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. Defence argued this is refutation by counterexample, not equivocation—mental-state theorists claim to explain the phenomenon that requires institutional elements
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed the thesis offers concrete falsification conditions: demonstrate mental states suffice in institutional contexts or that the judge's utterance is actually redundant
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence absorbed by acknowledging commitment-theoretic literature exists but claiming stronger conclusion or polemical value—the core insight is recognized in existing work
🔧 Survives as

Mental-state accounts of common ground (like Stalnaker's) fail because institutional testimony can be non-redundant even when conveying mutually known content, as the judge case demonstrates—this supports commitment-theoretic approaches and shows why mental-state definitions remain inadequate despite their continued influence

Flaw

The thesis presents as novel discovery what commitment theorists (Gunlogson, Farkas & Bruce) already established: that public commitment/conversational record cannot reduce to mental states

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "the shared assumption that common ground can be adequately understood through mental states like belief, acceptance, or knowledge," but this formulation significantly overstates the position held by actual theorists in this domain. Robert Stalnaker, the primary architect of mental-state accounts of common ground, explicitly defines common ground in terms of mutual belief or acceptance *for the purposes of conversation* — it's what participants are taking for granted in their exchange, not a pure psychological state divorced from pragmatic context. Crucially, Stalnaker's framework already accommodates the phenomenon described: when the judge says "The defendant is presumed innocent," this utterance can update the *conversational score* (what is officially on record as presupposed) even when the propositional content is already mutually believed. The mental-state theorist distinguishes between what is mutually believed in the room and what has been officially entered into the common ground of this particular exchange. The thesis attacks a crude psychologism — "common ground is just mutual belief, full stop" — that sophisticated mental-state theorists like Stalnaker do not hold. They already recognize that conversational common ground has normative and performative dimensions beyond mere shared psychology.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — The thesis addresses a real theoretical question about how mental states relate to conversational practice, but it likely mischaracterizes the target position by treating it as simpler and more psychologistic than defenders actually state it.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objector conflates two distinct theoretical moves that mental-state theorists make, and the thesis targets precisely the gap between them.

First, consider what Stalnaker actually says. Yes, he adds "for the purposes of conversation" — but this is a *restriction on scope*, not a departure from mental-state analysis. The common ground is still *constituted by* mutual belief or acceptance; the qualification merely specifies *which* beliefs count (those operative in this conversation). The architecture remains: mental states → common ground. What participants are "taking for granted" just is a mental state configuration with a particular functional role.

Second, the objector's escape route — distinguishing "what is mutually believed in the room" from "what has been officially entered into the common ground" — actually proves the thesis. If these can come apart, then common ground is NOT defined by the mental states after all. The judge case shows exactly this: the propositional content has the maximal mental-state configuration (mutual belief, mutual knowledge of mutual belief, etc.), yet it still needs to be "officially entered." But "officially entered" is a *performative, institutional* notion, not a mental-state one. The objector has conceded that something beyond mental states — official entry, conversational record — does the real work.

Third, the "conversational score" apparatus (Lewis/Stalnaker) was designed to track mental-state evolution, not to replace mental states with institutional facts. When defenders retreat to "what's on record" or "what's officially presupposed," they've abandoned the mental-state analysis for something else — precisely what the thesis claims they must do.

The thesis doesn't attack "crude psychologism." It attacks the claim that mental states *define* common ground, however sophisticated the packaging. The judge case shows that all the relevant mental states can be in place while the performative work remains undone.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection mislocates the target. Sophisticated mental-state theorists do add qualifications like "for purposes of conversation," but these qualifications either (a) remain within mental-state analysis — in which case the judge case still refutes them, since all conversationally-relevant mental states are present before the utterance, or (b) smuggle in non-mental-state elements like "official record" or "institutional entry" — in which case they've conceded the thesis.

The objector's own move — distinguishing mutual belief from "official entry into common ground" — is a concession that mental states don't suffice. If they did suffice, there would be nothing left for "official entry" to do.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to reveal something substantive about common ground by observing that testimony can be non-redundant even when conveying mutually known content. But this observation is actually a verbal stipulation about what "common ground" should mean, dressed up as a discovery about what it cannot be. The weak point is the premise that "non-redundancy reveals that common ground does work beyond tracking mental states." This assumes a particular definition of redundancy and then uses it to legislate what counts as common ground, rather than discovering a fact about an independently fixed phenomenon.

Consider: one could simply *define* "common ground" as "whatever makes testimony redundant in all contexts." Then the judge case would show that mutual knowledge isn't common ground—true by definition. Alternatively, define "common ground" as "mutual belief/knowledge operative in conversation." Then the judge case shows that performative utterances do additional work beyond reporting common ground—also true by definition. The thesis presents this as a discovery about the nature of common ground, but it's actually just choosing the second definition over the first. The supposedly problematic "prediction" that common-ground testimony should be redundant is not a prediction from mental-state theories—it's a stipulation about what would count as common ground if redundancy were the criterion. Mental-state theorists never claimed their account must make all testimony about common-ground contents redundant in every pragmatic dimension; they claimed to characterize what participants mutually presuppose. The thesis trades on equivocation about "redundant" (informationally vs. performatively) to make a definitional choice look like an empirical refutation.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — There's something here: the thesis does rely on intuitions about what common ground "must" explain to argue against mental-state definitions. But it's not purely stipulative—there's genuine disagreement about whether performative non-redundancy matters for defining common ground, making this a substantive theoretical dispute rather than mere wordplay.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objector claims the thesis merely stipulates what "common ground" means rather than discovering what it is. But this gets the dialectical structure backwards. The thesis isn't *stipulating* that common ground must make testimony redundant — it's *deriving* this consequence from what mental-state theorists themselves say common ground does.

Here's why the derivation isn't stipulative:

First, mental-state theorists explicitly characterize common ground as what conversational participants *take for granted* or *presuppose*. Stalnaker: "to presuppose something is to take it for granted, or at least to act as if one takes it for granted." But taking something for granted has built-in pragmatic consequences: if you genuinely take p for granted, then being told p should strike you as otiose. The redundancy prediction flows from *their* characterization, not from a definition imposed by the thesis.

Second, the objector's own formulation reveals this. They say mental-state theorists "claimed to characterize what participants mutually presuppose." But presupposition has pragmatic teeth: presupposed content is precisely what *doesn't need to be asserted* because it's already in place. If testimony asserting p is non-redundant, this is evidence that p wasn't genuinely presupposed — wasn't actually in the common ground. The thesis exploits this connection that mental-state theorists themselves rely on.

Third, the objector claims equivocation between "informationally redundant" and "performatively redundant." But this distinction doesn't save the mental-state view — it dooms it. If the judge's utterance is informationally redundant (everyone already believes it) but performatively non-redundant (it does institutional work), then the *performative* dimension is what makes it common ground for the proceeding. The mental states were already there; the performative act *establishes* common ground. This shows common ground is constituted by the performative dimension, not the mental states.

Fourth, this isn't "choosing a definition" — it's following explanatory demands. Common ground is invoked to explain conversational phenomena: what can be presupposed, what assertions are appropriate, what testimony is needed. The judge case shows that mental-state configurations don't determine these phenomena. That's an explanatory failure, not a definitional choice.

The objector says "mental-state theorists never claimed their account must make all testimony about common-ground contents redundant in every pragmatic dimension." But if common ground is what makes testimony redundant in *no* pragmatic dimension that matters for conversation, then it's not doing the explanatory work it was posited to do.

VERDICT

The defence holds, but barely, and reveals a deeper problem.

The objection correctly identifies that there's a theoretical choice point about what "common ground" should explain. But it's wrong to call this merely stipulative. The thesis leverages a genuine constraint: common ground theorists across traditions agree that common ground should explain *what moves are appropriate in conversation*. Mental-state accounts claim mental-state configurations do this explaining. The judge case shows they don't — the mental states are all in place, yet a testimonial move is still required and consequential.

However, the objection exposes a weakness: the thesis could be clearer that it's arguing from *explanatory failure* rather than from a supposed *prediction* that mental-state theories make. Mental-state theorists might not explicitly predict redundancy — but if their posited mental states don't explain the non-redundancy we observe, their account fails to explain what it was meant to explain.

The defence succeeds because the thesis isn't stipulating what common ground must be; it's showing that mental-state accounts fail to explain phenomena (like performative testimony) that any adequate account of common ground must explain. That's a substantive theoretical argument, not definitional legislation.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis equivocates on "common ground" between two readings, and the argument needs both to work.

On Reading 1, "common ground" means the psychological state of mutual belief/acceptance that conversational participants have. On Reading 2, it means the normative-institutional framework that structures what moves are appropriate and consequential in a discourse.

The argument's plausibility depends on Reading 1: it's initially compelling to think that if everyone mutually believes p, then testifying that p should be redundant. This makes the judge case seem puzzling—everyone already believes the defendant is presumed innocent, yet the utterance isn't redundant.

But the argument's interest depends on Reading 2: the conclusion is only significant if we're showing that common ground is constituted by performative-institutional acts rather than mental states. The judge's utterance "establishes" or "constitutes" common ground in this institutional sense.

The equivocation occurs at the inference: "testimony can be informative even when conveying mutually known content, therefore common ground cannot be defined by mental states." This only works if "common ground" means the same thing in both parts. But it doesn't. What the case actually shows is that institutional common ground (Reading 2) can be established by performative utterance even when psychological common ground (Reading 1) is already present. Mental-state theorists can accept this: there are two phenomena, and they're theorizing about the psychological one. The thesis trades on conflating them to make it seem like a single phenomenon that mental states fail to capture.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem that needs addressing. The thesis must show these are the same phenomenon, not just assert that "common ground" picks out a single thing that mental-state accounts fail to capture.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis equivocates between psychological and institutional readings of "common ground," treating them as separate phenomena that the thesis illicitly conflates. But this misunderstands the dialectical situation: the thesis argues that what mental-state theorists *thought* was one phenomenon (capturable by mental states) is actually shown by the judge case to require institutional-performative elements. That's not equivocation — that's refutation by counterexample.

Here's why the "two phenomena" response fails:

First, mental-state theorists don't present themselves as theorizing about only "psychological common ground" while leaving "institutional common ground" to someone else. Stalnaker, Lewis, and others offer their accounts as theories of *the* common ground that structures conversation and discourse generally — including institutional discourse. They're not restricting their domain to informal chat while exempting courtrooms. When Stalnaker says common ground is what participants presuppose "for the purposes of conversation," he means *all* conversation, including institutional settings. The thesis shows their account fails for a central class of cases.

Second, the objector's move — "there are two phenomena, and mental-state theorists are theorizing about the psychological one" — is precisely the concession the thesis seeks. If you grant that there's an *institutional* common ground that operates independently of mental states, and that this institutional common ground is what does the work in structuring discourse (determining what moves are appropriate, what's on record, what's presupposed for legal purposes), then you've conceded that mental states don't define *the* common ground that matters for conversational and institutional practice. You've admitted mental-state accounts don't capture the phenomenon they set out to capture.

Third, the "two phenomena" response creates an explanatory puzzle it cannot solve: why do we use the *same term* — "common ground" — for both? The natural answer is that we're tracking a single phenomenon with both psychological and institutional dimensions, and the thesis argues the institutional dimension is explanatorily prior. When the judge speaks, she doesn't create a *different kind* of common ground alongside the psychological one; she *establishes* common ground for the proceeding by performative means, where that common ground was not established by the mental states alone. That's one phenomenon with a surprising constitution, not two phenomena with coincidentally similar names.

Fourth, consider the explanatory direction. Mental-state theorists claim: mutual belief/acceptance *constitutes* common ground, which *in turn* makes certain conversational moves appropriate. The judge case breaks this chain. The mutual belief is present, but the conversational/institutional move is still needed. This shows the mutual belief doesn't constitute common ground after all — the performative act does. The objector wants to say there are two separate chains (mental states → psychological CG → informal conversational appropriateness; performative acts → institutional CG → formal conversational appropriateness). But this is *ad hoc*. The simpler explanation: there's one phenomenon (common ground), and mental states don't constitute it.

Fifth, the objection's own language reveals the problem. It says "institutional common ground can be established by performative utterance even when psychological common ground is already present." But if "psychological common ground" were really common ground, it would *already establish* what the performative utterance establishes. The fact that the utterance is still needed shows that what the objector calls "psychological common ground" isn't actually common ground at all — it's just mutual belief, which is necessary but not sufficient.

The thesis doesn't equivocate. It argues that what looks like one phenomenon (common ground) cannot be what mental-state theorists say it is (a configuration of beliefs/acceptances), because cases like the judge show that phenomenon requires performative-institutional constitution. The objector's response — "there are two phenomena" — is a retreat, not a refutation.

VERDICT

The defence holds.

The equivocation charge fails because the thesis isn't covertly switching between two meanings of "common ground." It's arguing that mental-state theorists misidentified what constitutes the single phenomenon they were trying to explain. The judge case is a counterexample: here's a situation where all the mental-state conditions are met, yet common ground (in the sense that structures what moves are appropriate and consequential) still needs to be established performatively.

The objector's escape — "there are two different phenomena, psychological and institutional" — actually concedes the thesis. If institutional common ground operates independently of mental states and does the real work in structuring discourse, then mental-state accounts have failed to capture common ground as it functions in conversational practice. You can't save a theory by restricting its domain to cases where it works while admitting it fails for central instances like institutional discourse.

The thesis stands: common ground cannot be defined by mental states because the judge case shows mental states are insufficient to constitute common ground even when they're all in place. That's a substantive discovery about what common ground is, not an equivocation about what the term means.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis is unfalsifiable because it protects itself through strategic redefinition of what counts as "genuine common ground" versus "mere mental states." Whenever mental-state theorists point to a case where mutual belief does make testimony redundant, the thesis can respond: "That's just psychological mutual belief, not real common ground." Whenever they point to cases where testimony isn't redundant despite mutual belief, the thesis says: "See, mental states don't constitute common ground!" The weak point is the premise that "non-redundancy reveals that common ground does work beyond tracking mental states."

Watch how immunity works: If testimony about mutually-believed p IS redundant in some context, the thesis can say "that context doesn't involve institutional/performative dimensions, so it doesn't test whether mental states suffice for common ground generally." If testimony about mutually-believed p is NOT redundant, the thesis says "this proves mental states don't constitute common ground." The judge case is presented as decisive, but any apparent counterexample—a case where mutual belief DOES make testimony redundant and DOES exhaust what common ground requires—gets reclassified as "not involving the institutional dimension" or "not the kind of common ground that matters for structuring discourse."

The defender's own moves reveal this: mental-state theorists who restrict their domain are accused of "concession," but mental-state theorists who claim broader domain are accused of "explanatory failure." The thesis wins either way by controlling what counts as the phenomenon to be explained.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — There's something here about how "institutional dimension" and "structuring discourse" remain underspecified in ways that could allow selective case-counting, but the thesis does offer a concrete case (the judge) with specified features (mutual knowledge + non-redundant testimony) that genuinely challenges mental-state accounts. The case isn't obviously redefinable away.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The unfalsifiability charge fails because it misrepresents the thesis's dialectical structure. The thesis doesn't protect itself by redefining what counts as "genuine common ground" — it offers a specific criterion and a concrete counterexample.

First, the thesis provides a clear test: if mental states constitute common ground, then when all the relevant mental states are in place (mutual belief, mutual knowledge of mutual belief, etc.), common ground should be established. The judge case meets this condition — all mental states are present — yet shows that common ground for the proceeding still requires performative establishment. That's a straightforward counterexample structure, not an unfalsifiable immunization strategy.

Second, the objection mischaracterizes the dialectical options. The thesis doesn't say "any time testimony is redundant, that's not real common ground" or "any time testimony isn't redundant, mental states fail." The argument is more specific: in cases where (a) all the mental-state conditions that theorists specify are satisfied, yet (b) testimony is still required to establish common ground, this shows mental states are insufficient. The judge case satisfies both conditions. This is falsifiable: show a case where mental states suffice without performative establishment in institutional contexts, and the thesis fails.

Third, the objection claims the thesis can dismiss counterexamples as "not involving the institutional dimension." But this gets the burden of proof backwards. Mental-state theorists claim their account works *generally* — for conversation as such, including institutional settings. The thesis provides a counterexample from that domain. The burden is on mental-state theorists to either (a) show the judge case doesn't actually involve mutual knowledge, or (b) explain why institutional discourse should be exempted from their theory. Neither move is available: (a) is empirically false, and (b) concedes that mental-state accounts don't capture common ground in central cases.

Fourth, consider what would falsify the thesis. Show that the judge's utterance *is* redundant after all — that it does no work beyond reporting what everyone already believes. Or show that in institutional contexts, mental states alone *do* determine what moves are appropriate without performative establishment. Or provide an alternative explanation of why the utterance is non-redundant that doesn't appeal to performative-institutional constitution. These are concrete empirical and theoretical challenges. The thesis is falsifiable.

Fifth, the objection says mental-state theorists are accused of "concession" if they restrict domain and "explanatory failure" if they claim broader domain. But this isn't immunization — it's a genuine dilemma for the position. If mental-state accounts restrict to non-institutional contexts, they've abandoned the claim to explain common ground generally (concession). If they claim to cover institutional contexts, the judge case shows they fail (explanatory failure). That's not unfalsifiability; that's a theory facing a problem it cannot solve either way.

Sixth, the objection claims "institutional dimension" remains underspecified in ways that allow selective case-counting. But the thesis specifies it clearly enough: the institutional dimension is what makes the judge's utterance *constitutive* of the legal proceeding rather than merely *reportive* of existing mental states. The utterance doesn't just describe what everyone believes; it *establishes* what's on record for legal purposes. That's a clear, observable distinction.

The thesis isn't unfalsifiable. It makes a specific claim: mental states are insufficient to constitute common ground because performative-institutional acts do work that mental states cannot do, as shown by the judge case. This is falsifiable by showing either that the judge case doesn't have the features claimed, or that mental states can do the work after all, or that the work doesn't need doing.

VERDICT

The defence holds completely.

The unfalsifiability charge collapses under examination. The thesis offers a concrete case with specifiable features (mutual knowledge present + performative establishment required) that challenges mental-state accounts. That's precisely the structure of a falsifiable empirical-cum-theoretical claim.

The objection tries to construct a dilemma: either the thesis dismisses cases where mental states work (by calling them "not institutional"), or it dismisses cases where mental states don't work (by calling this "proof they fail"). But this is a false dilemma. The thesis's actual structure is: mental-state theorists claim mental states constitute common ground generally; here's a central case (institutional discourse) where they don't; therefore the general claim fails. That's straightforward modus tollens, not immunization.

The objector's complaint that mental-state theorists face a dilemma (concession if they restrict, failure if they don't) is not evidence of unfalsifiability — it's evidence that the thesis has identified a genuine problem for the position. A theory that must either abandon its explanatory ambitions or face counterexamples is not being unfairly treated; it's being refuted.

The thesis stands. It's falsifiable, and the judge case is a legitimate test case that mental-state accounts fail.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to reveal that "common ground cannot be defined by any mental state" because testimony can be non-redundant even when conveying mutually known content. However, this position is already well-established in the pragmatics literature, particularly in work distinguishing common ground from public commitment or conversational record. The weak point is that the thesis presents as a novel discovery what is actually a known distinction in the field.

Specifically, Gunlogson (2001) and later work by Farkas & Bruce (2010) on commitment spaces argues that what structures discourse is not mutual belief but public commitment—what has been placed "on the record" through speech acts. Similarly, Thomason's work on accommodation (1990) and Clark & Marshall's (1981) earlier discussions distinguish between what is mutually believed and what has been explicitly established in discourse. The judge case is a standard example of this phenomenon: the utterance performs the institutional act of placing content on the record, which is precisely what these theorists argue is distinct from and not reducible to mental states. Even Stalnaker himself, in later work, acknowledges the need to distinguish the common ground (as a body of presuppositions) from what is merely mutually believed, introducing apparatus like "assertion" as updating the conversational record in ways that go beyond mental-state tracking. The thesis's core insight—that performative-institutional acts constitute common ground rather than mental states—is the established position of commitment-theoretic approaches to discourse, not a refutation of them.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. If the thesis's central claim is already the accepted view among theorists who distinguish commitment/record from mental states, then it's not revealing a problem for "mental-state accounts" but rather restating what non-mental-state accounts already say. The thesis may be attacking a position that has already been abandoned or significantly revised in the literature.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis merely restates what commitment-theoretic approaches already establish. But this misunderstands the thesis's target and contribution. The thesis isn't claiming to *introduce* the distinction between mental states and public commitment — it's arguing that this distinction *refutes* the possibility of defining common ground by mental states, which many theorists still attempt.

First, the objection overstates the consensus. Mental-state accounts remain influential and actively defended. Stalnaker's framework is still widely used as the baseline theory of common ground in philosophy of language and formal semantics. Many theorists continue to work within mental-state frameworks, treating public commitment apparatus as *tracking* or *implementing* underlying mental-state configurations rather than replacing them. The thesis targets this ongoing theoretical stance, not a position everyone has abandoned.

Second, the objection conflates *recognizing a phenomenon* with *drawing the right conclusion from it*. Yes, Gunlogson, Farkas & Bruce, and others recognize that public commitment differs from mutual belief. But many theorists treat this as showing there are *two things* — mental-state common ground and public commitment — rather than concluding that mental states *cannot constitute* common ground. The thesis's contribution is the *inference*: the judge case doesn't just show commitment differs from belief; it shows mental states are *insufficient* to define what common ground is, because the performative work is constitutive, not supplementary.

Third, even Stalnaker's acknowledgment that the objection cites actually supports the thesis rather than refuting it. If Stalnaker "in later work" needs to introduce apparatus beyond mental states (like assertion as updating the conversational record), this is evidence that his original mental-state account was inadequate — precisely what the thesis argues. The thesis isn't claiming no one has ever noticed this; it's claiming the inadequacy is deeper than often recognized. Patching mental-state accounts with "conversational record" apparatus doesn't save them if the record-updating is doing the real constitutive work.

Fourth, the objection says commitment-theoretic approaches make the thesis's "core insight" their "established position." But this is too quick. Commitment theorists often present their view as *compatible with* mental-state accounts, treating commitment as a distinct layer that coordinates with underlying beliefs. The thesis makes a stronger claim: mental states *cannot* define common ground because institutional-performative constitution is not just different from mental-state tracking but *incompatible* with mental states being definitional. That's a more radical claim than most commitment theorists make.

Fifth, consider the dialectical situation. If the objection is right that commitment-theoretic approaches already establish the thesis's conclusion, then the thesis successfully *sides with* the right position against mental-state accounts that remain influential. That's not a weakness — it's correctly identifying which side of an ongoing debate has the better arguments. The thesis's contribution would be providing a particularly clear case (the judge) that shows why commitment theorists are right and mental-state theorists are wrong.

Sixth, the thesis's formulation — "common ground cannot be defined by any mental state" — is stronger than what most commitment theorists claim. Many say commitment *differs from* mental states, or that we need *both* mental states and public commitment. The thesis says mental states are *definitionally inadequate* — that's a claim about the nature of common ground, not just about conversational architecture. Even if commitment theorists have the resources to make this claim, many don't explicitly draw this conclusion.

Seventh, the objection assumes that if others have recognized the phenomenon, the thesis adds nothing. But philosophical progress often consists in seeing the full implications of recognized phenomena. If theorists acknowledge the commitment/belief distinction but continue trying to define common ground in mental-state terms (perhaps treating commitment as derivative), the thesis's contribution is showing this cannot work — the judge case proves mental states are not just incomplete but fundamentally the wrong kind of thing.

VERDICT

The defence partially succeeds, but the objection identifies a real weakness.

The objection is correct that the thesis's core insight — that public commitment or conversational record cannot be reduced to mental states — is recognized in the literature. Commitment-theoretic approaches do make this distinction, and sophisticated theorists are aware of cases like the judge example.

However, the defence successfully shows that the thesis isn't merely restating known positions. There are three ways the thesis could still contribute:

1. Polemical value: If mental-state accounts remain influential (and they do — Stalnaker's framework is still widely used), showing clearly why they fail has value even if some theorists already reject them.

2. Stronger conclusion: The thesis claims mental states *cannot define* common ground, which is more radical than saying commitment and belief are distinct phenomena. Many theorists try to have both, treating them as compatible. The thesis argues they're incompatible as *definitions* of common ground.

3. Clearer argument: Even if the conclusion is available in the literature, the judge case may provide an unusually clear demonstration of why mental-state accounts fail.

But the objection succeeds in showing a significant limitation: the thesis presents itself as revealing a problem for "the shared assumption that common ground can be adequately understood through mental states," when in fact this assumption has been challenged and arguably defeated by commitment theorists. The thesis would be stronger if it explicitly positioned itself within this existing debate rather than presenting the insight as novel.

The thesis survives, but as a contribution to an ongoing debate rather than as a revolutionary discovery. It provides a clear case for why commitment theorists are right against mental-state theorists, but it doesn't establish new theoretical territory. That's still philosophically valuable — clarifying and strengthening the case against mental-state accounts — but it's not what the thesis's framing suggests.

The real question is whether the thesis's specific argument (via the judge case and the redundancy consideration) adds something beyond what Gunlogson, Farkas & Bruce, and others have already established. If it does, the contribution is real but incremental. If it doesn't, the thesis restates known positions without acknowledgment, which is a serious flaw in scholarly terms even if the position itself is correct.

R2. Common ground must be distinguished from common resource: pretense and strategic discourse show that propositions can be conversationally operative (available for anaphora, presupposition, inference) without being in common ground, revealing that context tracks what's available for use, not what's mutually accepted.

Scores
promise 4/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · dead
Move · Target
distinction — The assumption that a single notion of common ground handles both the role of tracking mutual acceptance and the role of licensing presupposition and anaphora
Sketch

The literature treats 'common ground' as doing two jobs: specifying what's mutually accepted/believed, and specifying what's available for conversational use (grounding presuppositions, anaphora, etc.). This distinction cleaves these roles. In a pretense, the proposition 'Sherlock Holmes lives on Baker Street' is available for anaphoric reference ('He lives there with Watson'), presuppositional constructions ('Holmes's violin'), and inference within the pretense—but it's not in common ground because nobody accepts or believes it, and everyone knows this. The key premise is that conversational operativity is a matter of what resources participants are jointly tracking and managing, which is orthogonal to what they mutually accept as true. Common ground (properly so-called) is still a mental-state notion, but it's not what does the work in licensing presupposition and anaphora—that's done by common resource, the set of propositions participants are jointly treating as available for conversational work, regardless of attitude.

Appraiser (blind)
Proposes a clean conceptual distinction (common ground vs. common resource) that could reframe debates about presupposition and pretense, though the distinction itself needs defense.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, answered. Defence clarified the target as Stalnaker's identification of conversational acceptance with operativity, not his belief/presupposition distinction
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence provided independent criteria but these collapsed into the use/mention distinction, making the thesis trivially true rather than substantive
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, answered. Defence gave three independent tests distinguishing acceptance from resource-management, though this victory revealed the thesis had become trivial
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence argued the target was literature's misuse of Stalnaker, but this conceded the thesis misdirects—the cure should be returning to Stalnaker, not splitting his framework
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence tried restricting common resource to joint representational tracking, but this distinction collapsed as any operative case can be redescribed as acceptance-for-some-purpose
🔧 Survives as

The literature often misapplies Stalnaker's common ground framework by conflating acceptance-for-conversational-purposes with actual belief; correctly applying Stalnaker's distinction between presupposition (what's treated as accepted for conversation) and belief shows that pretense, fiction-discussion, and reported speech involve meta-level common ground (mutual acceptance that the fiction says P, that the report claims P) which licenses the conversational operations without requiring object-level acceptance

Flaw
