The participant-replacement argument is clever but likely seen as a special case rather than decisive, since mental-state theorists can reply that institutional roles carry mental-state inheritance conditions.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, answered. The objection claimed both theorists use role-relative rather than person-indexed notions; the defence showed institutional cases involve participants who lack acceptance even qua role-occupants.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, answered. The objection argued the reasoning would eliminate mental foundations for all conversational phenomena; the defence showed common ground has unique persistence properties that speaker meaning and reference lack.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 4/5, answered. The objection claimed institutional record status differs from common ground proper; the defence showed institutional records exhibit all functional properties Stalnaker uses to identify common ground.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. The objection claimed mere terminological stipulation; the defence showed institutional cases realize the precise functional profile both theorists use to define their target phenomenon.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. The objection claimed equivocation between person-indexed and role-indexed states; the defence distinguished recognizing procedural requirements from accepting content, showing even role-occupants lack the requisite acceptance.
Survives as

Stalnaker's and Yalcin's accounts both fail because they require common ground to supervene on participants' states, but institutional common ground can persist when role-occupants recognize procedural requirements to presuppose certain content without accepting that content even for purposes of the conversation.

Merged in (1)
claimed shared content: Common ground cannot supervene on participants' mental states because it persists through complete replacement of participants.
  • (2/5) Common ground cannot be a mental state because it persists through participant replacement in ongoing institutional conversations, which is impossible for any supervenience base of individual or joint mental states.
full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The objection misrepresents both targets. Stalnaker's account does not require common ground to supervene on *participants'* states in the sense of being tied to particular individuals. His canonical formulation defines common ground as what is mutually accepted *for purposes of the conversation* — it is a property of the conversational context, not a set of individual mental states. When a new participant enters and accepts the conversational role, they thereby accept what has been established; the common ground persists because the *functional role* of accepting-for-conversation-purposes continues. Similarly, Yalcin's knowledge-of-acceptance view concerns what is mutually known to be accepted in the conversation, not what is known by specific individuals qua individuals. Both accounts are compatible with role-succession because "participant" in their frameworks means "occupant of a conversational role," not "this particular person with their idiosyncratic psychology." The thesis attacks a psychologistic reading neither theorist holds, mistaking "acceptance by participants" for "acceptance by these particular people" rather than "acceptance by whoever occupies participant-roles."

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious misreading that undermines the objection. Both Stalnaker (particularly in *Context and Content*) and Yalcin explicitly treat common ground as context-constituted rather than person-indexed. The institutional cases would need to show something incompatible with role-relative acceptance, which they do not obviously do.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection stands even granting the role-relative reading. The institutional cases reveal that common ground can persist when *no one currently in the conversation* accepts what is in common ground, even in their role as conversational participant.

Consider a parliamentary committee hearing testimony over weeks. On Monday, Members A, B, and C establish that witness testimony T is accepted into the record. By Friday, due to scheduled rotation, Members D, E, and F are present—none of whom were there Monday. The procedural rules dictate that T remains in the common ground of the hearing. But here is the crucial point: Members D, E, and F need not *accept* T, even for purposes of this conversation. They may think T is false, wish it weren't on record, and actively plan to challenge it. What matters is only that they *recognize T's status in the record*.

This defeats the role-relative reading because even qua participants in this conversation, D, E, and F do not accept T. What persists is not "acceptance by whoever occupies the role" but rather "what the institutional rules mark as established," which can come apart from any participant's acceptance.

The same point applies to Yalcin: it is not mutually known that the current participants accept T. What is mutually known is that T has institutional standing—a different matter entirely. The common ground supervenes not on states of participants (even role-indexed participants) but on institutional record-keeping, which can float free of all present participants' attitudes.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The role-relative reading救 Stalnaker and Yalcin only if role-occupants necessarily accept what their role commits them to. But institutional common ground demonstrates precisely that this is false: one can occupy the participant-role while rejecting what is institutionally established as common ground, so long as one recognizes its procedural status. The objection succeeds in showing that common ground in these contexts supervenes on institutional facts, not participant states.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. If this argument worked, it would prove that *no* conversational phenomena supervene on participants' states, which is absurd. The reasoning is: institutional rules can determine status X independently of current participants' attitudes, therefore X doesn't supervene on participant states. But apply this to speaker meaning: in parliamentary proceedings, the Speaker of the House has institutional authority to rule what someone's utterance "means for purposes of the record," even overriding what the utterer intended. By the thesis's logic, this shows speaker meaning doesn't supervene on speakers' intentions—it supervenes on institutional record-keeping that "can float free of all present participants' attitudes." Similarly for reference: if the chair rules "the gentleman's question refers to Bill S.123," that reference is established for the record regardless of what the questioner actually intended to refer to. The argument form—"institutional procedures can fix conversational status X independent of participants' mental states, therefore X-in-general doesn't supervene on mental states"—would eliminate the mental foundations of all conversational phenomena. The problem is equivocation: parliamentary common ground is a *technical, institutional* notion, not the ordinary conversational common ground Stalnaker and Yalcin theorize about. Their accounts concern everyday conversation where there are no record-keepers or procedural rules. The institutional cases are simply a different phenomenon requiring a different analysis.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This seriously damages the objection. The argument does generalize to unacceptable conclusions about speaker meaning and reference, suggesting the institutional cases are sui generis rather than counterexamples to theories of ordinary conversational common ground.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The proves-too-much objection fails because speaker meaning and reference do not have the persistence properties that common ground exhibits in institutional settings, and this asymmetry is theoretically significant.

When the parliamentary Speaker rules on what an utterance "means for the record," this creates an *institutional interpretation* that indeed floats free of speaker intention—but crucially, the speaker's original meaning does not thereby persist in the conversation. The speaker can immediately clarify: "That's not what I meant." What persists is a legal fiction, a recorded interpretation, while the conversational reality of speaker meaning remains tied to the speaker's state. Similarly with reference: the chair's ruling creates an *official* reference for procedural purposes, but the questioner's actual reference—what they were talking about—remains what they intended. We recognize these as two different things: the institutional overlay versus the conversational reality.

But with common ground in institutional settings, there is no analogous gap. When parliamentary procedure dictates that testimony T is in common ground, there is no separate "conversational common ground" that differs from the institutional one. The participants cannot say "That's in the official record but not in our actual common ground"—the institutional common ground *is* the common ground operative in their conversation. They must navigate around it, presuppose it in their questions, avoid contradicting it without procedural moves to reopen it. It functions exactly as Stalnaker says common ground functions: as the background of shared assumptions against which utterances are interpreted.

The asymmetry reveals that institutional common ground is not a mere "technical notion" separate from conversational common ground—it *is* conversational common ground in these contexts, but constituted by institutional rules rather than participant states. This shows that the supervenience claim fails: the same conversational phenomenon (common ground qua background of mutual assumptions) can be grounded differently in different settings.

VERDICT

The defence fails. The asymmetry claim does not hold up. In institutional settings, participants can and do distinguish between the official record and what is actually conversationally common ground. When Members D, E, and F inherit testimony T, they can perfectly well conduct sidebars, informal discussions, or even formal deliberations where they explicitly say "T is on the record, but let's be clear among ourselves that we all think it's false." Here they are distinguishing the institutional record from their actual conversational common ground—precisely the gap the defence claims doesn't exist.

Moreover, the defence concedes too much: it grants that "institutional common ground" can be constituted by rules rather than states, then tries to quarantine this as a special case. But Stalnaker and Yalcin offer *general* theories of common ground—theories meant to apply wherever the phenomenon occurs. If institutional contexts are genuine instances of common ground (and the defence admits they are, since they function "exactly as Stalnaker says"), then the theories must account for them. The objection succeeds: these are counterexamples showing that common ground does not always supervene on participant states, even role-indexed ones.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The institutional cases are not counterexamples because they are not instances of common ground at all—they are instances of *official record* or *procedural status*, which are different phenomena that institutional participants must track but which do not constitute the conversational common ground of their actual exchange.

Consider the parliamentary committee case more carefully. When Members D, E, and F discuss how to proceed, they operate with their own common ground: they mutually accept (for purposes of their conversation) that they are committee members, that they are reviewing testimony, that certain procedures apply, and crucially, that testimony T has official status in the record. This last item—"T has official status"—is in their common ground. But T itself need not be. They accept that T is on record; they do not accept T.

The thesis equivocates between two things: (1) the proposition that testimony T has been officially entered, and (2) the proposition that T (the content of the testimony) is true or accepted. Stalnaker's account predicts exactly what we observe: (1) is in common ground because all participants accept it; (2) is not in common ground because they do not accept it. The institutional rules determine what gets official status, but what is in conversational common ground remains what participants mutually accept—including their mutual acceptance of what has official status.

The weak point is the assumption that "what the institutional rules mark as established" and "what is in common ground" are the same thing. They are not. Institutional standing is one thing; conversational common ground is another. The former can be *about* the latter (it's common ground that X has official status) without being identical to it.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious challenge. The thesis needs to show that the institutional record itself, not merely facts about the institutional record, constitutes common ground. The equivocation between content and status is a genuine problem that significantly weakens the counterexample.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The counterexample objection fails because it misunderstands how institutional common ground actually functions in conversational practice. The claim that participants only accept "T has official status" rather than T itself cannot account for the normative constraints these institutional settings impose on conversation.

Return to the parliamentary committee. When Member D questions a new witness on Friday, she cannot felicitously say "Let's start from scratch—tell me whether you saw the defendant at the scene." The witness and other members will object: "That's already been established. Witness testimony T is on record that the defendant was at the scene." Member D must instead say something like "Given what's already established about the defendant's presence, can you tell me..." The conversational move of *presupposing* the defendant's presence is mandatory, not optional.

This is the signature of common ground in Stalnaker's sense: it is what must be taken for granted, what cannot be questioned without special procedural moves (like motions to strike from the record), what operates as the background against which new contributions are evaluated. Member D cannot coherently maintain "I accept that T has official status, but I don't accept T itself" while simultaneously being *required* to presuppose T's content in her questions. The presupposition relation holds between her utterances and T's content, not between her utterances and the meta-fact about T's status.

The objection tries to distinguish "accepting that T is on record" from "accepting T," but conversational practice collapses this distinction. If Member D must presuppose that the defendant was at the scene (T's content), then that content functions as common ground—it is what Stalnaker calls "accepted for purposes of the conversation." The institutional rules enforce this acceptance through procedural constraints, but the result is genuine common ground: the set of propositions that participants must take for granted.

The equivocation charge reverses: it is the objection that equivocates between "acceptance" as a voluntary mental attitude and "acceptance" as Stalnaker's technical term for what is taken-as-given in conversation. Institutional rules can make propositions taken-as-given without making them voluntarily believed. That is precisely what the counterexample demonstrates: common ground (qua what-must-be-presupposed) can be constituted by institutional fiat rather than by participant states.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection's distinction between "T has official status" and "T itself" cannot be maintained once we examine actual conversational constraints. When institutional rules require participants to presuppose certain content—to treat it as background, to build on it, to avoid contradicting it without special procedures—that content is functioning as common ground in precisely Stalnaker's sense, regardless of participants' private attitudes toward it.

The objection is correct that there is a difference between believing T and being required to presuppose T, but this difference undermines Stalnaker's account rather than saving it. Stalnaker defines common ground as what is mutually accepted for purposes of the conversation—but "acceptance" in his framework is supposed to be a mental state of participants (albeit a context-relative one), not a status imposed by external rules. The institutional cases show that what-must-be-presupposed can come apart from what-participants-accept, even in their role as conversational participants.

The counterexample stands: institutional common ground is genuine common ground (it has all the functional properties Stalnaker identifies), but it supervenes on institutional rules rather than participant states. This refutes the supervenience claim for both Stalnaker and Yalcin.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents itself as revealing a substantive failure in Stalnaker's and Yalcin's accounts, but it merely stipulates a technical sense of "common ground" and then observes that this stipulated notion behaves differently from what those theorists discuss. The weak point is the undefended assumption that institutional procedural records constitute "common ground" in the same sense that Stalnaker and Yalcin theorize about.

The thesis trades on "common ground" having an ordinary language sense (roughly: shared understanding or mutually accepted background) that makes it seem like parliamentary records and conversational common ground must be the same phenomenon. But Stalnaker and Yalcin offer technical definitions of a theoretical posit designed to explain certain conversational dynamics—presupposition projection, felicity conditions, information flow. Their claim is: "There is a conversational phenomenon with these functional properties, and it supervenes on participant states." The institutional cases introduce something else—official records with procedural force—and simply label it "common ground" without showing it has the same functional properties or is the same theoretical kind.

The thesis's "discovery" reduces to: "If we use 'common ground' to mean institutional record-keeping, then common ground doesn't supervene on participant states." But this is just a verbal stipulation. Stalnaker and Yalcin are not claiming that everything anyone might call "common ground" supervenes on participant states—they are making claims about a specific conversational-pragmatic phenomenon. Showing that parliamentary procedure uses similar vocabulary proves nothing unless the phenomena are genuinely identical, which is precisely what the thesis assumes rather than establishes.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This has some force in highlighting that the thesis assumes rather than argues for the identity of institutional records with conversational common ground. However, the defence's arguments about presupposition and functional role do provide some evidence that these are the same phenomenon, not merely homonymous uses of a term. The triviality charge would be stronger if the institutional cases clearly lacked the functional properties Stalnaker identifies, but the thesis makes a reasonable case that they share those properties while differing in their grounds.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The triviality objection fails because the institutional cases exhibit precisely the functional properties that Stalnaker and Yalcin use to identify common ground as a theoretical posit, making this a genuine counterexample rather than a verbal stipulation.

Stalnaker characterizes common ground by specific functional roles: it determines what is taken for granted in conversation, constrains what can be felicitously asserted (you cannot assert what is already common ground), governs presupposition projection, and defines the context set (the set of worlds compatible with what is commonly accepted). The institutional cases display all these properties:

Taken-for-granted status: Testimony T on the parliamentary record must be treated as given—participants cannot question it without procedural motions.

Assertion constraints: A member cannot felicitously assert T as new information on Friday if it was established on Monday; doing so prompts "That's already on record."

Presupposition projection: Questions must presuppose T's content ("Given the defendant's presence, what time did he arrive?"), and presuppositions project exactly as Stalnaker's theory predicts.

Context set: The institutional record constrains what possibilities remain open for discussion—once T is established, conversational moves that assume not-T are out of bounds.

These are not superficial similarities. The institutional record plays exactly the explanatory role in conversational dynamics that Stalnaker assigns to common ground. When Yalcin discusses mutual knowledge of acceptance, he is trying to explain why certain updates are infelicitous and why presuppositions behave as they do—the very phenomena that institutional records also govern.

The objection demands that the thesis "show the phenomena are genuinely identical" rather than assuming it, but this demand is backwards. Stalnaker and Yalcin identify common ground *by its functional role*—they are functionalists about this conversational posit. The institutional cases realize that functional role through different grounds (institutional rules rather than participant states). This is not stipulation; it is showing that the same functionally-defined phenomenon admits multiple realizations, which refutes the supervenience claim.

The objection's real move is to retreat: "Well, Stalnaker and Yalcin only meant to theorize about non-institutional conversation." But they present their accounts as theories of common ground *as such*, not as theories restricted to informal chat. Stalnaker's formal framework in *Context and Content* is explicitly meant to model assertion and presupposition generally, including in structured contexts. If the account cannot handle institutional cases that exhibit all the relevant functional properties, that is a substantive failure, not a terminological misunderstanding.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The triviality objection would work only if the institutional cases were labeled "common ground" arbitrarily, without sharing the functional properties that make common ground theoretically interesting. But the thesis establishes that institutional records exhibit the precise functional profile—presupposition behavior, assertion constraints, context-set restriction—that Stalnaker and Yalcin use to identify their target phenomenon.

The objection's suggestion that Stalnaker and Yalcin theorize only about a restricted domain (non-institutional conversation) is an ad hoc retreat unsupported by their texts. Both present general theories of conversational common ground, and Stalnaker's formal framework is meant to apply wherever the functional properties appear. The institutional cases show that this functionally-defined phenomenon can be grounded in institutional rules rather than participant states.

This is a genuine counterexample: it identifies cases where something with all the functional hallmarks of common ground (as Stalnaker and Yalcin characterize it) fails to supervene on participant states. The thesis succeeds in showing that both accounts fail because they make false supervenience claims about a phenomenon that admits multiple realizations.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "participants' states" between (1) mental states of individuals qua individuals, and (2) mental states of role-occupants qua role-occupants. The argument is plausible against reading (1) but uninteresting; interesting against reading (2) but implausible.

Plausible but uninteresting (reading 1): If "participants' states" means the mental states of particular individuals like Senator Smith or Judge Jones, then yes, common ground can persist through personnel changes. But neither Stalnaker nor Yalcin makes the crude claim that common ground supervenes on *these particular people's* psychology. This reading makes the thesis a trivial observation that conversational roles can be transferred—something no theorist denies.

Interesting but implausible (reading 2): If "participants' states" means the mental states of whoever-occupies-the-participant-roles (role-indexed states), then the claim becomes interesting—it would show that common ground can float free even of role-occupant states. But the institutional cases fail to establish this. When Member D inherits the parliamentary role, she thereby inherits commitments to presuppose what's on record. Her role-indexed state *does* include accepting-for-purposes-of-this-conversation that T must be treated as given, even if she personally doubts T. The institutional rules constitute what it is to occupy the participant-role, and occupying that role means having certain conversational commitments. The persistence is explained by role-continuity, not by common ground floating free of role-occupant states.

The argument needs both readings: it gets plausibility from the obvious fact that particular individuals can be replaced (reading 1), but gets interest only from the claim that role-occupant states don't matter either (reading 2). It cannot establish both.

STRENGTH: 3/5

This is a genuine problem that the thesis must address. The defence's moves about "acceptance as technical term" and "presupposition requirements" can be read as defending reading (2)—that even role-occupants need not accept T—but this remains contentious. The institutional rules might simply *constitute* what role-acceptance means in these contexts, rather than replacing it. However, the equivocation is not fatal: the thesis can potentially run on reading (2) alone if it successfully establishes that role-occupants genuinely lack the relevant acceptances, which the defence attempts. The attack has force but the thesis is answerable.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The equivocation charge fails because the thesis runs on reading (2) alone and successfully establishes that role-occupant states, properly understood, do not ground institutional common ground.

The objection claims that occupying the parliamentary role *means* having certain conversational commitments, so Member D's role-indexed state includes "accepting-for-purposes-of-this-conversation that T must be treated as given." But this conflates two distinct things:

Recognizing a normative constraint (knowing that one must presuppose T to participate properly)

Accepting the content (taking T as given, treating T as true for purposes of the conversation)

Member D can have the first without the second. She knows the rules require her to presuppose T; she knows violating this brings procedural sanctions; she knows her questions must be framed to accommodate T. But none of this entails that she accepts T even "for purposes of this conversation." She might actively resist—internally framing her questions as "Given what the record falsely claims..." while outwardly conforming to procedural requirements. Her mental state is: "I must act as if T is accepted, though I do not accept it."

This is not mere personal doubt compatible with conversational acceptance. It is the absence of conversational acceptance itself. Stalnaker's notion of "acceptance for purposes of conversation" is supposed to be a genuine mental state—a context-relative propositional attitude that participants adopt. But Member D has no such attitude toward T. She has only a recognition that institutional rules require certain behaviors from her.

The objection's move—claiming institutional rules "constitute what role-acceptance means"—is precisely the concession that defeats Stalnaker and Yalcin. If we must redefine "acceptance" to mean "behavioral conformity to institutional requirements" rather than any mental state, then we have abandoned the original accounts. Stalnaker explicitly contrasts acceptance (a mental state) with mere behavioral conformity. The institutional cases force us to choose: either common ground sometimes exists without participant acceptance (refuting the supervenience claim), or we redefine acceptance so radically that it is no longer a mental state at all (abandoning the theory).

The thesis runs cleanly on reading (2): even role-indexed participant states—the mental states of whoever occupies participant roles, qua occupants of those roles—do not suffice for institutional common ground. What suffices is institutional rule-compliance, which is a different kind of thing entirely.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The equivocation charge depends on blurring the distinction between accepting-a-proposition and recognizing-a-requirement-to-act-as-if-one-accepts-it. Once this distinction is clear, the institutional cases establish that common ground can exist when role-occupants have only the second (recognition of procedural requirements) without the first (acceptance of content).

The objection's suggestion that institutional rules "constitute what role-acceptance means" is not a defence of Stalnaker and Yalcin—it is their abandonment. If "acceptance" must be redefined as behavioral conformity to institutional norms rather than a mental state, then the accounts have been replaced rather than vindicated. Both theorists ground common ground in mental states (acceptance, knowledge of acceptance); showing that institutional common ground requires only behavioral conformity refutes the supervenience claim.

The thesis succeeds on reading (2) alone: common ground in institutional settings does not supervene on role-indexed participant states because participants can occupy roles, conform to procedural requirements, and presuppose institutional content without accepting that content even for purposes of the conversation. The counterexample stands.

O3. Public commitment views are unstable because they must either collapse into mental-state views (to explain why commitments bind) or eliminate the participants' perspective entirely (making disagreement about what's common ground impossible).

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 4/5 · survives
Move · Target
instability — Public commitment approaches to common ground
Sketch

Pure public commitment theories face a dilemma: either the commitments bind participants because participants recognize/accept them as binding (in which case we're back to a mental-state theory with public commitments as mere evidence), or commitments bind independently of any participant attitudes. If the latter, then when participants disagree about what the common ground is, there's no room for both being wrong—one must simply not know the objective facts about what moves were made. But this eliminates the familiar phenomenon of negotiations over what's been established, where both parties can be wrong about what their prior exchanges really committed them to. The key premise is that the bindingness of commitments requires a mental-state uptake condition that reintroduces precisely what public-commitment views aimed to avoid.

Appraiser (blind)
The dilemma is interesting but the argument that public-commitment views must collapse has likely been anticipated and addressed by defenders of those views.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. The objection claimed the thesis strawmanned actual theorists, but the defence showed the thesis targets theoretical instability, not explicit endorsements, and that cited theorists may exemplify rather than refute the instability.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. Lewis's rule-based account offered a genuine middle position, but the defence successfully pushed the dilemma up one level: rules themselves either bind through acceptance or independently.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. The objection claimed the thesis merely stipulated terminology, but the defence showed it makes a substantive claim about explanatory priority and metaphysical grounding, not labels.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, answered. This was the strongest attack, claiming the thesis slid between strong and weak readings of 'mental-state theory,' but the defence showed it consistently tracks one criterion: explanatory priority in grounding normative force.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 4/5, answered. The objection charged that the thesis reclassifies all counterexamples, but the defence argued the disjunction is genuinely exhaustive and gave a clear falsification condition: show bindingness neither mental-state-grounded nor attitude-independent.
Survives as

Public commitment views are unstable because they must either collapse into mental-state views (by grounding the bindingness of commitments in participant recognition/acceptance) or eliminate the participants' perspective entirely (by making commitments bind independently of any participant attitudes), and apparent middle positions (rules, conventions, intersubjective scorekeeping) face the same dilemma about what grounds their normative force.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "public commitment approaches to common ground" as holding that commitments bind "independently of any participant attitudes." But the major public commitment theorists—particularly Robert Brandom and Matthias Brune—explicitly build participant recognition into their accounts. Brandom's scorekeeping model makes commitment attribution a matter of intersubjective perspective-taking, not objective facts independent of participants. Similarly, Stalnaker's common ground framework (though he focuses on presupposition) treats common ground as what participants mutually recognize as shared, not as a third-realm entity. The thesis attacks a "pure" public commitment view where commitments exist wholly independently of participant uptake, but this appears to be a strawman—the actual theorists in this space don't defend commitment-bindingness as attitude-independent in the way required for the dilemma to get purchase. The weak point is the characterization of the target position in the second horn of the dilemma: actual public commitment theorists don't hold that commitments "bind independently of any participant attitudes."

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This is a weak objection. While major theorists do include participant perspectives, there may be versions of public commitment theory (particularly in formal semantics of common ground) that treat it more objectively. The thesis might be targeting a theoretical possibility rather than misattributing to actual holders. Without access to texts, I cannot confidently say no one holds the stronger view.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes what "independently of participant attitudes" means in the thesis. The defence has three parts:

First, the dilemma does not require that anyone explicitly endorses attitude-independence. It claims public commitment views are *unstable* — they tend toward one horn or the other when pressed. Even if Brandom includes "intersubjective perspective-taking," the question is whether this perspective-taking is doing the real work of making commitments binding, or whether it's merely tracking commitments that already bind. If the former, we have collapsed into mental states. If the latter, the commitment's normative force exists prior to and independently of the perspective-taking, which is the second horn.

Second, the objection's own examples support the thesis. Take Brandom's scorekeeping: when scorekeeper A attributes commitment C to speaker B, what makes A's attribution correct or incorrect? Either (i) it's correct because B has the relevant mental states (recognition, acceptance, intention), which reintroduces mental states as fundamental, or (ii) it's correct because of B's public moves regardless of B's mental states, which makes the commitment attitude-independent in the relevant sense. The fact that we describe this in terms of "perspective-taking" does not answer which of these grounds the correctness conditions.

Third, formal semantics treatments of common ground in the Stalnaker tradition often do treat it as the set of propositions mutually presupposed — a set that can be objectively characterized by the conversational record, and about which participants can simply be mistaken. When theorists say common ground is "what participants mutually recognize," they face exactly the thesis's question: is this mutual recognition constitutive of common ground (mental states doing the work) or merely epistemic access to an independently constituted common ground (attitude-independence)? The thesis claims you cannot stably occupy the middle.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection attacks a strawman version of the thesis — one that requires explicit endorsement of attitude-independence — when the thesis actually claims that public commitment views are *forced toward* attitude-independence when they try to avoid collapsing into mental-state views. The objection does not engage with the instability argument itself: the claim that intermediate positions are unstable. Citing theorists who use both "public commitment" language and "participant recognition" language does not defeat the thesis; it potentially exemplifies the instability the thesis diagnoses. The objection fails to show that these theorists have a stable way of combining both elements rather than oscillating between horns.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. Consider Lewis's account of conversational score in "Scorekeeping in a Language Game" (1979). Lewis treats presupposition accommodation as a rule-governed public phenomenon: when a speaker presupposes P, the conversational score changes to include P in the common ground *unless* participants object. This gives us a stable middle position that escapes the dilemma. The commitments bind because of the public rule ("what is presupposed becomes common ground if unchallenged"), not because of mental states and not wholly independently of participants. When two participants disagree about what's common ground after an exchange, they can both be wrong about whether the accommodation rule was properly triggered—perhaps neither noticed an implicit objection, or both misheard what was presupposed. The normative force comes from the *rule* (a public, social-conventional fact), not from mental uptake (avoiding horn one) and not from attitude-independent commitment facts (avoiding horn two). Participants can negotiate what the conversational record shows about whether accommodation occurred, making both fallible about the rule's application. The weak point in the thesis is the assumption that only mental states or attitude-independent facts can ground bindingness, ignoring social-conventional rules as a third source of normativity.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem requiring an answer. Lewis-style rule-based accounts do seem to offer a middle path where the source of normativity is neither mental states nor wholly attitude-independent facts, but conventional rules. However, the thesis might respond that rules themselves either bind because participants accept them (collapsing to mental states) or bind independently of acceptance (attitude-independence), pushing the dilemma up one level.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection relocates the dilemma but does not escape it. The defence proceeds in three stages:

First, the rule-based account simply pushes the question back one level. Lewis's accommodation rule states that presupposed content becomes common ground "if unchallenged." But what makes this rule binding on participants? Either (i) the rule binds because participants accept or recognize it as governing their practice—in which case mental states (acceptance of the rule) are doing the fundamental work, or (ii) the rule binds independently of whether participants accept it—perhaps as a constitutive rule of the practice they're engaged in. If (i), we've collapsed to mental states: the common ground is ultimately grounded in participant attitudes toward the rule. If (ii), we have attitude-independence: the rule determines what's common ground regardless of participant uptake, which is precisely the second horn.

Second, the objection's own example of disagreement reveals the instability. When both participants are "wrong about whether the accommodation rule was properly triggered," what makes them wrong? The objection suggests they might have "misheard what was presupposed" or "neither noticed an implicit objection." But notice: if what they misheard or failed to notice are *public facts* (the acoustic events, the observable behavior), then the rule is binding them to commitments based on public events independently of their recognition—that's attitude-independence. If instead what matters is what they *took* to be presupposed or *took* to be an objection, then their mental states are constitutive after all. The rule cannot float free of both.

Third, the "social-conventional" nature of rules does not provide a third category. Social conventions are themselves either grounded in participant attitudes (as Lewis himself argued in *Convention*—conventions exist because of patterns of mutual expectation and preference) or they're reified into attitude-independent normative facts. A convention that binds *because participants accept it* gives mental states the foundational role. A convention that binds *even when participants don't accept it* (perhaps because they're participants in a practice whether they recognize it or not) makes the normative force attitude-independent. The thesis's dilemma applies to conventional rules just as it applies to direct commitments.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection identifies a genuine theoretical move—appealing to rules rather than direct commitments—but this move does not escape the dilemma; it merely relocates it. The question "what makes commitments bind?" becomes "what makes rules bind?" and the same two answers remain available: participant attitudes or attitude-independence. The objection fails because it treats "social-conventional rules" as a third source of normativity without explaining how rules can bind in a way that's neither grounded in participant acceptance (mental states) nor independent of participant acceptance (attitude-independence). The thesis survives: public commitment views remain unstable because the appeal to rules, conventions, or any other intermediate mechanism eventually faces the same dilemma about the source of normative force.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents itself as identifying an instability or dilemma for public commitment views, but it's actually just stipulating how we should use the term "mental-state theory." The supposed discovery is that any view which makes participant recognition/acceptance relevant to bindingness counts as a "mental-state theory." But this is merely a verbal stipulation about what gets labeled "mental-state." The original motivation for public commitment views was to avoid making common ground purely private or inaccessible—to give it an objective, publicly observable dimension. A view can perfectly well accomplish this while still incorporating participant uptake: common ground is constituted by public moves (utterances, gestures, observable behaviors) that participants recognize as commitment-generating. This makes common ground publicly accessible and objective in the relevant sense—it's not hidden in anyone's head, it's manifest in the conversational record—while still being sensitive to participant perspectives. The thesis just declares by fiat that any such view "collapses into" mental-state theory, but this is trivial re-labeling, not a substantive discovery. The weak point is the claim that incorporating participant recognition means "we're back to a mental-state theory"—this treats "mental-state theory" so broadly that the distinction between public and private approaches loses its original point, making the thesis a terminological stipulation rather than a philosophical insight.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This attack has some force but is ultimately weak. The thesis does make a substantive claim about where the normative force is grounded, not just about labels. If participant mental states are doing the fundamental work of making commitments bind, that does seem to undermine the distinctive appeal of public commitment approaches, regardless of whether we call it "collapsing" or something else. The thesis is tracking a real theoretical question about the source of normativity, not just stipulating terminology.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses labels with explanatory priority, and confuses accessibility with grounding. The defence has three parts:

First, the thesis is not about what we call things but about what explains what. The original dispute between mental-state and public-commitment theories concerns the *grounds* of common ground: is common ground fundamentally constituted by mental states (beliefs, intentions, mutual knowledge) with public behavior as mere evidence, or is it fundamentally constituted by public commitments with mental states as derivative or secondary? This is a substantive metaphysical question about explanatory priority, not a terminological one. When the thesis says a view "collapses into mental-state theory," it means: mental states turn out to be doing the foundational explanatory work after all. That's a claim about theoretical structure, not about labels.

Second, the objection's proposed middle position actually concedes the thesis's point. The objection says: "common ground is constituted by public moves that participants recognize as commitment-generating." But now ask: what makes a public move commitment-generating? The objection's answer is: participant recognition. So participant recognition is what gives public moves their commitment-generating force. That means mental states (recognition) are explanatorily prior to the public commitments—the commitments bind *because* they're recognized as binding. This is precisely what the thesis means by "collapsing into mental-state theory": mental states are doing the fundamental work, even if we gesture at public moves in our formulation. The public moves are now just the *objects* of the mental states that do the real work.

Third, accessibility is orthogonal to the thesis's concern. The objection says the view "makes common ground publicly accessible and objective in the relevant sense—it's not hidden in anyone's head, it's manifest in the conversational record." But the thesis never denies that public-commitment views can make common ground *epistemically accessible*. The question is what *grounds* the common ground—what makes it the case that certain commitments are in force. A view that says "commitments are in force because participants recognize them as such" has located the grounds in mental states, even if those mental states are reliably trackable via public behavior. The thesis's instability claim is about metaphysical grounding, not epistemic access. The objection attacks a claim the thesis never made.

VERDICT

The defence holds completely. The objection fails to engage with the thesis's actual content. The thesis makes a claim about explanatory priority and metaphysical grounding: either mental states ground the commitments (by making them binding through recognition/acceptance) or commitments bind independently of mental states. This is not a terminological stipulation but a substantive disjunction about where normative force comes from. The objection's proposed middle position—public moves that participants recognize as binding—actually exemplifies the first horn: if participant recognition is what makes the moves binding, then mental states are explanatorily fundamental. The objection's point about accessibility is simply irrelevant to the thesis's concern with grounding. The thesis survives intact: it identifies a real instability about the source of normative force, not a verbal trick about how to apply labels.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "mental-state theory" between a strong reading (where mental states are metaphysically constitutive and epistemically primary) and a weak reading (where mental states play any explanatory role whatsoever). The argument needs both readings to work.

The thesis gains plausibility from the strong reading: surely public commitment theorists wanted to avoid views where common ground is *purely* mental—hidden beliefs and intentions that public behavior merely evidences, where we can only access common ground by mind-reading. On this reading, "collapsing into mental-state theory" means returning to the problematic features that motivated public approaches: privacy, inaccessibility, and treating public moves as mere symptoms.

But the argument only works on the weak reading: any view where participant attitudes play *any* constitutive role counts as "mental-state theory." The defender's own responses demonstrate this. When Lewis appeals to rules that bind "if unchallenged," the defence insists this "collapses to mental states" because participants must accept the rules. When the counterexample offers "public moves that participants recognize as commitment-generating," the defence says recognition makes mental states "explanatorily fundamental."

These conclusions only follow if "mental-state theory" means "any view where mental states matter at all." But on that reading, the collapse is uninteresting—of course participant attitudes matter *somehow* in an account of conversational commitments between participants. The original motivation for public commitment views wasn't to eliminate mental states entirely (an absurd goal) but to avoid making them primary and making public behavior merely evidential.

The thesis cannot run on either reading alone: on the strong reading, the first horn doesn't threaten public commitment views (they can include mental states without making them primary); on the weak reading, the first horn is trivial (every theory "collapses" because every theory includes mental states somewhere).

Weak point: The premise that "the bindingness of commitments requires a mental-state uptake condition that reintroduces precisely what public-commitment views aimed to avoid."

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious objection requiring a real answer. The thesis does seem to slide between "any mental-state involvement" and "the problematic features of mental-state-primary theories," and the argument appears to need both readings. However, the thesis might survive by clarifying that it's specifically about *explanatory priority* or *grounding*, not mere involvement—and that locating grounding in mental states does reintroduce the original problems even if mental states are publicly trackable.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies what remains constant across the thesis's argument. The thesis operates with a single, consistent criterion throughout: explanatory priority in grounding normative force. There is no equivocation between strong and weak readings—there is one reading applied consistently.

The defence proceeds in three stages:

First, the criterion is univocal: what grounds the bindingness of commitments? When the thesis asks whether mental states are doing the fundamental work, it's asking a precise question: what makes it the case that a commitment binds a participant? Is the answer ultimately cashed out in terms of that participant's mental states (beliefs, acceptances, recognitions, intentions), or in terms of something else? This is not "any involvement whatsoever" versus "purely mental"—it's a question about the bottom level of explanation. When we trace the explanation of why a commitment binds down to bedrock, do we end at mental states or not?

Second, the objection's "strong reading" is actually irrelevant to the thesis. The objection says the strong reading concerns privacy, inaccessibility, and public behavior as "mere symptoms." But notice: the thesis never claims that views collapsing to the first horn must make common ground *epistemically inaccessible* or *private*. A view can make mental states the metaphysical ground of commitments while still making those mental states reliably trackable via public behavior. The thesis's point is about *what's doing the grounding work*, not about epistemic access. The objection imports concerns about privacy and accessibility that the thesis never invoked, then complains the thesis equivocates by not consistently tracking these imported concerns.

Third, the objection's examples actually demonstrate the thesis's consistent application of its criterion. Take the Lewis case: the thesis asks what makes the accommodation rule binding. If the answer is "participants accept it," then participant acceptance (a mental state) is what grounds the rule's normative force—that's the criterion being applied. Take the "public moves that participants recognize as binding" case: the thesis asks what makes these moves binding. If the answer is "participant recognition," then recognition (a mental state) grounds the bindingness—same criterion. The thesis consistently asks: *what grounds the normative force?* If the answer bottoms out in mental states, that's the first horn. If not, the second horn.

The objection claims this makes the first horn "trivial" because "every theory includes mental states somewhere." But this misses the point entirely. The thesis doesn't claim *including* mental states anywhere makes you a mental-state theory. It claims that if mental states are what ultimately *grounds the normative force of commitments*, then you haven't escaped mental-state theories of common ground—you've just added public-behavior epicycles. The public commitment theorist's distinctive claim was supposed to be that *public commitments themselves* bind, not that they bind because participants have certain mental states toward them.

Consider an analogy: A property dualist might say physical states are reliably correlated with mental states and give us epistemic access to them, but mental states are still metaphysically fundamental. A physicalist would say this "collapses into" dualism because it makes mental states explanatorily basic. The property dualist cannot reply "you're equivocating—I'm not saying mental states are purely private and inaccessible!" The physicalist's point is about grounding, not accessibility. The thesis makes the parallel move: a view that grounds commitment-bindingness in mental states has made mental states explanatorily basic, even if those mental states are publicly trackable.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection fails because it misidentifies what the thesis is tracking. The thesis has one consistent criterion: explanatory priority in grounding normative force. It never invokes privacy or inaccessibility as part of what makes something a "mental-state theory"—those are red herrings the objection introduces. The thesis's claim is metaphysical: if you trace the explanation of why commitments bind down to bedrock and you end at mental states (acceptance, recognition, intention), you've made mental states foundational, regardless of whether those mental states are publicly accessible.

The objection's charge of equivocation depends on attributing two different readings to the thesis, but the thesis actually uses one reading consistently: mental states are doing the fundamental grounding work. The objection confuses this with questions about epistemic access and privacy that the thesis never raised. When the thesis says views "collapse into mental-state theory," it means they locate the ultimate ground of normative force in mental states—a clear, consistent, non-trivial claim that the objection has not defeated.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis is structured to be immune from counterexamples through systematic redefinition. Any proposed middle position between mental-state grounding and attitude-independence gets reclassified as actually being one horn or the other, ensuring the dilemma remains exhaustive.

Consider how the thesis handles attempted counterexamples:

Lewis's rule-based account: Initially appears to offer a third option (social-conventional rules as the source of normativity). But the thesis responds by asking what makes rules binding, then insists this question admits only two answers: participant acceptance (reclassified as mental-state theory) or attitude-independence (reclassified as the second horn). The rule-based position is not allowed to be its own answer.

Public moves with participant recognition: Appears to combine public objectivity with participant perspective. But the thesis declares that if recognition makes moves binding, then mental states are "explanatorily fundamental"—reclassified as horn one. If moves bind regardless of recognition—reclassified as horn two.

Brandom's scorekeeping: Involves intersubjective perspective-taking that seems neither purely mental nor attitude-independent. But the thesis insists we must ask whether perspective-taking is "doing the real work" or "merely tracking" prior commitments—forcing reclassification into one horn or the other.

The pattern is consistent: any proposed position is subjected to the question "but what *really* grounds the bindingness?" and any answer is sorted into the two pre-established categories. The thesis protects itself by treating "mental-state grounding" and "attitude-independence" as an exhaustive disjunction that applies to every possible answer about normative force, then declaring that any view must ultimately give one of these two answers.

The weak point is the premise that the dilemma is exhaustive—that every possible account of what makes commitments binding must reduce to either mental-state grounding or attitude-independence. This exhaustiveness is maintained not by argument but by definitional fiat: whatever answer you give gets reclassified as really being one or the other.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem requiring a real answer. The thesis does appear to operate with a framework that automatically sorts any proposed middle position into one of two categories, making it difficult to see what could count as a genuine counterexample. However, the thesis might respond that this isn't unfalsifiability but rather correct identification of a genuine metaphysical exhaustiveness—that there really are only two possible grounds for normative force, and apparent middle positions genuinely do reduce to one or the other upon analysis.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses principled metaphysical analysis with definitional gerrymandering. The thesis is not making itself unfalsifiable through arbitrary reclassification—it is applying a legitimate and genuinely exhaustive metaphysical distinction. The defence has three parts:

First, some disjunctions really are exhaustive, and recognizing this is not a fallacy. Consider: "Either the number of stars is finite or infinite." Any proposed middle position ("the number is indefinitely large," "the number is transfinite") gets "reclassified" as one horn or the other upon analysis. This is not unfalsifiability—it's the correct recognition that certain metaphysical categories are genuinely exhaustive. The thesis claims that for any normative fact (including the bindingness of commitments), either that fact obtains in virtue of mental states or it obtains independently of mental states. This is not definitional fiat—it's a substantive metaphysical claim about the space of possible groundings for normative facts.

Second, the objection provides no candidate answer that escapes the disjunction—it only complains that proposed answers get sorted. The objection lists Lewis's rules, public moves with recognition, and Brandom's scorekeeping, but notice: it never explains how any of these *actually escapes* the question "does this bind in virtue of mental states or not?" Instead, it complains that the thesis asks this question and sorts the answers. But that's exactly what the thesis should do if its disjunction is correct! The objection needed to show either (a) a coherent third category of grounding that's neither mental-state-dependent nor attitude-independent, or (b) that the thesis misclassifies some particular case. It does neither—it just protests that cases get classified at all.

Third, the thesis gives a clear falsification condition: show that commitments can bind in a way that's neither grounded in mental states nor independent of them. What would this look like? It would be a case where: (i) the commitment's bindingness is not ultimately explained by any participant's mental states (beliefs, acceptances, recognitions, intentions), AND (ii) the commitment's bindingness is not a fact that obtains independently of all participant mental states. The objection needs to articulate what such a case would be, not just assert that the thesis won't allow one.

The objection's examples actually demonstrate why the disjunction is exhaustive rather than showing unfalsifiability:

- Rules: A rule either binds because participants accept/recognize it (mental-state-dependent) or it binds regardless of whether they do (attitude-independent). What third option is there? The objection cannot say.

- Public moves with recognition: Either the recognition is what makes the move binding (mental-state ground) or the move binds independently and recognition merely tracks this (attitude-independent). What third option is there? The objection cannot say.

The thesis is falsifiable in principle: show a coherent account where bindingness is neither mental-state-grounded nor attitude-independent. The objection has not done this. It has only shown that the thesis analyzes proposed middle positions—which is what the thesis should do if its disjunction is correct.

Consider an analogy: Someone claims "all events are either deterministic or indeterministic." An objector complains: "This is unfalsifiable! Whenever I propose a middle position—quantum superposition, probabilistic causation, emergent agency—you just reclassify it as really deterministic or really indeterministic." But this complaint fails if the disjunction really is exhaustive. The proper response is: "Yes, I analyze your proposals and show which category they fall into, because those are the only categories. If you think there's a third, articulate it."

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection fails to distinguish between illegitimate unfalsifiability (protecting a thesis through arbitrary redefinition) and legitimate exhaustiveness (correctly identifying that a metaphysical disjunction covers all cases). The thesis claims that normative bindingness either depends on mental states or doesn't—this is a substantive metaphysical claim, not a definitional trick.

The objection needed to either (a) articulate a third category of grounding that's neither mental-state-dependent nor attitude-independent, or (b) show that the thesis misclassifies specific cases by forcing them into the wrong horn. It does neither. Instead, it merely complains that the thesis analyzes proposed middle positions and determines which horn they fall under—but this is exactly what the thesis should do if its disjunction is genuinely exhaustive.

The thesis remains falsifiable: produce a coherent account of how commitments can bind in a way that's neither grounded in mental states nor independent of them. Until the objection does this, the charge of unfalsifiability fails. The thesis survives: its disjunction is not protective gerrymanering but a legitimate and exhaustive metaphysical distinction about the possible grounds of normative force.

O4. Treating common ground as mutual knowledge of public commitments commits you to rejecting the standard update semantics for presupposition, because presuppositions would no longer be admittance conditions on the context set but constraints on legitimate uptake of commitments.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 3/5 · survives
Move · Target
commitment — Public commitment theorists who want to keep standard dynamic semantics machinery
Sketch

If common ground is public commitments rather than shared mental states, then when a speaker presupposes p, they're not testing whether p is in the interlocutors' shared belief set (Stalnaker) or mutually known as accepted (Yalcin). They're marking p as a commitment they're treating as already actionable. The key premise is that commitments have a different normative structure than mental states: you can be entitled to invoke a commitment (because it was established by prior speech acts) even when you're not entitled to assume a mental state (because you don't know what's in others' heads). This means presupposition failure isn't context-set mismatch but illegitimate invocation of a commitment. So presupposition projection would need to be reanalyzed as tracking which commitments an utterance attempts to make actionable, not which propositions it requires to be antecedently believed/accepted.

Appraiser (blind)
The claim about update semantics implications is technically interesting but seems more like a consequence to be worked out than a thesis that would reframe the debate itself.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, answered. The objection claimed no theorist holds both commitments, but the defence identified actual hybrid work (Asher & Lascarides, Maier, Gauker) and clarified the target is the formal apparatus, not Stalnaker's metaphysics specifically.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, answered. The objection argued the logic would prohibit all metaphysical reinterpretation of formal tools, but the defence showed presupposition semantics is special because its operations (admittance conditions, set-intersection) are defined by reference to doxastic states, unlike genuinely neutral mathematical structures.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 2/5, answered. The 'Sorry' case only showed extensional agreement in uncontroversial cases; the defence provided the challenge-retraction variant where the frameworks give different verdicts, proving the operations genuinely differ.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 1/5, answered. The objection claimed the thesis was analytically true by definition, but the defence showed it makes substantive empirical claims about when frameworks give different verdicts (challenge-retraction case), not mere definitional consequences.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 2/5, answered. The objection claimed ambiguity between narrow and broad readings of 'standard update semantics,' but the defence clarified the target is the specific explanatory architecture (information-state contexts, elimination-based updates) shared across the dynamic semantic tradition, not arbitrary formalization.
Survives as

Treating common ground as public commitments commits you to rejecting the standard update semantics for presupposition, because that framework's core explanatory architecture—modeling contexts as information states that get narrowed by assertion and using admittance conditions defined by set-membership—cannot represent the normative structure of commitment scorekeeping where entitlements are speaker-relative and survive challenge until withdrawal.

full exchange (9 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis targets "public commitment theorists who want to keep standard dynamic semantics machinery," but this mischaracterizes the actual positions in this literature. Theorists like Brandom explicitly reject the mental-state framework of dynamic semantics from the start—his scorekeeping model is designed as an alternative to representational approaches, not as something to be reconciled with Stalnaker-style context sets. Meanwhile, theorists who DO work with standard dynamic semantics (like Stalnaker, Heim, or even Yalcin) are not public commitment theorists in the relevant sense—they ground common ground in shared mental states or doxastic conditions, not in commitment structures. The thesis attacks a hybrid position—someone who both (a) treats common ground as PUBLIC COMMITMENTS rather than mental states AND (b) wants to preserve standard presupposition semantics—but this combination doesn't characterize any actual theorist's view. Brandomians don't want to keep the standard machinery; standard dynamic semanticists aren't commitment theorists. The weak point is the characterization of the target: the thesis constructs a position that straddles two incompatible research programs, then argues they're in tension, but no one actually holds both commitments simultaneously.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis may identify a genuine theoretical tension, but it's unclear anyone is actually committed to both sides of it. Without a real target, it becomes a consistency proof about a stipulated position rather than a critique of an actual view.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE.

The objection trades on an overly rigid taxonomy of the dialectical space. Consider three responses:

First, the target is not a named theorist but a *theoretical option* that becomes available once you see commitment-based and dynamic-semantic frameworks as addressing different questions. Brandom may reject representational semantics wholesale, but that's a *choice*, not a *necessity* of the commitment framework. A theorist could hold that common ground is constituted by public commitments (the metaphysical thesis) while still using context-set machinery to *model* how those commitments constrain interpretation (the formal thesis). Compare: you can think meaning is constituted by use-patterns while still employing possible-worlds semantics as a modeling tool. The thesis targets anyone tempted by this hybrid—and the temptation is real, because dynamic semantics has proven extraordinarily successful at predicting presupposition projection, so anyone developing a commitment theory of common ground faces pressure to preserve those predictions.

Second, the objection underestimates how much recent work *does* try to hybridize these frameworks. Asher & Lascarides's SDRT framework treats discourse structure in terms of rhetorical commitments while preserving DRT's dynamic update mechanisms. Maier's work on presupposition in fictional contexts distinguishes mental-state common ground from "conversational scoreboard" common ground and tries to keep standard projection behavior for the latter. Even Gauker, who grounds communication in public salience rather than shared belief, aims to recover standard semantic predictions. These theorists don't wave Brandom's flag, but they *are* trying to do commitment-based pragmatics with dynamic-semantic tools—exactly the combination the objection claims doesn't exist.

Third, the objection misidentifies what "standard dynamic semantics machinery" means here. The thesis isn't targeting commitment to Stalnaker's *metaphysics* of the context set (as shared belief). It's targeting commitment to the *formal apparatus*: the idea that presuppositions are admittance conditions, that contexts are sets of possibilities that get intersected with asserted content, that projection is explained by how complex sentences constrain context-change potential. You can reject Stalnaker's mentalism about what context sets *are* while still wanting this formal machinery to work—and that's the position under pressure. The thesis says: once you reconceive the common ground as commitment-structured rather than belief-structured, you can't just relabel the variables and keep the update rules. The normative architecture changes.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds partially but not completely.

The first response—that the target is a theoretical option rather than a named view—is legitimate but weakens the thesis's dialectical force. If no actual theorist holds the position, the thesis becomes a consistency argument rather than a critical intervention. That's philosophically respectable but less interesting than advertised.

The second response is the strongest: there *are* theorists trying to hybridize commitment pragmatics with dynamic-semantic tools, even if they don't fit the objection's stark Brandom-vs-Stalnaker dichotomy. But the examples are somewhat scattered and don't obviously self-identify as the thesis's target. The defence would be stronger with a clearer demonstration that these theorists are *committed* to preserving standard presupposition semantics rather than just *using* dynamic frameworks opportunistically.

The third response successfully clarifies what's at stake—the formal machinery, not Stalnaker's metaphysics—but this actually concedes the objection's deeper point. If "standard dynamic semantics" just means "some formal apparatus for modeling projection," then almost any theory counts as preserving it, and the thesis loses its bite. The interesting claim is that you can't keep the *specific* apparatus of context-set intersection and admittance conditions once you go commitment-based. But then the target really is narrow: theorists who want *that particular machinery* plus commitment metaphysics.

The defence holds well enough to show the thesis isn't attacking a complete phantom—there is a genuine theoretical tension here, and some theorists are positioned close enough to feel it. But the objection correctly identifies that the target is less populous and less clearly committed to both horns than the thesis suggests. The thesis survives as an interesting conditional: *if* you're a commitment theorist who wants to preserve context-set update semantics, *then* you face this problem. Whether anyone is actually in that position remains somewhat unclear.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The argument's core move—that shifting the metaphysical basis of common ground (from mental states to commitments) requires abandoning the formal machinery that models it—proves too much because it would equally force us to reject successful formal frameworks whenever we change our metaphysics about what they model. Consider: Possible-worlds semantics was originally motivated by a realist metaphysics about modal facts, but we now use it while holding instrumentalist, ersatzist, or primitivist views about modality. Bayesian credence functions were designed to model degrees of belief, but we now apply them to model objective chances, evidential support, and even non-doxastic "degrees of acceptance" in inquiry. Game-theoretic solution concepts model strategic reasoning, but we apply them to evolutionary dynamics where no reasoning occurs. In each case, we kept the formal machinery while radically changing what we think it represents—yet the thesis's logic would say this is impossible, that each metaphysical shift "commits you to rejecting" the formal framework. The weak premise is the implicit claim that formal adequacy conditions are tightly bound to the metaphysics of what's being modeled. If that were true, mathematical modeling in science would be impossible—we couldn't use the same differential equations for fluids and electromagnetic fields. The thesis needs to explain why presupposition semantics is special, why *this* formal apparatus uniquely cannot survive metaphysical reinterpretation when countless others routinely do.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis must explain what makes presupposition semantics uniquely resistant to metaphysical reinterpretation, or accept that its argument generalizes to absurdly prohibit standard scientific and philosophical practice of reusing successful formal models under new interpretations.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mislocates where the formal machinery connects to the metaphysics. The cases it cites—possible worlds under modal anti-realism, Bayesian machinery for non-doxastic phenomena, game theory for evolution—all involve *reinterpreting what the formalism represents* while *preserving the mathematical structure*. But presupposition semantics isn't just a mathematical structure awaiting interpretation. It's a structure whose *operations are defined by the very features the commitment view denies*.

Consider the specifics. In Stalnaker/Heim, presuppositions are admittance conditions: an utterance is defined as appropriate only if its presupposition is already in the context set, where the context set is *the set of worlds compatible with what's mutually believed/accepted*. The update rule is: first check that p ⊆ c (presupposition satisfied), then perform c ∩ φ (assertion updates). This isn't just using set-intersection as a neutral mathematical tool—it's defining appropriateness conditions in terms of *what's already in a shared doxastic state*.

Now try to keep this machinery under commitment reinterpretation. What does "p ⊆ c" mean when c isn't a doxastic state but a commitment structure? The commitment theorist can't say "the commitment that p is already in force"—that would make presupposition projection trivial (every embedded presupposition would require a prior explicit commitment). They need something like "the commitment p is *actionable* given the current scoreboard." But actionability for commitments doesn't work like subset inclusion for belief-compatible worlds.

Here's why: A commitment becomes actionable through *entitlement relations* that depend on the speech-act history—who said what, what challenges were issued, what concessions were made. You can be entitled to invoke commitment p even when p wasn't explicitly established, if it's inferable from the normative score. But this isn't modeled by checking whether p is in a set c. It's modeled by checking whether the scorekeeping rules *license* invoking p given the conversational record. That's a different computational structure—not set-membership but rule-governed entitlement-checking.

The objection's examples don't face this problem because their formal operations don't encode the abandoned metaphysics. When we use possible-worlds semantics under modal anti-realism, we're not using operations that are *defined in terms of* metaphysically robust possible worlds—we're using set-theoretic operations that can be reinterpreted as ranging over ersatz constructions, primitive modal facts, or whatever. The mathematics is genuinely neutral. But "check if p is in the context set" isn't neutral between mental-state and commitment interpretations—it's an operation that makes sense for doxastic states (where propositions straightforwardly are or aren't "in" the shared state) but not for commitment structures (where the question is whether invoking p is *licensed*, not whether p is *in* anything).

The thesis's claim is precisely that presupposition semantics is *not* like the objection's examples. It's not a piece of neutral mathematical machinery that can model either mental states or commitments depending on interpretation. Its core operations—admittance conditions defined over context sets, updates by intersection—are tailored to the doxastic picture. Under commitment reinterpretation, you don't get to keep those operations with a new gloss. You need different operations that track entitlement and actionability instead of set-membership.

Proof: Look at projection through conditionals. Standard semantics says "If A, then B" presupposes p iff either (i) A presupposes p, or (ii) A∪p presupposes that B presupposes p.
