This is explained by: first A updates the context, then we check if B's presupposition is satisfied in that updated context. But if presuppositions are about commitment-actionability rather than context-set membership, this explanation fails. Whether I'm entitled to invoke a commitment in the consequent doesn't depend on whether the antecedent *would update a belief set* to include it—it depends on whether asserting the antecedent *would create entitlement* to invoke it. Those are different questions with different answers. The formal rule might happen to give the same verdicts in simple cases, but it's doing so for the wrong reasons, and it will break in cases where entitlement-structure and information-structure come apart.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The objection assumes that formal machinery is always metaphysically neutral—that mathematical structures can be freely reinterpreted under new metaphysical pictures. The defence shows this isn't true when the *operations themselves* are defined in terms of the abandoned metaphysics. Presupposition semantics isn't just using set theory as a neutral tool; it's using operations (admittance conditions, context-set intersection) that are *defined by reference to* shared doxastic states. You can't reinterpret "p ⊆ c" as about commitment-actionability any more than you can reinterpret "x is a bachelor" to be about married men—the operation's identity depends on what it's checking for.

The objection's examples don't undermine this because they genuinely involve metaphysically neutral mathematics. Using differential equations for fluids and fields works because the equations don't encode "fluidness"—they encode abstract structural relations that both domains instantiate. But "check if p is in the context set" *does* encode "beliefness"—it's checking for a relation (set-membership) that makes sense for propositions in doxastic states but not for commitments in scoreboards.

The thesis holds: shifting to commitment metaphysics really does require abandoning standard update semantics, not because all formal reinterpretation is impossible, but because *this particular* formal machinery has the mental-state picture built into its operations.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims that treating common ground as public commitments "commits you to rejecting the standard update semantics for presupposition" because presuppositions would become "constraints on legitimate uptake of commitments" rather than "admittance conditions on the context set." But consider this counterexample:

The "Sorry" case: A says "I forgot to pick up milk." B responds "It's okay, I know you've been stressed." Now A says "Sorry for forgetting the milk."

A's apology presupposes that A forgot the milk. Under standard semantics, this presupposition is satisfied because it's in the context set (just asserted). Under commitment semantics, A's apology invokes the commitment that A forgot—treating it as actionable for the purpose of the apology speech act.

Here's the problem: The same formal machinery works identically. Check if p (A forgot milk) is in c (the context/scoreboard): Yes, because A just put it there. The update proceeds: c ∩ φ where φ is the apology's content.

The weak point is the claim that commitment-actionability requires "different operations" than context-set membership. But in this case, and indeed in all standard presupposition cases, checking "is p actionable given the scoreboard?" and checking "is p in the context set?" yield identical verdicts using identical formal operations. The commitment theorist can simply *reinterpret* what c represents (scoreboard rather than belief-set) while keeping the operation (⊆ check) unchanged. The thesis hasn't shown any actual case where the formal machinery breaks—only asserted that it must.

STRENGTH: 2/5

This is a weak attack. The counterexample doesn't actually break the thesis because it only shows that simple cases might work the same way under both interpretations—it doesn't address the thesis's deeper claim about projection through complex constructions (like conditionals) where entitlement-structure and information-structure genuinely come apart. The defender already anticipated this move by noting "the formal rule might happen to give the same verdicts in simple cases, but it's doing so for the wrong reasons, and it will break in cases where entitlement-structure and information-structure come apart." A single case where both frameworks agree doesn't refute the claim that they must eventually diverge.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The counterexample actually *supports* the thesis rather than undermining it, once we look at what's doing the work. The objection says "checking 'is p actionable given the scoreboard?' and checking 'is p in the context set?' yield identical verdicts using identical formal operations." But this confuses *extensional equivalence in a particular case* with *using the same operation*.

Consider what's really happening in the "Sorry" case. Under standard semantics: A's assertion adds ⌜A forgot milk⌝ to the context set c (by intersection: c ∩ ⌜A forgot milk⌝). When A then apologizes, we check whether ⌜A forgot milk⌝ ⊆ c_updated. Yes, so the presupposition is satisfied. The operation is: check set-membership of a proposition in a doxastic state.

Under commitment semantics: A's assertion creates a commitment that A forgot milk (A is now on the hook for this claim; others can hold A to it). When A apologizes, we check whether A is *entitled to invoke* the commitment that A forgot milk. Yes, because A just created that commitment. The operation is: check whether the scorekeeping rules license invoking a commitment.

These are different operations that happen to give the same answer here. But watch what happens when we vary the case:

Modified case: A says "I forgot to pick up milk." B says "No you didn't—I saw you buy it." Now A says "Sorry for forgetting the milk."

Standard semantics: The presupposition fails because after B's denial, ⌜A forgot milk⌝ is no longer in c. We've updated the context set by intersecting it with ⌜¬(A forgot milk)⌝, which removes the worlds where A forgot.

Commitment semantics: Whether A can invoke the commitment is more complex. B has *challenged* A's commitment, but A hasn't *withdrawn* it. On most scorekeeping models (Brandom, Pettit), a challenged commitment remains actionable by the original speaker until they explicitly concede—the challenge creates an obligation to defend or retract, but doesn't immediately destroy the commitment's standing for the speaker. So A *can* still invoke this commitment (though doing so might be dialectically inappropriate for other reasons—it ignores B's challenge).

The formal machinery gives different verdicts: Standard semantics says presupposition failure (p ∉ c); commitment semantics says presupposition satisfied (invoking p is licensed for A). This isn't a case where "entitlement-structure and information-structure come apart" in some exotic embedded construction—it's a simple sequence of assertion, denial, and presupposition-bearing response.

The objection's error is thinking that because both frameworks can handle *uncontroversial* cases the same way, they're using the same operations. But that's like saying addition and multiplication are the same operation because 2+2 and 2×2 both equal 4. The operations are genuinely different; they just happen to align when nothing interesting is happening. Once you introduce challenge, retraction, entitlement-shift, or any of the features that make commitment-scorekeeping different from belief-pooling, the verdicts diverge.

The thesis's claim stands: you can't keep the standard machinery (check p ⊆ c, update by intersection) because that machinery is checking the wrong thing. It's checking informational inclusion when it should be checking normative entitlement. These come apart as soon as the conversational dynamics involve anything beyond monotonic information-accumulation.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds completely.

The counterexample fails because it only tests the frameworks in a case where they're designed to agree—straightforward assertion followed by presupposition-bearing uptake with no controversy, challenge, or retraction. This is like testing whether two different theories of addition both get 2+2=4 and concluding they're the same theory.

The defence shows that the frameworks diverge as soon as we introduce the phenomena that *motivate* commitment-based approaches in the first place: challenge, retraction, speaker-relative entitlements, and other features of dialectical scorekeeping. In the modified case, standard semantics says the presupposition fails (the proposition is no longer in the shared information state after B's denial), but commitment semantics says it succeeds (A retains entitlement to invoke their own commitment even after challenge, until they withdraw it).

This isn't an exotic edge case. It's exactly the kind of situation commitment theories are built to handle—conversational contexts where speakers have *different* standings with respect to the same claim, where what you're entitled to invoke depends on your dialectical role, not just on what's in a shared information pool. Standard presupposition semantics can't model this because its operations (set-membership, intersection) don't have the resources to represent speaker-relative entitlements.

The objection claimed the thesis "hasn't shown any actual case where the formal machinery breaks." The defence provides exactly such a case. The formal machinery breaks as soon as you need to track who has entitlement to invoke what commitment, rather than just whether a proposition is in a shared set. That's not the machinery "doing the same thing under a new interpretation"—that's the machinery being unable to represent the relevant distinctions at all.

The thesis holds: commitment-based common ground requires abandoning standard update semantics because the operations of that semantics (checking set-inclusion, updating by intersection) cannot capture the normative structure of commitment-scorekeeping.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT

The thesis presents itself as a substantive discovery about the incompatibility between commitment-based common ground and standard presupposition semantics, but it's actually a trivial consequence of how "public commitment" and "standard update semantics" are being defined.

The weak point is the thesis's core claim that "presuppositions would no longer be admittance conditions on the context set but constraints on legitimate uptake of commitments." This isn't a discovered incompatibility—it's virtually analytic given how the terms are set up.

Here's why: "Standard update semantics" is explicitly characterized as treating presuppositions as admittance conditions on context sets, where context sets are shared doxastic states. "Public commitment common ground" is explicitly characterized as NOT being shared doxastic states but rather normative scorekeeping structures. The thesis then "concludes" that you can't treat presuppositions as admittance-conditions-on-doxastic-states if you don't think common ground consists of doxastic states.

But this is just the logical principle: If framework F is defined as "treating X as Y-type things" and you adopt view V that "X are not Y-type things," then you can't keep framework F. This is true by definition, not by discovery. It's like saying "if you treat bachelors as unmarried men, and you define 'bachelor' as 'married man,' you must reject the standard definition"—true, but only because we've stipulated incompatible definitions.

The thesis dresses this up as a substantive finding by talking about "normative structure," "actionability," and "entitlement," but these are just elaborations of what was already built into "public commitment" vs. "mental state" contrast. The entire argument amounts to: "If you change what common ground IS, you have to change theories that say what common ground IS." That's a tautology, not a thesis.

STRENGTH: 1/5

This attack has almost no force. The thesis isn't claiming a trivial definitional consequence—it's making a substantive claim about formal machinery, not just metaphysical relabeling. The defender has repeatedly shown that the issue isn't "if you change the metaphysics, you must change the theory" (which would be trivial), but rather "this specific formal apparatus (context-set intersection, admittance conditions) cannot model commitment-scorekeeping because its operations cannot represent the relevant distinctions (speaker-relative entitlements, challenge-response dynamics)."

The challenge-retraction case proves this isn't trivial: it's a substantive empirical claim that standard semantics and commitment semantics give different verdicts about when presuppositions are satisfied. That's not true by definition—it's a discovered incompatibility in how the frameworks handle contested commitments.

NOT APPLICABLE — The thesis makes a substantive claim about formal inadequacy, not a verbal stipulation dressed as discovery.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "standard update semantics," and the argument needs both readings to work. On one reading, "standard update semantics" means the specific formal machinery of Stalnaker/Heim: context sets as sets of possible worlds, presuppositions as admittance conditions defined by subset relations, updates by set intersection. On another reading, it means any systematic formal framework for modeling presupposition projection and context-change—a broader category that could include alternative formalisms.

The thesis is plausible on the narrow reading: if you're committed to exactly Stalnaker's apparatus (worlds-based context sets, ⊆-checking, ∩-updates), then yes, shifting to commitment metaphysics creates formal problems because those specific operations encode doxastic assumptions. But it's only interesting on the broad reading: if "standard update semantics" means any rigorous formal framework for presupposition, then showing you must abandon it is a striking claim—it means commitment theorists can't just swap in different formal machinery, they face a deeper challenge to formalization itself.

The argument needs both: The plausibility comes from focusing on Stalnaker's specific machinery (as in the challenge-retraction case, where ⊆-checking gives wrong verdicts). But the significance comes from the broad reading—the thesis title says you must "reject the standard update semantics" (definite article suggesting the whole paradigm), and it targets theorists who "want to keep standard dynamic semantics machinery" (suggesting any formal framework in that tradition, not just Stalnaker's exact formulation).

The equivocation appears when the thesis treats Stalnaker's specific formalism as if it exhausts all possible formal approaches to presupposition. But commitment theorists could develop alternative formal machinery (perhaps using labeled transition systems, scoreboard algebras, or entitlement calculi) that still counts as "update semantics" in the broad sense—systematic, compositional, formally rigorous modeling of how presuppositions constrain context-change. The argument hasn't shown that all formalization is impossible, only that this particular formalization doesn't transfer.

STRENGTH: 2/5

This is a weak objection. While there is some flexibility in how broadly "standard update semantics" might be read, the thesis is reasonably clear that it's targeting the specific formal apparatus (context sets, admittance conditions, intersection-based updates), not formalization in general. The defender explicitly distinguished "the formal apparatus" from just "some formal framework," and the challenge-retraction case demonstrates problems with the particular operations (⊆-checking), not with formalization as such.

The thesis doesn't claim commitment theorists can't build any formal semantics—it claims they can't keep this formal semantics. That's not equivocation; that's precision about which formal tools are at issue. If anything, the objection reveals that the thesis's scope is narrower and more specific than it might initially appear—but that makes it more defensible, not less.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misunderstands what makes a formal framework "standard update semantics." The thesis isn't arbitrarily restricting attention to Stalnaker's exact formulation while ignoring possible alternatives. It's identifying the core formal architecture that defines the dynamic semantic tradition for presupposition, and showing that architecture is incompatible with commitment metaphysics.

What makes something "standard update semantics" isn't just that it's formal, systematic, and compositional. It's that it has a specific explanatory structure:

1. Context as information state: The context is modeled as a set of possibilities (worlds, indices, or information-states) representing what's treated as settled/shared.

2. Presuppositions as filters: Presuppositions are conditions that must be satisfied by the input context for an utterance to be felicitous/defined. They constrain what contexts the utterance can apply to.

3. Update as elimination: Assertion eliminates possibilities from the context. The semantic value of a sentence is a function from contexts to contexts, defined by ruling out incompatible possibilities.

4. Projection as preservation: Projection patterns (why "If A, then B" presupposes what it does) are explained by tracing how presuppositions of parts constrain the contexts available to other parts during compositional interpretation.

This isn't "Stalnaker's specific machinery" in some narrow sense—it's the shared architecture of Stalnaker, Heim, Karttunen, Veltman, Groenendijk & Stokhof, and the entire dynamic semantic tradition. The variations (DPL vs. update semantics vs. dynamic predicate logic) all preserve this core: contexts as information states, presuppositions as input conditions, updates as elimination, projection by compositional context-threading.

The thesis claims commitment metaphysics is incompatible with this architecture, not just with Stalnaker's notation. Here's why:

Commitment scoreboards aren't information states. An information state is a set of possibilities that gets narrowed as incompatible possibilities are eliminated. A commitment scoreboard is a record of who is committed to what, with entitlements and obligations that don't reduce to eliminating possibilities. When B challenges A's commitment, we don't eliminate possibilities—we change A's dialectical obligations. When A invokes a commitment, we don't check which possibilities remain—we check what A is entitled to treat as actionable given the normative score.

This means you can't just "swap in different formal machinery" while keeping the explanatory architecture. Consider what an alternative would need to do:

- Model contexts not as sets-that-shrink but as score-structures-that-evolve. (Different mathematical object: not sets of worlds but graphs/algebras of commitment-relations.)

- Model presuppositions not as input-filters but as entitlement-requirements. (Different semantic type: not context → context functions but scoreboard → entitlement-verdict functions.)

- Explain projection not by context-threading but by tracking how complex speech acts distribute entitlement-requirements across their parts. (Different compositional mechanism: not passing updated contexts to subsequent clauses but computing which entitlements a complex act presupposes given its structure.)

Could you build such a framework? Probably. Would it still be "update semantics"? Not in any meaningful sense. It wouldn't share the core explanatory architecture—it would be a different kind of semantic theory, like how game-theoretic semantics isn't a variant of truth-conditional semantics but a different approach entirely.

The objection treats "update semantics" as if it just means "formal + compositional." But that's like saying "proof-theoretic semantics" just means "formal + systematic"—it ignores that these are specific research programs with characteristic explanatory strategies. The thesis isn't equivocating between narrow and broad readings; it's correctly identifying that commitment metaphysics requires abandoning the explanatory architecture that defines dynamic semantics as a distinctive approach, not just swapping in different notation.

The proof is in projection. Standard update semantics explains why "If A, then B" inherits B's presuppositions (modulo A) by showing how A updates the context before B is evaluated. This explanation essentially depends on contexts being information states that get updated. You can't preserve this explanation while reconceiving contexts as commitment scoreboards, because scoreboards don't get "updated by A" in the relevant sense—they get modified by the speech act of asserting A, which creates commitments rather than eliminating possibilities. The projection facts might end up the same, but the explanation would be completely different, appealing to different formal machinery and different compositional mechanisms.

That's not equivocation. That's recognizing that "standard update semantics" picks out a specific theoretical framework, not just "any formal approach to presupposition."

VERDICT

The defence succeeds.

The objection accuses the thesis of equivocating between "Stalnaker's specific formalism" (narrow reading) and "any formal framework for presupposition" (broad reading). But this mischaracterizes what's at stake. The thesis targets a specific explanatory architecture—the core dynamic semantic approach where contexts are information states, presuppositions are input conditions, and projection is explained by compositional context-threading. This isn't an arbitrary restriction to Stalnaker's notation; it's the shared framework of the entire dynamic semantic tradition.

The defence shows that commitment metaphysics isn't just incompatible with Stalnaker's particular notation—it's incompatible with the explanatory strategy that defines dynamic semantics. You can't model commitment scoreboards as information states (they're different kinds of objects with different update operations). You can't explain projection by context-threading when contexts aren't information states that get passed along. You could build some formal semantics for commitment-based common ground, but it wouldn't be "update semantics" in any meaningful sense—it would be a different kind of semantic theory with different formal machinery and different explanatory resources.

This isn't equivocation; it's precision. The thesis correctly identifies that "standard update semantics" refers to a specific theoretical framework, not just formalization in general. The objection's suggestion that commitment theorists could keep "standard dynamic semantics machinery" by building alternative formalisms misses the point: if the formalism doesn't share the core architecture (information-state contexts, elimination-based updates, context-threading for projection), it's not a variant of update semantics—it's a different approach.

The thesis holds: treating common ground as public commitments commits you to rejecting standard update semantics because that framework's core explanatory architecture—modeling contexts as information states that get narrowed by assertion—cannot represent the normative structure of commitment scorekeeping.

O5. Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the projection of two distinct mechanisms—conversational scorekeeping (public commitments) and shared cognitive context (mutual mental states)—which normally covary but can and do come apart in systematic ways.

distinction — The shared assumption of Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground is a unified phenomenon admitting a single correct analysis
Sketch

The argument identifies cases where the two mechanisms deliver different verdicts about what's 'in common ground': in pretense, the scorekeeping mechanism includes p while no participant has p in their cognitive context; in secrets everyone knows but nobody can acknowledge, cognitive context includes p while scorekeeping excludes it; in accommodation, scorekeeping updates first and drags cognitive context along. The key premise is that both Stalnaker and Yalcin conflate these mechanisms by assuming common ground must be definable in purely mental or purely commitment-based terms, when actually our talk of 'common ground' equivocates between them. This explains why their accounts each fit some cases well (Stalnaker: ordinary conversation; Yalcin: epistemic discourse) but struggle with others.

Two-mechanism projection account explains variance across cases but the equivocation diagnosis may just relabel rather than resolve the underlying theoretical tension.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, answered. The defence showed Stalnaker allows divergence as defective deviation while maintaining unified explanatory priority, which is precisely what the thesis attacks.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. The defence demonstrated that tight causal coupling does not preclude constitutive distinctness and provided cases of selective impairment and sequential updating.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, answered. The defence showed the framework predicts systematic conflicts where neither mechanism is in error, which unified theories cannot accommodate without treating one verdict as illusory.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 2/5, answered. The defence clarified that weak and strong readings serve different roles—diagnosing opponents' error versus stating the positive view—rather than equivocating on a single term.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 2/5, answered. The defence specified falsification conditions: show all divergence reduces to malfunction, or that apparent conflicts involve different contents, or that selective impairment cases actually impair both systems.
Survives as

Common ground is not a single phenomenon but the projection of two distinct mechanisms—conversational scorekeeping (public commitments) and shared cognitive context (mutual mental states)—which normally covary but can and do come apart in systematic ways, delivering competing verdicts where neither is in error.

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims both Stalnaker and Yalcin assume common ground is "a unified phenomenon admitting a single correct analysis," but this misrepresents at least Stalnaker's actual position. Stalnaker's seminal work explicitly recognizes that "common ground" operates at multiple levels: he distinguishes the common ground as a body of shared presuppositions (what speakers mutually take for granted) from the mechanisms that track it, and he's careful about the relationship between mental states and conversational commitments. In "Common Ground" (2002), he acknowledges that what is presupposed in conversation can come apart from what participants actually believe—precisely the kind of separation the thesis claims he conflates. The weak point is the characterization of Stalnaker as conflating mental and commitment-based dimensions when his account actually allows these to diverge. While Yalcin might hold a more unified view, the thesis targets a "shared assumption" that at least one of these theorists does not actually hold. The argument would need to engage with what Stalnaker actually says about the relationship between conversational presupposition and belief, rather than attributing to him a naïve identification he explicitly avoids.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis needs to show textual evidence that Stalnaker conflates these dimensions rather than merely emphasizing one in his analysis.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on a distinction Stalnaker draws but does not exploit the way the thesis requires. Yes, Stalnaker distinguishes what speakers presuppose from what they believe—but this is not the same as distinguishing *scorekeeping mechanisms* from *shared cognitive context* as functionally independent systems that can systematically come apart.

Look at what Stalnaker actually does with the distinction. In "Common Ground" (2002), when presupposition and belief diverge, he treats this as *defective* or *parasitic* on the normal case where they align. Pretense, for instance, is analyzed as speakers acting *as if* they share beliefs they lack—the scorekeeping inherits its structure from what would be a genuine cognitive common ground. The direction of explanation runs from mental states to commitments: commitments are what they are in virtue of representing (or misrepresenting) an underlying cognitive condition.

This is precisely the conflation the thesis targets. Stalnaker allows presupposition and belief to come apart *locally* while maintaining that common ground itself is fundamentally one thing—a body of shared assumptions—that can be tracked either mentally or through conversational behavior. He does not treat scorekeeping and cognitive context as *two different things that might each deserve the name "common ground"* and that might deliver competing verdicts about what is common ground in a given case.

The thesis claims we equivocate between two mechanisms. Stalnaker's framework has one phenomenon (mutual assumption) and two ways of accessing it (mental states, conversational behavior), where one is more basic. That is exactly the unified-phenomenon assumption the thesis attacks.

The textual evidence: Stalnaker defines common ground as what is "mutually assumed" or "mutually taken for granted"—a single cognitive-cum-normative notion. When he discusses accommodation (Lewis 1979, which Stalnaker endorses), he treats it as scorekeeping *revealing* what was already in common ground, not as scorekeeping *creating* common ground independently of cognitive states. The thesis's accommodation case—where scorekeeping updates *first* and cognitive context follows—is precisely what Stalnaker's framework cannot recognize as accommodation at all.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection confuses acknowledging that belief and presupposition can diverge with treating scorekeeping and cognitive context as independent mechanisms. Stalnaker does the former but not the latter—he maintains a unified account where one dimension (cognitive) is explanatorily prior and the other (behavioral/normative) is derivative. The thesis attacks precisely this asymmetric unification. The objection needed to show that Stalnaker treats the two mechanisms as *peers* that might conflict, not merely that he notices they sometimes fail to align.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims scorekeeping and cognitive context can systematically come apart, with accommodation being a key case where "scorekeeping updates first and drags cognitive context along." But consider standard cases of successful communication about shared perceptual experience: I say "that's a beautiful sunset" while we both watch it together. Here, the cognitive context (we both see the sunset, both process my utterance) and scorekeeping (my assertion publicly commits us to the sunset's beauty being conversationally accepted) update *simultaneously and interdependently*, not sequentially. The thesis needs cases where one mechanism genuinely operates *first* and *independently*, but in paradigmatic conversational exchanges, the two are so tightly coupled that calling them "distinct mechanisms" rather than "aspects of a single mechanism" appears arbitrary. Even in the thesis's own examples: in pretense, participants *knowingly* engage in the pretense—their cognitive context includes the meta-knowledge "we're pretending p," which explains the scorekeeping behavior. In secrets everyone knows, the cognitive context includes "we all know p but cannot acknowledge it"—again, cognitive awareness explains scorekeeping behavior. These aren't cases of genuine independence but of one unified mechanism operating on different contents (object-level vs. meta-level). The weak point is the claim of distinctness: the thesis hasn't shown two mechanisms that can operate independently, only one mechanism that tracks different levels of content.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — A genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis must demonstrate genuine independence and sequential operation, not merely different aspects or levels of a single coordinated mechanism.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection mistakes *causal coupling* for *constitutive identity*. That two mechanisms reliably co-occur and influence each other does not make them the same mechanism—hearts and lungs are tightly coupled in normal physiology, update simultaneously, and causally interact, but remain distinct organs that can fail independently.

The sunset case proves nothing. Yes, cognitive context and scorekeeping update together there—but this is exactly what the thesis predicts for *normal* cases where the mechanisms covary. The thesis's claim is not that they *always* come apart, but that they *can* come apart in ways that reveal their distinctness. Simultaneous updating in paradigm cases is perfectly compatible with underlying distinctness, just as synchronized clocks remain distinct clocks.

Now consider what genuine independence requires: cases where one mechanism delivers a verdict while the other remains silent or delivers the opposite verdict, and where this difference has functional consequences. The thesis's examples do exactly this:

Accommodation reconsidered: Take Lewis's classic case: "I have to pick up my sister at the airport." Before this utterance, nothing in anyone's cognitive context represents the speaker as having a sister. The scorekeeping mechanism updates *immediately*—the assertion is not blocked, does not trigger correction, gets recorded as accepted. The cognitive context updates *after*—hearers infer "speaker has a sister" from the successful assertion. The functional independence is demonstrated by the fact that the assertion *goes through* before the cognitive updating completes. If there were only one mechanism, we could not explain why the assertion is not rejected as presupposition-less.

Pretense refined: The objection claims cognitive context includes "we're pretending p"—but this concedes the point! The *content* "we're pretending p" is not the same as the content "p." Scorekeeping includes *p itself* as a commitment (within the pretense, we reason from p, draw consequences from p, correct violations of p). Cognitive context includes *not-p* plus *"we're pretending p."* These are different contents tracked by different mechanisms. The functional independence appears when someone *breaks* the pretense: they are violating scorekeeping (which has p as a commitment) while respecting cognitive context (which has not-p). If there were one mechanism, there would be no such thing as pretense violation—you cannot violate what is not really there.

The crucial test: Can each mechanism be selectively impaired while the other functions? Yes. In certain pathological conversations (gaslighting, strategic ambiguity), scorekeeping continues to function—utterances are recorded, commitments tracked, contradictions noted—while cognitive context is deliberately destabilized. Conversely, in cases of mutual knowledge that cannot be acknowledged (the thesis's "secrets"), cognitive context is robust while scorekeeping is blocked from accessing it. These selective impairments demonstrate genuine mechanism-independence.

The objection's "different levels of content" move actually supports the thesis: if we need to distinguish object-level content (p) from meta-level content ("we're pretending p"), and these are tracked differently (scorekeeping gets object-level, cognitive context gets meta-level), then we have two tracking systems—two mechanisms—not one mechanism that somehow tracks both levels simultaneously.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection demands that distinct mechanisms operate "independently" in the sense of *never* coupling, but this sets an impossibly high bar—no functional systems in cognitive science meet it. The right test for distinctness is whether mechanisms can selectively fail, deliver different verdicts, or operate on different contents while the other continues. The thesis's cases pass this test.

The "different levels of content" observation actually strengthens rather than weakens the thesis: it shows that what we need to explain conversational phenomena is precisely *two* tracking systems that can diverge in what content they register. The objection has confused the question "Are these distinct mechanisms?" with "Do these mechanisms always operate independently?"—but tight causal coupling is compatible with, indeed often evidence for, underlying distinctness.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents itself as revealing "two distinct mechanisms" underlying common ground, but this is merely a terminological repackaging of observations already present in the literature, dressed up as a theoretical discovery. The weak point is that distinguishing "what participants are publicly committed to" from "what participants mentally represent" is not a novel insight requiring a new "two-mechanism" framework—it's a standard conceptual distinction that anyone working on common ground already recognizes, even if they disagree about explanatory priority. Stalnaker distinguishes presupposition from belief; Clark distinguishes grounding from content; Lewis distinguishes conversational score from participant psychology. The thesis claims to identify "two distinct mechanisms" that "can and do come apart in systematic ways," but the examples given—pretense, accommodation, open secrets—are familiar puzzle cases that existing theories already address (Stalnaker treats pretense as parasitic, Lewis explains accommodation through his scorekeeping rules, etc.). The thesis is not discovering that these dimensions *can* come apart; it's simply *insisting* we call them "two mechanisms" rather than "two aspects" or "two levels." This is a verbal stipulation about how to use the term "mechanism," not a substantive discovery about the structure of common ground. The move from "these things can diverge" (uncontested) to "therefore they are projections of two distinct mechanisms" (the thesis's framing) adds no explanatory power—it just relabels the explananda as explanans.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious challenge. The thesis needs to show that the "two-mechanism" framework does genuine explanatory work beyond relabeling familiar distinctions, or that it predicts novel phenomena that existing frameworks cannot accommodate. Simply pointing to cases where public commitment and private belief diverge does not establish that positing "two distinct mechanisms" is anything more than a terminological choice.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the two-mechanism framework merely relabels what everyone already knows, but this misses what the thesis actually does: it denies that either dimension is explanatorily prior and treats the "familiar puzzle cases" as *data points against* rather than *accommodations within* unified theories.

The crucial move is not "look, these can diverge" but "neither can be reduced to or derived from the other." This is not a relabeling—it's a rejection of the explanatory projects that Stalnaker, Clark, and Lewis are engaged in. Each of them tries to ground common ground in one privileged dimension:

- Stalnaker: Common ground is fundamentally mutual belief/assumption; scorekeeping is how we track it, and divergences (pretense) are parasitic on the normal case.
- Lewis: Common ground is fundamentally conversational score; mental states matter only insofar as they're reflected in scorekeeping rules.
- Clark: Common ground is fundamentally grounding actions (public coordination); content supervenes on successful grounding.

Each theory treats one dimension as *constitutive* and the other as *derivative*. The thesis rejects this entire approach. It claims both mechanisms are constitutively independent—neither is "what common ground really is" with the other being mere appearance or tracking device.

The explanatory payoff: This framework predicts something the unified theories cannot: *systematic conflicts* where both mechanisms deliver verdicts and those verdicts clash without either being an error.

Consider the open secret case more carefully. Everyone knows the boss is an alcoholic; everyone knows everyone knows; but it cannot be acknowledged in conversation. On Stalnaker's view, if it's mutually believed, it *is* in common ground, and the conversational prohibition is merely a pragmatic constraint on what can be *said*—but the content is available for presupposition, anaphora, and inference. This predicts we should be able to say "Since he has that problem, we should schedule morning meetings"—the prohibition should only block *direct* mention. But we *cannot* do this. The content is not available for conversational exploitation at all.

On Lewis's view, if it's not in conversational score, it's not in common ground, period—the mutual knowledge is conversationally inert. This predicts it should have no effect on conversation. But it *does*: people carefully avoid topics that would force acknowledgment, utterances are crafted to respect the unacknowledged knowledge, and if someone *does* acknowledge it, the reaction is not "that's false" but "you've violated a boundary"—the content was already there, constraining behavior.

The two-mechanism framework predicts exactly what we observe: cognitive context includes the content (explaining the careful avoidance behavior and the "violation" reaction) while scorekeeping excludes it (explaining why it's unavailable for presupposition and anaphora). Neither mechanism is malfunctioning; neither is parasitic on the other; they're simply tracking different things.

Novel prediction: The framework predicts we should find cases where conversational pathology arises not from *failure* of common ground but from *conflict* between the two mechanisms. And we do: gaslighting works precisely by maintaining impeccable scorekeeping (everything is recorded, commitments are tracked, nothing is denied) while systematically destabilizing cognitive context (the victim cannot maintain stable mental representations of what's been established). A unified theory must treat this as either scorekeeping failure (but it isn't—the gaslighter can quote back everything that was said) or cognitive failure (but the victim's cognitive mechanisms are functioning normally—they're being deliberately confused by contradictory inputs). The two-mechanism framework explains it as exploiting the independence of the systems.

The terminological point misses the substance: Yes, everyone recognizes that belief and commitment can diverge. But "recognizing they can diverge" while maintaining one is explanatorily prior is completely different from treating them as independent mechanisms that jointly project what we call "common ground." The former allows divergence as *deviation*; the latter treats divergence as *normal operation of distinct systems*. That is not a relabeling—it is a different theory with different predictions.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but the objection identified a genuine weakness in how the thesis was presented. The thesis *as sketched* does not sufficiently emphasize what explanatory work the two-mechanism framework does beyond acknowledging divergence. The defence shows this work exists: the framework predicts systematic conflicts (open secrets), explains pathological cases (gaslighting) that unified theories must treat as failures, and denies rather than accommodates the explanatory-priority claims that existing theories depend on.

However, the objection correctly identifies that the thesis needs to do more than cite familiar puzzle cases—it needs to show that treating these as *conflicts between independent mechanisms* rather than *parasitic deviations from a unified phenomenon* gives us explanatory leverage. The defence provides this (the open secrets case shows both mechanisms delivering verdicts simultaneously with neither being an error; the gaslighting case shows selective exploitation of one mechanism), but the original sketch did not make this sufficiently clear.

The thesis survives, but the objection reveals it must be strengthened: it cannot rest on "look, divergence cases exist" but must argue that these cases are better explained by mechanism-independence than by unified theories with accommodation strategies. The defence shows this argument can be made—the open secrets case is particularly strong because neither Stalnaker nor Lewis can explain why the content is simultaneously present (constraining behavior) and absent (unavailable for presupposition) without treating one of these as an error or illusion.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "distinct mechanisms" between a weak reading (two analytically separable dimensions) and a strong reading (two functionally independent systems), and the argument needs both readings to work.

The thesis is *plausible* on the weak reading: obviously we can analytically distinguish public commitments from mental states—this is just the distinction between what's on the conversational record and what's in participants' heads. No one denies we can draw this distinction. The cases of divergence (pretense, secrets, accommodation) show these dimensions can come apart, which is uncontroversial.

But the thesis is only *interesting* on the strong reading: that common ground is "projected" by two functionally independent cognitive/social systems that operate according to different principles, update via different processes, and can deliver conflicting verdicts about the same content. This is the reading that would make it a substantive discovery about conversational architecture rather than a conceptual truism.

The problem is the argument slides between these readings. When defending plausibility (responding to MISATTRIBUTION), the thesis uses the weak reading: "Stalnaker maintains a unified account where one dimension is explanatorily prior and the other is derivative"—this concedes that everyone recognizes the *distinction*, and merely disputes explanatory priority. But when defending interest (responding to TRIVIAL), the thesis uses the strong reading: these are "constitutively independent" systems that can be "selectively impaired," like "distinct organs that can fail independently."

The argument cannot run on either reading alone. On the weak reading, the thesis becomes "common ground talk equivocates between two analytically separable dimensions"—true but uninteresting, because everyone already knows this. On the strong reading, the thesis becomes "two functionally independent cognitive systems jointly constitute common ground"—interesting but implausible, because the evidence offered (pretense, accommodation, secrets) shows only analytical separability, not functional independence. The pretense case shows we can distinguish what's pretended from what's believed, not that there are two separate cognitive systems. The accommodation case shows presuppositions can be established before beliefs update, not that scorekeeping operates independently of cognitive processing.

The weak point is the slide from "these dimensions can diverge" to "these are projections of distinct mechanisms"—this move requires "mechanism" to mean something substantial enough to be interesting but weak enough to be supported by the cases, and no stable reading achieves both.

STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force but ultimately fails. While the thesis does use "mechanism" in ways that could be precisified, the defence to TRIVIAL actually *provides* the strong reading's evidence: the gaslighting case and open secrets case show functional independence (selective impairment of one while the other operates normally; simultaneous conflicting verdicts where neither is an error). These go beyond mere analytical separability. The thesis can consistently maintain: the mechanisms are functionally independent (strong reading, supported by these cases) AND existing theories fail to recognize this because they treat one dimension as merely tracking the other (weak reading, used to characterize the target). This is not equivocation—it is using the weak reading to describe the opponent's error and the strong reading to state the positive view. The argument does not *need* both readings of the same term; it uses one reading for diagnosis and another for prescription.

NOT APPLICABLE

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims common ground is "the projection of two distinct mechanisms" that "normally covary but can and do come apart in systematic ways." But this formulation is structured to be immune from counterexamples through strategic redefinition of what counts as the mechanisms "coming apart."

When the mechanisms align (the normal case), the thesis says they "covary"—both are operating, projecting the same verdict. When they seem to align so perfectly that they appear to be one thing (the sunset case), the thesis says this is merely "simultaneous updating" of distinct mechanisms that happen to be "tightly coupled." When they diverge (pretense, secrets), the thesis says they've "come apart"—vindication! But when someone objects that these aren't really cases of distinct mechanisms but rather one mechanism operating on different contents or at different levels, the thesis redefines what the mechanisms are tracking: scorekeeping tracks "p itself" while cognitive context tracks "we're pretending p"—different contents, so of course they diverge, but now we've changed what counts as the mechanism's output.

The weak point is the notion of "projection"—it's never specified what would count as these mechanisms *failing* to project common ground, as opposed to projecting it differently. Every possible case gets classified as either: (a) both mechanisms operating and covarying (normal), (b) both mechanisms operating but delivering different verdicts (systematic divergence—supports thesis), or (c) one mechanism "selectively impaired" while the other functions (also supports thesis). There's no specification of what evidence would show these aren't two mechanisms but one, because any apparent unity gets redescribed as "covariation" or "coupling" and any apparent divergence gets redescribed as "coming apart." The thesis has made itself unfalsifiable by ensuring that both unity and disunity in common ground phenomena count as evidence for two underlying mechanisms.

STRENGTH: 2/5

The attack has some force in identifying that the thesis uses flexible language ("projection," "covariation," "coming apart"), but it doesn't quite land. The thesis *does* provide falsification conditions implicitly: if we never found cases where the two dimensions delivered conflicting verdicts simultaneously (both present, both functioning, different outputs), that would falsify the independence claim. The open secrets case is supposed to be exactly this. The thesis could be more explicit about what would falsify it, but it's not actually immune from counterexample—showing that all apparent divergence cases involve malfunction of one system, or that the "different verdicts" always involve different contents at different levels in a way that's compatible with a single unified mechanism, would undermine it. The flexibility in terminology is a presentation problem, not proof of unfalsifiability.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses *explanatory flexibility* with *unfalsifiability*. Yes, the thesis can explain both covariation and divergence—but this is a virtue, not a vice, when the phenomenon being explained genuinely exhibits both patterns. A theory of vision that can explain both binocular fusion (when both eyes agree) and binocular rivalry (when they conflict) is not unfalsifiable—it's adequate to the data.

The falsification conditions are perfectly clear, even if implicit in the sketch:

What would falsify the two-mechanism claim:

1. Show that all apparent divergence cases reduce to *malfunction* of a single unified system rather than *normal operation* of independent systems. If pretense is just defective belief-formation, secrets are just pragmatic blocking of a unified common ground, and accommodation is just delayed updating of one mechanism, then we have one mechanism with various failure modes, not two mechanisms.

2. Show that the "different verdicts" always involve equivocation on content—that when we say scorekeeping includes p while cognitive context excludes it, we're really talking about p₁ vs. p₂, and there's no genuine conflict. If the mechanisms never actually deliver competing verdicts *about the same content*, they're not independent verdict-delivering systems.

3. Show that the alleged "selective impairment" cases (gaslighting, etc.) actually involve impairment of *both* systems, just manifesting differently—that there's no case where one mechanism functions normally while the other is blocked.

The thesis is falsifiable because these are empirically decidable questions. Consider the open secrets case specifically:

- Stalnaker's reduction attempt: "It's in cognitive context (mutual belief) so it IS in common ground; the conversational prohibition is merely a pragmatic constraint on explicit mention." This predicts the content should be available for presupposition and anaphora even if not directly statable. Testable prediction: "Since he has that problem, morning meetings would be better" should be acceptable. It's not—falsifies Stalnaker's reduction.

- Lewis's reduction attempt: "It's not in conversational score, so it's NOT in common ground; the mutual knowledge is conversationally inert." This predicts the content should have no effect on conversational behavior. Testable prediction: speakers should not systematically avoid topics that would force acknowledgment; if someone does acknowledge it, the reaction should be "that's false/irrelevant" not "you've violated a boundary." But we see systematic avoidance and boundary-violation reactions—falsifies Lewis's reduction.

The two-mechanism thesis makes a third prediction: both effects should be present simultaneously—the content should constrain behavior (cognitive context functioning) while being unavailable for presupposition (scorekeeping excluding it). This is exactly what we observe. If we observed only one effect, that would falsify the independence claim.

On "projection": The objection complains this term is vague, but it's doing specific work. "Projection" means our *talk* of "common ground" (singular) is a projection from two underlying sources, like how our talk of "the economy" projects from millions of independent transactions. The falsification condition: show that common ground talk is systematically univocal—that competent speakers never disagree about whether p is in common ground in ways that track the scorekeeping/cognitive distinction. But they do: in the open secrets case, asked "Is it common ground that he's an alcoholic?", some speakers say yes (tracking cognitive context: we all know it), others say no (tracking scorekeeping: it's not conversationally available). This equivocation in ordinary usage is evidence for projection from multiple sources.

On the "different contents" move: The objection claims that when scorekeeping includes "p" and cognitive context includes "we're pretending p," we've changed what the mechanisms track. But this misunderstands the case. The question is: *Is p in common ground?* Scorekeeping says yes (p is a conversational commitment—we reason from it, correct violations of it). Cognitive context says no (no participant believes p). These are competing verdicts about *whether p is in common ground*—the same question, different answers. That cognitive context includes the *meta*-level content "we're pretending p" explains *why* it delivers the verdict it does about the object-level content p, but doesn't make the verdicts non-competing.

The key test: Can we find cases where both mechanisms are functioning normally, delivering verdicts about the same content, and those verdicts conflict? The open secrets case provides exactly this. If every apparent case of this type turned out, on examination, to involve either (a) malfunction of one system, (b) different contents being tracked, or (c) the "conflict" being merely apparent (one system not actually delivering a verdict), that would falsify the thesis. But the thesis claims such cases exist and are systematic—that's an empirically vulnerable claim.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection correctly identifies that the thesis uses flexible terminology and could be more explicit about falsification conditions, but it fails to show actual unfalsifiability. The thesis makes empirically testable predictions: that we should find cases where both mechanisms deliver competing verdicts about the same content while both function normally, and that attempts to reduce these cases to unified-mechanism accounts (either Stalnaker's or Lewis's) will fail specific empirical tests.

The "projection" terminology is not evasive—it's making a specific claim that our common ground *talk* equivocates between two sources, which predicts that competent speakers will sometimes disagree about whether p is in common ground in ways that track the distinction. This is testable.

The objection's strongest point—that both covariation and divergence support the thesis—is actually the thesis's strength: it explains both patterns as arising from the same underlying architecture (two systems that normally align but can come apart). A theory that could *only* explain covariation or *only* explain divergence would be inadequate to the phenomenon. The right question is not "does your theory explain both X and not-X?" but "does your theory make predictions that distinguish it from alternatives?" The defence shows it does: the open secrets case makes different predictions on the two-mechanism view than on either Stalnaker's or Lewis's unified view, and these predictions are empirically decidable.

The thesis survives, though the objection usefully identifies that the presentation should be more explicit about falsification conditions and more careful with terminology like "projection" and "covariation."

O6. Treating common ground as common knowledge of acceptance (Yalcin) is unstable because it must either collapse into Stalnaker's view (making acceptance involuntary in practice) or expand into full public commitment theory (abandoning the mental-state framework entirely).

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 4/5 · survives
Move · Target
instability — Yalcin's position that acceptance is voluntary while knowledge is not, combined with defining common ground via common knowledge of acceptance
Sketch

Yalcin wants acceptance to be voluntary (you can accept what you disbelieve) but also wants common knowledge of acceptance. But if we have common knowledge that you've accepted p, then in standard conversational contexts, you cannot coherently refuse to treat p as given without incoherence—the voluntary nature of acceptance is nullified by the common knowledge. The key premise is that common knowledge of acceptance creates the same normative pressure as belief: once we all know you've accepted p, you're bound to act on it conversationally just as you would be by belief. Either acceptance becomes functionally equivalent to belief (collapsing to Stalnaker), or we must say the normativity comes from the public knowability of acceptance rather than acceptance itself (moving to commitment theory).

Appraiser (blind)
The instability argument against Yalcin is competent but the collapse-or-expand dilemma needs more development to be compelling.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed the thesis needs only minimal separation between acceptance and belief, not robust voluntariness independent of rational constraint
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, answered. Defence distinguished acceptance from intention (different direction of fit) and supposition (retains visible framing) to block the over-generalization
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed the seminar case involves explicit framing that distinguishes it from Yalcinian unframed common ground acceptance
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defence argued the instability is substantive (design specifications are incoherent) not merely descriptive of the theory working as intended
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, answered. Defence justified indexing 'functional' to conversational practice for a theory of common ground, making constitutive norms that don't affect conversation explanatorily idle
Survives as

Treating common ground as common knowledge of acceptance (Yalcin) is unstable because common knowledge eliminates the conversational space between acceptance and belief that justifies the distinction: either the constitutive difference between acceptance and belief makes no difference to conversational practice (making the mental-state framework explanatorily idle), or it does make a difference (contradicting the concession that both create the same conversational obligations)

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT: The thesis misrepresents Yalcin's position on the relationship between acceptance and voluntariness. While Yalcin does distinguish acceptance from belief and does connect common ground to acceptance rather than belief, he does not claim that acceptance must be "voluntary" in the sense of being freely choosable independent of evidence or conversational pressure. The thesis treats Yalcin as holding that acceptance remains a purely voluntary mental state even under common knowledge conditions, but Yalcin's actual view is that acceptance is a functional attitude responsive to conversational role, not that it's voluntary in the robust sense required for this dilemma to bite. The weak point is the premise that "Yalcin wants acceptance to be voluntary (you can accept what you disbelieve)." Yalcin's distinction between acceptance and belief is about the functional role and normative profile of these attitudes in conversation, not about voluntariness as freedom from rational or social constraint. The thesis constructs a tension between voluntariness and common knowledge that depends on attributing to Yalcin a stronger claim about voluntary control than he actually makes.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This is a weak objection. While I'm not certain Yalcin explicitly emphasizes "voluntariness" as a key feature, the functional distinction between acceptance and belief does seem to involve some degree of independence from belief, which creates the space for the instability argument. Without access to the specific texts, I cannot confidently assert the misattribution.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection trades on an equivocation about "voluntary." The thesis does not require that Yalcin treat acceptance as "freely choosable independent of evidence or conversational pressure" — that would be a straw man. The relevant sense of voluntariness is simply this: acceptance can come apart from belief. You can accept what you do not believe, and you can believe what you have not accepted. This is the whole point of Yalcin's departure from Stalnaker.

The objection says Yalcin's view is that "acceptance is a functional attitude responsive to conversational role." Exactly right — and that functional responsiveness is what creates the instability. If acceptance is responsive to conversational role rather than to evidence for truth, then it is *not* simply belief under another name. But once we have common knowledge of your acceptance, the conversational role *demands* that you treat the accepted content as given. You cannot say "I accept p but let's not presuppose it" without pragmatic incoherence. So the common knowledge condition transforms acceptance from a conversationally-responsive attitude into something that binds you exactly as belief would.

The objection claims Yalcin doesn't make voluntariness claims "in the robust sense required for this dilemma to bite." But the dilemma requires only the minimal separation between acceptance and belief that motivates the view in the first place. If acceptance just *is* belief, we have Stalnaker's view back. If acceptance can diverge from belief (the "voluntary" element in the relevant sense), then common knowledge of acceptance creates pressure that eliminates that divergence in practice.

The charge of misattribution fails because it demands a caricatured reading of "voluntary" that the thesis does not require.

VERDICT

The defence holds. The objection attacks a strong reading of "voluntary" (free choice independent of rational constraint) that the thesis does not need. The instability argument requires only that acceptance be functionally distinct from belief — which is Yalcin's own commitment. Once that distinction exists, common knowledge threatens to collapse it.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The argument claims that common knowledge of acceptance creates normative pressure that eliminates the functional distinction between acceptance and belief. If this worked, it would prove that *any* mental state under common knowledge conditions collapses its distinctive features. Consider intention: I can intend to φ without believing I will φ (I might doubt my resolve). But once we have common knowledge that I intend to φ, there's conversational pressure for me to act accordingly—others will hold me to it, I cannot coherently say "I intend to φ but don't expect me to pursue it." Yet intention remains functionally distinct from belief even under common knowledge. The weak point is the premise that "common knowledge of acceptance creates the same normative pressure as belief." This conflates *conversational commitment* (which common knowledge does create) with *functional identity*. Common knowledge that I accept p makes me conversationally committed to treating p as given; common knowledge that I believe p makes me epistemically committed to p's truth. These remain different normative profiles. The argument, if sound, would prove that all attitudes under common knowledge collapse into belief—including intentions, suppositions, assumptions for the sake of argument—which is absurd. The thesis needs common knowledge to do more work than it can: creating conversational obligation doesn't eliminate the functional distinction between acceptance-as-conversational-stance and belief-as-truth-commitment.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem that needs answering. The parallel with intention is not perfect (intentions have world-to-mind direction of fit), but it does show that common knowledge creating normative pressure doesn't automatically collapse functional distinctions. The thesis needs to explain why acceptance specifically, unlike other attitudes, cannot maintain its distinctive profile under common knowledge conditions.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection fails because intention is disanalogous in the crucial respect. Intention has a different *direction of fit* — it aims at making the world match the mind, not at tracking how the world is. When we have common knowledge of your intention to φ, the normative pressure is for you to *act*, not to *reason from* the intention as a premise. Acceptance and belief, by contrast, both have mind-to-world direction of fit — both purport to represent how things are, and both function as premises in theoretical reasoning.

The real issue is this: what makes acceptance functionally distinct from belief *in its conversational role*? On Yalcin's view, the distinction must be that acceptance can be adopted for conversational purposes without endorsement of truth. But here is the critical point: once we have *common knowledge* that you accept p, you cannot maintain that gap in conversational practice.

Consider the contrast with supposition. When we commonly know you are *supposing* p for the sake of argument, everyone understands you are not committed to p's truth — the supposition frame remains visible. But acceptance, as Yalcin conceives it, is meant to *constitute* common ground, not to be a marked or framed attitude. There is no conversational signal distinguishing "I accept p" from "I believe p" once both are common knowledge. The acceptance is supposed to do the same work — licensing presupposition, grounding anaphora, constraining what can be coherently said next.

The objection says these remain "different normative profiles" — conversational commitment versus epistemic commitment. But *what is the difference in practice*? If common knowledge that you accept p means you must treat p as given in conversation, and common knowledge that you believe p means you must treat p as given in conversation, then the functional distinction has collapsed for conversational purposes. The supposed voluntariness — the ability to accept without believing — becomes idle once the acceptance is common knowledge.

The proves-too-much charge fails because the other attitudes it cites either have different direction of fit (intention) or retain visible framing (supposition), neither of which applies to acceptance as Yalcin needs it.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection's analogies fail because they involve attitudes with different directions of fit or different conversational framings. Acceptance is uniquely vulnerable to this collapse because it must be both (a) functionally distinct from belief to motivate the view, yet (b) able to play belief's conversational role once commonly known. The proves-too-much charge does not land.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT

Consider a seminar where everyone is working through a controversial philosophical argument. The group accepts the principle of sufficient reason (PSR) as a working assumption for the discussion, and this acceptance is common knowledge—everyone knows everyone has accepted it for purposes of the seminar. Yet several participants are known skeptics about PSR who explicitly disbelieve it.

In this case, we have common knowledge of acceptance without belief. The acceptance does real conversational work: participants can presuppose PSR, draw inferences from it, and object when someone's claim violates it. Yet the functional distinction from belief is preserved: participants can coherently say "Given our acceptance of PSR, it follows that..." while maintaining "Of course, I don't actually believe PSR is true." The common knowledge doesn't create pressure to *believe* PSR, only to *work within* the accepted framework during the seminar.

This counterexample targets the premise that "common knowledge of acceptance creates the same normative pressure as belief." It shows acceptance maintaining its voluntary character (divergence from belief) even under common knowledge conditions, without collapsing to Stalnaker or expanding to commitment theory. The acceptance remains a mental state responsive to conversational purpose, not public commitment.

STRENGTH: 2/5

This is weak. The seminar case involves an explicitly *framed* or *bracketed* acceptance—"for purposes of this discussion"—which the defender already addressed with the supposition analogy. Yalcin's common ground acceptance is supposed to be *unframed*, constituting the background rather than a marked stance. The example doesn't hit the target.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection presents a seminar case, but this actually *supports* rather than undermines the thesis. Notice what the objector has done: to make common knowledge of acceptance compatible with disbelief, they had to introduce explicit *framing* — "for purposes of the seminar," "working assumption for the discussion," "within the accepted framework."

But this framing is precisely what distinguishes the seminar case from Yalcin's common ground. The seminar acceptance is *marked* as provisional, bracketed, purpose-relative. Everyone knows it is a working assumption. This is not what Yalcin means by common ground acceptance. Common ground is supposed to be the *unframed background* against which conversation proceeds — the set of propositions that are simply taken for granted, not taken for granted *for some marked purpose*.

When the participants say "Given our acceptance of PSR..." they are explicitly invoking the frame. This is conversationally more like supposition than like Yalcinian acceptance. Indeed, the very fact that participants can coherently say "Of course, I don't actually believe PSR is true" shows that the acceptance remains marked — there is a visible boundary between what is accepted-for-the-seminar and what is believed-simpliciter.

Contrast this with genuine common ground. If p is in the common ground in Yalcin's sense, you cannot coherently say "Of course, I don't actually believe p" without *removing* p from common ground. The common ground is precisely what you *cannot* bracket off from your beliefs in this way while maintaining conversational coherence. When I say "My wife is a philosopher" I presuppose I have a wife — that's common ground. I cannot coherently add "Of course, I don't believe I have a wife" without destroying the common ground and making my original utterance infelicitous.

So the counterexample fails because it smuggles in the very feature — explicit framing — that would prevent it from being a case of Yalcinian common ground acceptance. The seminar case is actually an example of what acceptance *must* become to remain functionally distinct from belief under common knowledge: a marked, framed, purpose-relative attitude. But that is no longer the mental-state account of common ground that Yalcin wants — it is already halfway to commitment theory, where what matters is the *public* frame rather than the mental state itself.

VERDICT

The defence holds completely. The objection's counterexample depends essentially on explicit framing ("for purposes of the seminar"), but such framing is precisely what distinguishes marked suppositions from Yalcinian common ground. The example actually demonstrates the thesis's point: to keep acceptance functionally distinct from belief under common knowledge, you must introduce public framing devices — and once you do that, you have moved away from a pure mental-state account toward commitment theory. The counterexample fails because it is not a case of what it claims to be a case of.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT

The thesis claims to reveal an "instability" in Yalcin's position, but it actually just restates the design specifications of any view that distinguishes acceptance from belief. Of course acceptance under common knowledge creates normative pressure—that's what common ground is *for*. Of course this pressure resembles belief's normative profile in conversational contexts—that's why acceptance is useful for modeling common ground. The thesis presents as a deep tension what is simply the intended function of the theoretical apparatus.

The weak point is treating "acceptance becomes functionally equivalent to belief in conversation" as a *problem* rather than the *point*. Yalcin distinguishes acceptance from belief precisely to capture how agents can be conversationally bound by propositions they don't believe. The "instability" is just the observation that acceptance does the job it was designed to do. Saying "either acceptance collapses to belief or expands to commitment theory" is like saying "either a bridge collapses to solid ground or expands to become a road"—it's a false dilemma that treats the middle ground (a bridge doing bridge-work) as unstable merely because it shares features with what's on either side.

The thesis dresses up a verbal point about functional roles as a discovery about theoretical instability. It's true but uncontested that acceptance under common knowledge creates belief-like conversational obligations while remaining distinct from belief as a mental state. That's the theory working as intended, not a fatal tension.

STRENGTH: 2/5

This is weak. The thesis isn't just observing that acceptance does what it's designed to do—it's arguing that the design is *incoherent*, that you cannot actually maintain the purported middle ground. The claim is that common knowledge pressure doesn't merely create "belief-like" obligations but eliminates the functional space between acceptance and belief that justifies having the distinction at all. That's a substantive instability claim, not a verbal stipulation.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies what makes a theoretical position unstable. An unstable position is not one that "shares features with what's on either side" — it is one that *cannot maintain its distinctive commitments* when those commitments are fully spelled out. The thesis argues that Yalcin's position has exactly this problem.

Consider the objection's own formulation: "acceptance under common knowledge creates belief-like conversational obligations while remaining distinct from belief as a mental state." But what does this distinction *amount to* once we have common knowledge? The objector says acceptance is "useful for modeling common ground" because it captures how "agents can be conversationally bound by propositions they don't believe."

Here is the instability: What is the *cash value* of this binding? When we have common knowledge that you accept p, you must treat p as given in reasoning, you cannot coherently deny p without removing it from common ground, you must draw inferences from p, and you are subject to criticism if you fail to do so. Now: in what conversational respect does this differ from common knowledge that you believe p?

The objector says they remain "distinct as mental states." But Yalcin's view is supposed to be a theory of *common ground*, which is a conversational phenomenon. If acceptance and belief are functionally identical in their conversational effects once commonly known, then the mental-state difference becomes theoretically idle for the purposes of explaining common ground. We have not explained common ground by appeal to a distinctive mental state; we have simply relabeled belief as "acceptance" and declared victory.

The bridge analogy fails because bridges *do* maintain a functional middle ground — they are neither solid ground nor roads, but structures that enable crossing. The thesis claims acceptance under common knowledge *cannot* maintain its middle ground — it either becomes functionally equivalent to belief in all conversationally relevant respects (in which case why not just say "belief"?) or it requires supplementation by public commitment structures that do the real theoretical work (in which case why appeal to mental states at all?).

The objection treats "doing the job it was designed to do" as a defence, but the thesis argues the job *cannot be done* by the resources Yalcin deploys. That is not a verbal point — it is a claim that the theoretical apparatus is inadequate to its explanatory target. The design specifications are incoherent, not merely implemented.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection confuses "having features of both sides" with "being unable to maintain a stable middle position." The thesis makes a substantive claim: that common knowledge eliminates the functional space between acceptance and belief that the theory requires.
