The objection has not shown this is merely "the theory working as intended" — it has simply asserted that acceptance can remain distinct from belief while doing belief's conversational work, without explaining how that distinction remains non-idle. The triviality charge fails because it does not engage with the core instability claim: that the purported middle ground collapses when its commitments are made explicit.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "functionally equivalent" (or "functional distinction"). On one reading, acceptance and belief are functionally equivalent when they produce the same *conversational obligations* — both require treating p as given, drawing inferences from p, etc. On another reading, they are functionally distinct when they have different *constitutive norms* — belief aims at truth and is responsive to evidence, while acceptance is responsive to conversational purpose and can diverge from evidence.

The argument needs both readings. The thesis is *interesting* only if "functional equivalence" means equivalence in constitutive norms — that would show acceptance really has collapsed into belief. But the argument is *plausible* only if "functional equivalence" means merely producing similar conversational obligations — and that's compatible with the attitudes remaining distinct in their constitutive norms and responsive conditions.

The weak point is the premise that "common knowledge of acceptance creates the same normative pressure as belief." This is true for conversational obligations (both commonly-known attitudes require treating p as given) but false for constitutive norms (acceptance remains responsive to conversational role, belief to evidence). The argument trades on sliding between these senses: it establishes similarity in conversational obligations, then concludes collapse in constitutive norms. But Yalcin can maintain that acceptance and belief are functionally distinct in what makes them the attitudes they are, even while granting they produce similar conversational effects under common knowledge conditions.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This is a serious problem. The thesis repeatedly uses "functionally equivalent" and "functional distinction" without clearly distinguishing conversational effects from constitutive norms. The argument does seem to establish only that the *conversational effects* are similar, but then concludes that the attitudes themselves have collapsed. Yalcin could reasonably respond that attitudes can be constitutively distinct (different formation conditions, different norms) while producing similar behavioral/conversational outputs in specific conditions.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection draws a distinction between "conversational obligations" and "constitutive norms," claiming the thesis illicitly slides from the former to the latter. But this distinction cannot save Yalcin's position, because *for a theory of common ground*, conversational function is what matters.

Return to the theoretical context. Yalcin proposes acceptance instead of belief as the basis for common ground precisely because of how these attitudes function *in conversation*. If the distinction between acceptance and belief makes no difference to conversational practice once we have common knowledge, then the distinction does no theoretical work in explaining common ground. The objection concedes that "both commonly-known attitudes require treating p as given" — but treating p as given *is what common ground is*.

The objector says acceptance and belief can remain "constitutively distinct" even while producing "similar conversational effects." But consider what this means: acceptance is supposedly responsive to "conversational purpose" rather than evidence. Yet once acceptance is common knowledge, what conversational purpose could justify *not* treating the accepted proposition as given? The conversational purpose that made acceptance useful — enabling coordination without requiring belief — is defeated by the common knowledge condition. Under common knowledge, you *must* treat p as given whether you accepted it or believed it. The "responsiveness to conversational purpose" has become idle.

Here is the key point the objection misses: constitutive norms matter only insofar as they generate *different patterns of rational constraint*. If acceptance and belief, once commonly known, generate identical patterns of conversational constraint — and the objection concedes they do — then for purposes of theorizing about common ground (which is constituted by these constraints), the constitutive difference is explanatorily inert.

The objection says the attitudes can be "constitutively distinct" in "what makes them the attitudes they are" even while producing "similar conversational effects." But this is exactly the instability the thesis identifies. Either:

(a) The constitutive difference makes a practical difference to how conversation proceeds — in which case we do not yet have "similar conversational effects," and the objection's concession is withdrawn; or

(b) The constitutive difference makes no practical difference to how conversation proceeds — in which case we are just positing a mental-state difference that does no explanatory work, and we should ask why we need "acceptance" at all rather than just using "belief."

The objection's distinction between constitutive norms and conversational effects only helps Yalcin if constitutive norms can remain distinct *while making no difference to conversational practice*. But then we have abandoned the idea that common ground is explained by these mental states — the real explanation must appeal to whatever *does* constrain conversational practice, which will be public commitment structures, not private mental states with idle constitutive differences.

The equivocation charge fails because the thesis uses "functional" in precisely the right sense for evaluating a theory of common ground: functional = conversationally efficacious. Constitutive norms that make no difference to conversational practice are not "functional distinctions" in the relevant theoretical sense.

VERDICT

The defence holds, though this is the strongest objection yet. The objection correctly identifies that the thesis moves from "similar conversational obligations" to "collapse of the attitudes," and this move does require justification. But the justification is available: for a theory of *common ground*, which is a conversational phenomenon, constitutive norms matter only insofar as they shape conversational practice. If acceptance and belief produce identical conversational constraints under common knowledge (which the objection concedes), then their constitutive difference becomes explanatorily idle for theorizing about common ground. The objection's distinction between constitutive norms and conversational effects does not save Yalcin's position — it exposes exactly the instability the thesis identifies. Either the constitutive difference makes a conversational difference (in which case the objection's concession fails), or it doesn't (in which case the mental-state framework is doing no work). The equivocation charge does not land because "functional" is correctly indexed to the explanatory target: common ground as a conversational phenomenon.

O7. Common ground is the minimal information structure that would rationalize the discourse's trajectory for an interpreter, making it answerable to actual discourse moves but not constituted by participants' mental states.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 0/5 · worst 3/5 · survives
Move · Target
reframing — The shared assumption that common ground is determined by participant-level facts
Sketch

Both sides assume common ground is determined by facts about participants (their acceptances, commitments, or knowledge). But consider: when we interpret historical discourse, we attribute a common ground to rationalize what was said, even when we lack access to participants' mental states. This isn't mere epistemological limitation—the common ground we attribute is constrained by but not identical to what participants accepted or knew. The argument turns on a Davidsonian point about interpretation: common ground is a theoretical posit we attribute to make sense of discourse, characterized by a principle of interpretive charity. In live discourse, participants are themselves interpreters (of each other), so they're implicitly attributing a common ground to rationalize ongoing exchanges. The pretense cases are easy: the common ground interpreter-participants attribute includes pretended content because that rationalizes the moves being made. This makes common ground neither mental nor public-structural but interpretive—a constraint on successful interpretation.

Appraiser (blind)
The Davidsonian interpretive approach is competent but the payoff is incremental—interpretive charity is already widely discussed in this literature.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 3/5, answered. Defence showed that despite theorists' 'context-level' language, their analytical machinery reduces to participant attitudes—the objection's claim they 'already moved beyond' psychologism was too quick.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 3/5, answered. Defence established that rationalizing discourse as failed communication (attributing lack of common ground) defeats the vacuity worry—the interpretive constraint is substantive, not formal.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 1/5, answered. The case actually supported the thesis by showing irrelevant mental-state differences don't affect common ground—objector's own rating acknowledged this was weak.
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defence demonstrated divergent verdicts in pretense, historical interpretation, and modal cases—extensional overlap in easy cases doesn't establish theoretical identity.
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 3/5, answered. Defence identified a Davidsonian middle position between purely descriptive and robustly normative readings, though acknowledged the thesis needs more explicit articulation of this interpretive constraint.
Survives as

Common ground is the minimal information structure that would rationalize the discourse's trajectory for an interpreter (where rationalization means making moves maximally intelligible as coordinated communication under interpretive charity), making it answerable to actual discourse moves but not constituted by participants' mental states.

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims "both sides assume common ground is determined by facts about participants (their acceptances, commitments, or knowledge)" but this mischaracterizes the actual positions held in the common ground literature. Stalnaker explicitly argues that common ground is NOT simply the sum of participants' mental states but rather what is mutually presupposed in the conversation—a normative, context-level construct. Clark's collaborative theory likewise treats common ground as jointly constructed through coordination, not reducible to individual mental states. The "public-structural" view mentioned isn't committed to grounding common ground in "participant-level facts" at all—it's precisely an attempt to locate common ground at the discourse level rather than in individual psychology. The thesis attacks a psychologistic view that its named targets (those holding "shared assumptions" about participant-determination) have already moved beyond. The Davidsonian reframing may have merit, but it's offered as a solution to a problem that Stalnaker, Clark, and others weren't actually facing. The weak premise is the characterization of "both sides" as making this shared assumption about participant-level determination.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis presents itself as resolving a debate, but the debate as characterized doesn't match what major theorists actually hold. The interpretive approach might still be valuable, but not as an alternative to positions nobody defends.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE.

The objection trades on an ambiguity in "participant-level facts." Return to what Stalnaker and Clark actually do when they theorize common ground, not what they say they're doing.

Stalnaker: Yes, he says common ground is what is mutually presupposed, a "normative, context-level construct." But look at his analytical machinery. Mutual presupposition is cashed out as: A presupposes p, B presupposes p, A presupposes that B presupposes p, B presupposes that A presupposes p, and so on. This is an infinite hierarchy of attitudes held by participants. The "context-level" talk is a convenient façon de parler, but the reduction goes through participant attitudes. When Stalnaker asks "what is the common ground after this utterance?" his method is to ask what presuppositions the participants now hold. The theoretical posit is built from participant-level materials.

Clark: The "joint construction through coordination" still bottoms out in what participants mutually know or believe they mutually know. Clark's grounding criterion asks whether participants have sufficient evidence to believe the other has understood—this is still a fact about participants' epistemic states, however collaborative the process that generates it.

The thesis's target is precisely this: even when theorists invoke "context-level" or "normative" language, their accounts remain answerable to facts about what participants accept, know, or presuppose. The Davidsonian move is to say: no, common ground is what an interpreter must attribute to rationalize the discourse, and this is constrained by but not reducerable to any set of participant facts.

The "public-structural" view the objection mentions: if it truly locates common ground at the discourse level independent of participant states, then it's an ally, not a target. But most self-described "public" views (including Stalnaker's official position) still cash out in terms of what's mutually manifest or available to participants—participant-level facts again, just public ones.

VERDICT.

The defence partially succeeds but reveals a crucial ambiguity in the thesis. If "participant-level facts" means facts constituted by participant mental states (even mutual or coordinated ones), then Stalnaker and Clark do rely on these, and the thesis correctly identifies their shared commitment. The objection's claim that Stalnaker "already moved beyond" psychologism is too quick—mutual presupposition is still a psychological construction, just an interpersonal one.

However, the defence exposes that the thesis needs to be clearer about what counts as "participant-level." If some theorists genuinely offer discourse-level accounts that don't reduce to any participant states (even mutual ones), the thesis must either exclude them from its target or explain why they still face the interpretive challenge.

The objection succeeds in showing the thesis is imprecise about its target, but fails to show that target is empty. The defence holds well enough to demand the objection do more work showing that Stalnaker's and Clark's actual analytical practice is independent of participant states in the way the thesis denies.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. If common ground is "the minimal information structure that would rationalize the discourse's trajectory for an interpreter," this criterion applies far too broadly and licenses attributing common ground where there clearly is none. Consider a discourse where A systematically misunderstands B's technical terms, leading to a confused exchange where they talk past each other. An interpreter could still construct a "minimal information structure" that rationalizes this trajectory—perhaps attributing to the common ground various false beliefs about what the terms mean, or meta-level ignorance about their disagreement. The interpretive charity principle would require attributing whatever makes their moves intelligible as conversational contributions. But intuitively, there IS no common ground here in the relevant sense—that's precisely why the conversation fails. The weak premise is that rationalizability-for-an-interpreter is sufficient for common ground attribution. If it were, every discourse trajectory, no matter how dysfunctional, would have some common ground (whatever rationalizes it), making the notion vacuous. The thesis needs common ground to do work distinguishing successful from unsuccessful communication, but the interpretive criterion makes it merely a label for "whatever an interpreter posits," which proves too much—it would make common ground present even in paradigm cases of its absence (mutual misunderstanding, talking past each other, failed communication).

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem requiring substantial response. The thesis risks making common ground unfalsifiable or present everywhere, undermining its explanatory role.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE.

The objection assumes that if an interpreter can rationalize a discourse, that rationalization must attribute common ground. But this gets the interpretive constraint backwards. The thesis says common ground is what rationalizes the discourse *as the discourse it is*—and talking-past-each-other is a different kind of discourse than cooperative information exchange.

Return to the misunderstanding case. What rationalizes the trajectory? Not a common ground rich with shared false beliefs about terminology. Rather: the interpreter attributes to each participant a *different* understanding of the terms, plus ignorance of this difference. This is precisely to attribute *lack* of common ground on the meaning of the terms. The moves are rationalized by the gap, not by a common ground that bridges it.

The interpretive principle isn't "attribute whatever makes the moves intelligible as something." It's "attribute what makes them intelligible as the *kind* of exchange they are." When we interpret the confused exchange as talking-past-each-other, we're saying: these moves make sense as what people do when they wrongly assume common ground they lack. The rationalization attributes a failure of common ground, not a peculiar common ground.

Compare: Davidsonian interpretation doesn't make every utterance true (that would prove too much). It makes utterances *mostly* true, and rationalizes the false ones as errors explicable given what is true. Similarly here: the interpretive approach doesn't make common ground present everywhere. It makes it present where attributing it rationalizes the moves better than attributing its absence.

The pretense case shows this clearly. Why attribute pretended content to common ground? Because treating the discourse as cooperative exchange proceeding on shared information requires it. The alternative—attributing no common ground about the pretense—would make the moves unintelligible as cooperative discourse. But in the misunderstanding case, the moves ARE unintelligible as fully cooperative discourse—and the interpretation reflects this by attributing fragmented or absent common ground.

The thesis doesn't make common ground unfalsifiable. It makes its absence falsifiable: common ground is absent when the best interpretation of the discourse is as failed or fragmented communication. That's a substantive constraint.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds. The objection misunderstands what "rationalizing the discourse's trajectory" requires. An interpreter doesn't just make moves barely intelligible—they interpret what kind of communicative event is occurring. Attributing lack of common ground can be precisely what rationalizes a discourse (as failed communication), just as attributing error can rationalize false utterances (as mistakes).

The "proves too much" worry assumes the interpretive criterion is purely formal: any rationalization will do. But interpretation is constrained by the need to make best sense of the discourse as a communicative phenomenon, and sometimes that means attributing communicative failure, not exotic success.

However, the defence reveals the thesis needs more explicit statement of what "rationalizing the discourse" means. It's not mere logical consistency with the moves, but something like: making the moves intelligible as the kind of communicative exchange they present themselves as being. With that clarification, the vacuity worry dissolves. The objection fails because it assumes a weaker interpretive constraint than the thesis actually requires.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. Consider a conversation between two physicists, Alice and Bob, discussing quantum entanglement at a conference. They have a productive 20-minute exchange about Bell inequalities, experimental tests, and interpretational questions. An interpreter (perhaps a historian of science, or us) can easily construct a minimal information structure rationalizing their discourse: shared understanding of quantum mechanics, Bell's theorem, standard experimental setups, etc.

Now the counterexample: Unbeknownst to anyone, Alice has a rare neurological condition causing her to experience completely different qualia when processing language—what she experiences as "understanding quantum mechanics" has a radically different phenomenological character than Bob's experience. Moreover, Alice's long-term memory encoding is anomalous: she'll remember this conversation entirely differently tomorrow, though right now her responses are perfectly appropriate.

According to the thesis, the common ground is "the minimal information structure that would rationalize the discourse's trajectory for an interpreter." The interpreter attributes shared understanding of quantum mechanics—and this attribution is entirely successful in rationalizing what was said. But here's the problem: Alice's actual mental states (bizarre qualia, anomalous memory encoding) are completely irrelevant to this common ground attribution, exactly as the thesis predicts by saying common ground is "not constituted by participants' mental states."

Yet intuitively, there IS common ground here—they genuinely share understanding of quantum mechanics. The thesis seems to give the right answer but for the wrong reason. It works not because common ground is independent of mental states, but because the *relevant* mental states (conceptual understanding, beliefs about physics) are actually shared, while the *irrelevant* ones (qualia, memory encoding details) differ. The thesis cannot distinguish relevant from irrelevant mental states because it rejects mental-state constitution entirely.

The weak premise is that common ground is "not constituted by participants' mental states." This case shows we need mental states in the story—just the right ones.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This is a weak objection. The case actually seems to support the thesis rather than undermine it. The thesis can simply say: exactly right, the common ground is constituted by what rationalizes the discourse, and Alice's weird qualia are irrelevant precisely because they don't affect what needs to be attributed to make sense of the exchange. The distinction between "relevant" and "irrelevant" mental states is doing no work—what makes states relevant just IS whether they figure in rationalizing the discourse. The thesis has a principled story about why qualia don't matter (they don't constrain interpretation), while the mental-state view must add ad hoc restrictions about which mental states count.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE.

The objection presents what it calls a counterexample but actually demonstrates the thesis's explanatory advantage. Focus on what's doing the work in the case.

The objection says "intuitively, there IS common ground here—they genuinely share understanding of quantum mechanics." Agreed. Now ask: what makes this intuition correct? Not the match in their phenomenology (which differs radically) or their memory encoding (which is anomalous in Alice's case). What makes it correct is that their discourse proceeds successfully as a cooperative exchange about quantum mechanics—their moves mutually cohere, build on each other, exhibit appropriate challenge and response about Bell inequalities.

The thesis explains this straightforwardly: common ground is what an interpreter must attribute to rationalize this successful exchange. The interpreter attributes shared understanding of quantum mechanics because that's what makes sense of the discourse trajectory. Alice's bizarre qualia and anomalous memory don't enter the picture because they don't constrain what must be attributed to rationalize the conversation.

The objection claims we need to distinguish "relevant" from "irrelevant" mental states and that the thesis cannot do this because it "rejects mental-state constitution entirely." But this misunderstands the dialectic. The thesis doesn't need to distinguish relevant from irrelevant mental states—it explains why that distinction seems necessary to mental-state theorists while being explanatorily idle.

Mental-state theorists face a problem: Alice and Bob's mental states differ dramatically (in qualia, in memory encoding, perhaps in computational architecture), yet common ground obtains. They must now add epicycles: "Well, not ALL mental states matter, only the conceptual/doxastic ones," or "Only mental states with the right functional role," or "Only mental states accessible to consciousness in the right way." Each restriction is ad hoc, motivated by the need to exclude cases like Alice's qualia.

The thesis has no such problem. It says: common ground is determined by what rationalizes the discourse. Alice's qualia are irrelevant not because they're the "wrong kind" of mental state, but because they place no constraints on interpretation. Her anomalous memory is irrelevant for the same reason—during the conversation, her responses are "perfectly appropriate," which is to say, they cohere with what's been established and move the discourse forward intelligibly.

The objection's final move is telling: "The thesis seems to give the right answer but for the wrong reason." This is backwards. Giving the right answer without ad hoc restrictions is precisely what we want from a theory. The mental-state view gives the right answer only after adding unprincipled qualifications about which mental states count. The interpretive view gives the right answer directly.

Consider what happens if Alice's memory anomaly were different: suppose mid-conversation she suddenly forgets everything said in the previous ten minutes. Now her responses become incoherent, non-sequiturs. What changes? Not whether her mental states "constitute" common ground in some metaphysical sense. What changes is that the discourse trajectory can no longer be rationalized as proceeding on stable shared information. An interpreter would now attribute breakdown of common ground—and be right to do so, because that's what makes sense of the conversational failure.

The thesis doesn't need to say "now her memory-states matter." It says: the discourse trajectory changed, therefore what rationalizes it changed, therefore the common ground attribution changes. Mental states matter when and because they affect the discourse in ways that constrain interpretation—which is exactly what the thesis predicts.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds completely. This is not a counterexample but a confirmation. The objection tries to show the thesis gives "the right answer for the wrong reason," but actually reveals that the thesis gives the right answer for a principled reason while mental-state views must add unprincipled restrictions.

The case of Alice's qualia and memory encoding is precisely what we'd expect if the thesis is correct: differences in mental states that don't affect the discourse trajectory don't affect common ground attribution. The mental-state theorist must explain why some mental-state differences matter and others don't. The interpretive theorist has a unified explanation: what matters is what constrains the interpretation of the discourse.

The objection's strength rating of 2/5 is accurate—it actually supports rather than undermines the thesis. The "weak premise" identified (that common ground is "not constituted by participants' mental states") is not weak at all; the case shows why that premise is needed to avoid the ad hoc restrictions mental-state theories require.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to offer a substantive reframing, but the core move is essentially terminological. When it says common ground is "the minimal information structure that would rationalize the discourse's trajectory for an interpreter," this is just redescribing what theorists already mean by common ground using different vocabulary. Stalnaker's "mutually presupposed propositions," Clark's "mutually known information," and the thesis's "information structure that rationalizes discourse for an interpreter" all pick out the same phenomenon—they're extensionally equivalent in their applications. The thesis presents the shift from "what participants mutually accept" to "what an interpreter attributes to rationalize discourse" as a deep theoretical advance, but this is merely a change in perspective on the same facts. When we ask "what's in the common ground after this utterance?" both approaches give identical answers—they must, because both are constrained by the same discourse evidence. The interpretive framing doesn't generate different predictions or solve problems the participant-based views couldn't handle; it just relocates the theoretical primitives from "mutual acceptance" to "interpretive rationalization." The weak premise is that this constitutes a genuine reframing rather than a notational variant. Like defining knowledge as "what a reliable process would deliver" versus "justified true belief"—these may frame the issue differently, but without divergent predictions or problem-solving power, the difference is merely verbal.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This attack has some initial plausibility but ultimately fails. The thesis does generate different verdicts: in the pretense case, participant-based views struggle to explain why pretended content enters common ground (participants don't genuinely accept it), while the interpretive view handles it straightforwardly (it rationalizes the discourse). The historical discourse case also shows divergence—we can attribute common ground to rationalize historical exchanges even when we're agnostic about what participants actually accepted. These aren't merely verbal differences; they're substantive disagreements about what determines common ground facts. The thesis isn't just relabeling the same extension but offering a different ground for that extension, with different modal and explanatory properties.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE.

The objection conflates extensional equivalence with theoretical identity, but this conflation is precisely what the thesis challenges. Consider the parallel: "temperature is mean molecular kinetic energy" and "temperature is what thermometers measure" might be extensionally equivalent, yet one is a reduction and the other an operational definition—they have radically different explanatory and modal profiles.

The thesis generates substantive divergences that the objection's own strength rating acknowledges but then dismisses too quickly:

Pretense cases: Participant-based views face a dilemma. Either pretended content is NOT in common ground (because participants don't genuinely accept it), making pretense-based discourse unintelligible as proceeding on shared information, or they must add epicycles about "acceptance-in-the-pretense" or "quasi-belief." The interpretive view has no such problem: pretended content is attributed to common ground because that's what rationalizes participants treating it as shared information in their discourse moves. This isn't a "different vocabulary for the same thing"—it's a different answer to what makes pretense content common ground.

Modal profile: Consider counterfactuals. Suppose Alice and Bob discuss quantum mechanics, but unbeknownst to them, both are confused about Bell's theorem in the same way—they share a misconception. Participant-based view: this misconception IS in their common ground (they mutually accept it). Interpretive view: it depends. If their discourse moves proceed smoothly and are rationalized by attributing correct understanding, then the common ground contains the correct content, and their shared misconception is irrelevant. The common ground is what rationalizes the discourse as the exchange it is, not what's in participants' heads.

Explanatory direction: The participant-based view says: determine what participants mutually accept, then predict discourse behavior. The interpretive view reverses this: examine discourse behavior, then determine what common ground must be attributed. These give different answers to "what explains what?" In cases where participants' mutual acceptances come apart from what rationalizes their discourse, the views diverge on which is authoritative.

The historical case: This is decisive. When interpreting historical discourse, we attribute common ground to make sense of the exchange, constrained by but not determined by evidence about participants' mental states. We might say: "Given how the discourse proceeded, they must have had X in common ground, even though we lack direct evidence they accepted X." The participant-based view cannot say this—if we lack evidence of mutual acceptance, we should be agnostic about common ground. The interpretive view can and must say it—the discourse trajectory itself is evidence for common ground attribution.

Normative force: When participants disagree about what's in common ground, who's right? Participant-based view: there's no fact of the matter beyond what each accepts about what's mutually accepted (and this can diverge). Interpretive view: there's a fact of the matter—what an ideal interpreter would attribute to rationalize the discourse. This gives common ground a normative dimension that participant-based views struggle to capture.

The objection says "both approaches give identical answers" when we ask what's in common ground after an utterance. But this is false. After an utterance in a pretense, the participant-based view must either deny the pretense content is common ground (wrong answer) or add special machinery for pretense-acceptance (ad hoc). The interpretive view simply asks: what rationalizes the subsequent discourse? If participants proceed as if the pretense content is shared, it's attributed to common ground. Different method, different answer in hard cases.

The comparison to knowledge definitions fails. "Justified true belief" and "reliably produced belief" aren't mere notational variants—they give different verdicts on Gettier cases, barn facade cases, etc. Similarly here: the thesis isn't just relabeling. It's offering a different account of what constitutes common ground facts, with different predictions in cases where mutual acceptance comes apart from interpretive rationalization.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds. The objection's claim of "extensional equivalence" is false—the views diverge in pretense cases, historical interpretation, cases of shared misconception, and normative disputes about what's in common ground. Even if they often agreed in central cases (which is expected—both are trying to capture the same phenomenon), theoretical identity requires more than frequent agreement. It requires same explanatory structure, same modal profile, same verdicts in hard cases.

The objection's strength rating of 2/5 is correct, but its reasoning is backwards. It acknowledges the thesis "generates different verdicts" in pretense and historical cases, then dismisses these as insufficient to show "substantive disagreement." But generating different verdicts in systematic ways IS substantive disagreement. The objection needed to show these apparent divergences are illusory or unprincipled—it doesn't.

The "merely verbal" charge fails because the thesis offers a different ground for common ground facts (interpretive rationalization vs. participant acceptance), and different grounds generate different modal and explanatory profiles even when they pick out the same extension in easy cases. The defence successfully shows the difference is theoretical, not terminological.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis equivocates on "rationalize the discourse's trajectory" between two readings that cannot both be maintained. On one reading (call it DESCRIPTIVE), to rationalize a discourse is simply to make its moves intelligible as the speech acts they are—to show why utterance U₁ followed by U₂ makes sense as a sequence of communicative actions. On this reading, the thesis is plausible: we can indeed attribute information structures to make discourse moves intelligible without accessing mental states. But on this reading, the thesis is uninteresting—it merely says common ground is whatever we posit to explain conversational behavior, which is trivially true and doesn't resolve debates about what grounds common ground facts.

On the other reading (call it NORMATIVE), to rationalize a discourse is to show that the moves are appropriate or correct given what's established—to vindicate them as proceeding properly on shared information. On this reading, the thesis is interesting: it would explain why pretense content enters common ground (because it makes subsequent moves appropriate) and would distinguish successful from failed communication. But on this reading, the thesis is implausible: it requires the interpreter to make normative judgments about conversational appropriateness, and these judgments must be answerable to something—either participant intentions/acceptances (collapsing back to the participant-based view) or discourse conventions (which are themselves grounded in patterns of participant behavior).

The argument needs both readings. The defence against PROVES TOO MUCH uses the normative reading (talking-past-each-other is rationalized "as failed communication," not as exotic success—requiring normative standards). But the defence against COUNTEREXAMPLE uses the descriptive reading (Alice's qualia don't matter because they "don't constrain interpretation"—purely descriptive). The weak premise is the unified notion of "rationalize" doing this double duty.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem requiring clarification. The thesis needs to specify what "rationalizing" amounts to, and each precisification faces difficulties. However, there may be a middle position (something like "make optimally intelligible as cooperative discourse") that threads between purely descriptive and robustly normative readings. The equivocation is real but potentially resolvable with more careful statement of the interpretive constraint.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE.

The objection presents a false dichotomy. "Rationalizing the discourse" is neither purely descriptive (making moves barely intelligible) nor robustly normative (vindicating them as correct by independent standards). It's interpretive in Davidson's specific sense: attributing content that makes the discourse maximally intelligible as the kind of communicative activity it is.

Return to Davidson's principle of charity. It's not: "make the speakers' utterances true" (too normative) or "make their utterances intelligible as some kind of behavior" (too descriptive). It's: "interpret so as to maximize agreement and rationality while respecting constraints from behavior and context." This is a constitutive principle of interpretation—not an optional methodological nicety but what determines content attribution.

Apply this to discourse interpretation. To rationalize a discourse is to attribute a common ground that makes the moves maximally intelligible as *coordinated communicative acts*—as participants trying to exchange information, build on what's established, respond appropriately to what's said. This is neither purely descriptive nor externally normative. It's internally normative: the standard of "appropriate response" is given by the practice of coordinated communication itself, not by independent facts about what participants accept.

Against the descriptive reading: The objection says this would make the thesis "trivially true" and "uninteresting." But this misses what's at stake. The thesis claims common ground is constituted by interpretive rationalization, not merely tracked by it. On participant-based views, common ground facts obtain independently (grounded in mutual acceptance), and we use interpretation to discover them. On the interpretive view, there are no common ground facts prior to and independent of what interpretation attributes. This is substantive, not trivial.

Against the normative reading: The objection says interpretive judgments "must be answerable to something—either participant intentions/acceptances (collapsing back) or discourse conventions (grounded in participant behavior)." But this misunderstands interpretive constitution. The interpreter's judgments are answerable to the discourse itself—to the pattern of moves, their sequential coherence, their responsiveness to each other. These constrain interpretation without being reducible to participant mental states or conventional rules.

Consider the talking-past-each-other case again. Why does the interpreter attribute lack of common ground? Not because they consult independent normative standards about "correct" communication. Rather: the discourse moves exhibit a pattern (non-sequiturs, repeated clarification attempts, frustration markers) that is most coherently interpreted as proceeding on incompatible assumptions. The attribution of fragmented common ground is what makes best sense of this pattern as communicative activity.

Similarly, Alice's qualia case. Why don't her qualia constrain interpretation? Not because we've made a purely descriptive judgment that they're causally irrelevant. Rather: in interpreting the discourse as a coordinated exchange about quantum mechanics, nothing in the pattern of moves requires attributing phenomenological differences. The interpretation that makes best sense of the discourse attributes shared understanding of physics, and qualia differences are simply orthogonal to this interpretive project.

The middle position: Rationalizing discourse means attributing content that makes the moves optimally intelligible as participants attempting coordinated communication. This has normative dimension (it distinguishes better from worse interpretations, successful from failed coordination) without requiring external normative standards (the standard is internal to the practice of interpretation itself).

The objection says defences against different attacks use different readings. But check whether they actually do:

- PROVES TOO MUCH defence: Talking-past-each-other is rationalized "as failed communication." This uses the interpretive reading: the best interpretation of the discourse pattern attributes communicative failure, not exotic success. Not purely descriptive (it distinguishes failure from success) but not externally normative (the standard comes from making sense of the moves as communicative acts).

- COUNTEREXAMPLE defence: Alice's qualia "don't constrain interpretation." This also uses the interpretive reading: in attributing content to make the discourse optimally intelligible as coordinated exchange, qualia differences play no role. Not purely descriptive (we're not just noting causal irrelevance) but not externally normative (we're not checking against independent standards of correctness).

Both defences use the same middle notion: interpretation constrained by the goal of making discourse optimally intelligible as coordinated communication.

The grounding worry: The objection asks what interpretive judgments are "answerable to" if not participant states or conventions. Answer: the discourse trajectory itself, under the constitutive constraint of interpretive charity. This isn't circular. Compare: Davidson's radical interpretation doesn't presuppose meanings to discover meanings; it constitutes meanings through the interpretive process. Similarly here: common ground isn't presupposed to interpret discourse; it's constituted through interpreting discourse as coordinated communication.

VERDICT.

The defence succeeds in showing there's no equivocation, but reveals the thesis needs more explicit articulation of what "rationalizing" means. The objection correctly identifies that "rationalize" is doing crucial work and needs specification. But the dichotomy between "purely descriptive" and "robustly normative" is false.

The interpretive reading—make maximally intelligible as coordinated communication—threads between these poles. It has normative dimension (distinguishes better/worse interpretations, successful/failed coordination) without requiring external normative standards (the standard is internal to interpretation). It's not purely descriptive (not just causal explanation of behavior) but not robustly normative (not answerable to independent facts about correctness).

However, the defence exposes that the thesis would benefit from explicitly invoking Davidson's principle of charity or something similar as the interpretive constraint. Without this, "rationalize the discourse" is indeed ambiguous between readings the objection identifies. With it, there's a principled middle position.

The objection partially succeeds in demanding clarification but fails to show the thesis cannot provide it. The equivocation is apparent, not real, once we recognize the Davidsonian interpretive framework the thesis implicitly invokes. Strength rating of 3/5 is appropriate: genuine issue requiring response, but response is available within the thesis's resources.

O8. The voluntary/involuntary distinction between acceptance and knowledge tracks not a difference in mental state type, but a difference between context-internal and context-external sources of commitment.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · wounded
Move · Target
distinction — Yalcin's classification of attitudes by their voluntariness
Sketch

Yalcin thinks acceptance is voluntary (you can accept p for conversational purposes without believing it) while knowledge is involuntary (you cannot know at will). But the real distinction is between commitments whose source is a speech act within this conversation (these feel 'voluntary' because they're created by our discourse moves) and commitments imported from outside (these feel 'involuntary' because they're not up to us conversationally). The key premise is that what Yalcin calls 'accepting p' is really 'p being committed-to on the basis of our in-conversation moves,' while what he calls 'knowing p' is really 'p being committed-to on the basis of evidence available to us pre-conversation.' This reframes the debate: the question isn't about mental state types but about how conversational context relates to extra-conversational epistemic resources.

Appraiser (blind)
Reinterpreting the voluntary/involuntary distinction as about commitment sources is interesting but feels more like a friendly amendment to Yalcin than a fundamental challenge.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed the thesis engages Yalcin's operative framework commitments, not merely his explicit thematizations
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 3/5, unanswered. Defence distinguished application from theft but conceded Brandomian machinery should be acknowledged; this is absorption through narrowing scope
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 4/5, unanswered. Defence added multiple qualifications (domain restriction, commitment-creating vs content-generating, epistemic authority) to avoid overextension; the thesis survived by becoming narrower
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 3/5, answered. Defence successfully distinguished commitment-timing from commitment-source, showing mathematical proof reveals rather than creates constraints
  • TRIVIAL — landed 2/5, answered. Defence showed the thesis achieves ontological parsimony by reducing apparent mental state type differences to commitment-source differences
🔧 Survives as

The voluntary/involuntary distinction between acceptance and knowledge in Yalcin's framework tracks not a difference in mental state type but a difference between commitments created through discourse moves within conversational context and commitments imported as epistemically authoritative constraints from extra-conversational sources—a distinction that applies Brandomian scorekeeping machinery to dissolve an apparent ontological difference into a functional one

Flaw

The thesis required substantial narrowing through multiple qualifications (domain restrictions, commitment-type distinctions, authority conditions) to survive objections, and must acknowledge its Brandomian heritage

full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis attributes to Yalcin a view that acceptance is voluntary while knowledge is involuntary, and that this voluntariness distinction is Yalcin's basis for classifying these as different mental state types. However, Yalcin's actual work on epistemic modals and acceptance (particularly in "Epistemic Modals" and related papers) does not primarily classify acceptance versus knowledge by voluntariness. Yalcin's central concern is with how epistemic modals behave in embedded contexts and what this tells us about information-sensitive semantics. When Yalcin discusses acceptance, it's typically in the context of dynamic semantics and information states, not as a contrast with knowledge based on voluntary control. The voluntariness distinction is more characteristic of work by Cohen or Bratman on acceptance versus belief. The thesis appears to be attacking a position about voluntary acceptance versus involuntary knowledge that Yalcin doesn't centrally defend, making this a debate with a phantom opponent rather than with Yalcin's actual framework.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This is a weak objection. While Yalcin may not emphasize voluntariness as his primary distinction, he does work within frameworks where acceptance and knowledge play different functional roles, and the thesis might be charitably reconstructing an implicit commitment rather than claiming explicit textual support. The reframing offered might still engage productively with Yalcin's broader project even if it doesn't perfectly match his stated concerns.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses explicit thematization with operative commitment. Yalcin need not make voluntariness his "primary distinction" or "central concern" for the thesis to engage his view. What matters is whether the voluntary/involuntary contrast does work in distinguishing acceptance from knowledge in his framework, even if he doesn't foreground it.

Consider three points:

First, Yalcin's dynamic semantic treatment of acceptance inherently involves a voluntaristic element. When acceptance is modeled as updating an information state through conversational moves, the agent is represented as having control over what gets added to the conversational scoreboard. This is precisely the kind of "voluntary" commitment the thesis targets—not psychological voluntariness, but conversational agency. Knowledge, by contrast, enters his framework as a constraint on what's already available, not as something agents add by conversational fiat.

Second, the thesis explicitly offers a *reframing*. It doesn't claim Yalcin uses the word "voluntary"—it claims that what Yalcin treats as a difference in attitude type (acceptance vs. knowledge) is better understood as a difference in commitment source. The objection demands textual fidelity where conceptual engagement is what's offered.

Third, even if the voluntariness language comes from Cohen or Bratman, that doesn't make it irrelevant to Yalcin. If Yalcin's framework inherits or presupposes distinctions others make explicit, the thesis can illuminate that presupposition. The objection mistakes genealogy for validity.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection mistakes the thesis's dialectical strategy. The thesis isn't exegeting Yalcin's explicit claims about voluntariness—it's diagnosing what does the distinguishing work in his framework, whether or not he names it that way. A reframing can be legitimate even when it uses vocabulary the target doesn't employ, provided it captures the functional role of the distinction. The objection would need to show that voluntariness (understood as conversational agency over commitment-source) plays *no role whatever* in how Yalcin's acceptance differs from his knowledge. It hasn't shown that.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT. The distinction between context-internal and context-external sources of commitment is already a central feature of Robert Brandom's inferentialist framework in *Making It Explicit* (1994). Brandom explicitly distinguishes between commitments undertaken through assertional speech acts within a "game of giving and asking for reasons" (context-internal) and commitments that are inherited or preserved from prior contexts (context-external). His account of the "default and challenge" structure of entitlement already tracks how some commitments arise from conversational moves while others are imported as background conditions. The weak point in the thesis is the claim that this reframing is novel or distinctively illuminating for Yalcin's debate: it's actually just applying Brandom's existing apparatus. When the thesis says "commitments whose source is a speech act within this conversation" versus "commitments imported from outside," it's rehearsing Brandom's distinction between undertaken commitments (those we explicitly make) and inherited commitments (those we bring to conversation). Even the specific application to voluntary/involuntary phenomenology echoes Brandom's treatment of how agentive asserting differs from merely inheriting entitlements. The thesis presents as novel insight what is already a well-developed position in the inferentialist tradition.

STRENGTH: 3/5 — This is a genuine problem requiring an answer. While the thesis might still be valuable as an *application* of Brandomian machinery to Yalcin's specific case, it would need to acknowledge the precedent and explain what's gained by the translation. The objection has real force because it challenges the thesis's apparent originality.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection conflates structural similarity with theoretical identity. Yes, Brandom distinguishes undertaken from inherited commitments, but that distinction does different work in a different framework with different explanatory targets. Three reasons the thesis isn't "just applying Brandom":

First, *explanatory direction*. Brandom uses the commitment distinction to build a theory of conceptual content from social-practical scorekeeping. The thesis uses it to *dissolve* an apparent distinction between mental state types. These are opposite projects. Brandom moves from commitment-attribution to semantics; the thesis moves from putative mental state differences to commitment-source differences. That Brandom's machinery can be borrowed doesn't make the borrowing trivial—it makes it a successful reduction.

Second, *the target phenomenon*. Brandom isn't trying to explain voluntariness phenomenology or the acceptance/knowledge distinction. He's building inferentialism from the ground up. The thesis claims that what *looks like* a difference in attitude type (voluntary acceptance vs. involuntary knowledge) is *really* a difference in commitment source. This is a debunking move about a specific philosophical puzzle, not a general framework application. That the debunking uses Brandomian resources doesn't make it "already taken"—it makes those resources newly explanatory for this phenomenon.

Third, *context-relativity*. The thesis's specific claim is about *this conversation* versus *outside this conversation*—a synchronic, context-indexed distinction. Brandom's inherited/undertaken distinction is primarily diachronic (what I bring forward from past contexts versus what I now assert). The thesis needs something sharper: the difference between what's up for conversational negotiation *now* and what's treated as fixed input. This isn't quite Brandom's distinction, even if it's Brandom-adjacent.

The objection treats conceptual tools as non-reusable: if Brandom has a commitment-source distinction, no one else can use commitment-source to explain anything. But philosophical progress often involves recognizing that Framework A's primitive can explain Framework B's phenomenon. That's application, not theft.

VERDICT

The defence holds, but barely. The thesis survives because explaining voluntariness phenomenology via commitment-source is genuinely different from Brandom's project, even if it uses his tools. However, the thesis would be *much stronger* if it explicitly acknowledged the Brandomian machinery and argued for why this application is non-trivial. As it stands, the thesis looks like it's presenting as novel what should be credited as a Brandom-inspired dissolution. The objection doesn't kill the thesis, but it reveals a serious presentational weakness: the thesis needs to say "following Brandom's distinction between X and Y, we can now explain Yalcin's puzzle about Z" rather than implying the distinction itself is the contribution. The substantive move—that voluntariness tracks commitment-source rather than mental state type—can survive, but only if properly situated in the inferentialist tradition it's drawing from.

KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims that what appears to be a voluntary/involuntary distinction between acceptance and knowledge is really a distinction between context-internal and context-external sources of commitment. But if this reframing works, it would apply far too broadly and collapse distinctions we need to preserve. Consider: believing that it's raining (based on looking outside before the conversation) and desiring that it rain (a preference I bring to the conversation) are both context-external sources of commitment. By the thesis's logic, both should feel equally "involuntary" since neither is created by our discourse moves. Yet desires paradigmatically feel voluntary in a way beliefs don't—I can decide what to want for conversational purposes, but I can't decide what to believe. Similarly, remembering that Paris is in France (context-external) and imagining that Paris is in Germany (context-internal, created by our hypothetical reasoning) should pattern with knowledge and acceptance respectively. But memory doesn't feel involuntary in the same way knowledge does, and imagination doesn't feel voluntary in the way acceptance does. The weak point is the premise that context-internal versus context-external source suffices to explain the voluntary/involuntary phenomenology. If it did suffice, we'd expect all context-external commitments (beliefs, desires, memories, perceptions) to feel involuntary and all context-internal ones (acceptances, suppositions, imaginings, stipulations) to feel voluntary. But they don't pattern that way. The distinction proves too much—it would wrongly predict uniform phenomenology within each category.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem requiring a substantial answer. The thesis needs to explain why its proposed distinction tracks voluntariness for the acceptance/knowledge pair specifically without generating false predictions about other mental states that also divide along context-internal/external lines.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The objection assumes the thesis claims context-source *alone* explains voluntariness phenomenology across all mental states. But the thesis is narrower: it claims that *within the specific domain of epistemic commitments that Yalcin is theorizing*, what looks like a voluntary/involuntary difference between acceptance and knowledge is actually a context-source difference. This doesn't commit to explaining all voluntariness phenomenology everywhere.

Three lines of defence:

First, *domain restriction*. The thesis targets "acceptance and knowledge"—both epistemic attitudes toward propositions in Yalcin's framework. Desires aren't epistemic commitments; they're conative attitudes with different functional roles. The thesis can consistently hold that context-source explains the voluntary/involuntary contrast *for epistemic attitudes* without claiming it explains voluntariness for desires, intentions, or other attitude types. The objection's counterexamples (desire, imagination) switch domains. That's not "proving too much"—that's showing the explanation has boundaries.

Second, *the memory case backfires*. The objection says "memory doesn't feel involuntary in the same way knowledge does," but this actually *supports* the thesis. Remembering that Paris is in France feels less involuntary than knowing it *precisely because* memory can be conversationally deployed—I can choose whether to bring this memory into our discussion, whether to assert it, whether to let it guide my commitments here. The phenomenological difference between memory and knowledge isn't a counterexample; it's evidence that even among context-external resources, those that can be selectively mobilized in conversation feel less involuntary than those that constrain us automatically. The thesis can accommodate this: knowledge isn't just context-external, it's *epistemically authoritative* context-external input—it's what we *must* defer to, not merely what we happen to bring.

Third, *imagination versus acceptance*. The objection claims imagination (context-internal) doesn't feel voluntary like acceptance does. But there's a crucial difference: imaginative content typically doesn't create *commitments* in the scorekeeping sense. When I imagine Paris is in Germany, I'm not committing to defend that claim or treat it as a premise for inference in our conversation—I'm bracketing it as mere supposition. Acceptance, by contrast, *does* create such commitments. So the thesis can distinguish: context-internal *commitment-creation* feels voluntary; context-internal *content-generation without commitment* (like mere imagining) doesn't. The voluntariness tracks commitment-source specifically, not just content-source.

The objection's force depends on treating the thesis as a universal theory of voluntariness. But the thesis is a *local* explanation: it says that *for the acceptance/knowledge contrast Yalcin draws*, the apparent voluntary/involuntary difference reduces to commitment-source difference. Other mental states may involve other factors (conative vs. epistemic role, commitment-creating vs. non-commitment-creating, defeasible vs. authoritative status). The thesis doesn't "prove too much" unless it claims more than it does.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds, but reveals that the thesis needs crucial clarifications. The objection is right that context-source alone can't explain all voluntariness phenomenology across all mental states. But the thesis doesn't need that strong claim. It needs only that *within epistemic attitudes in Yalcin's framework*, the voluntary/involuntary contrast tracks context-source.

However, the defence exposes three things the thesis must make explicit to survive:

1. The domain restriction to epistemic commitments (not desires, intentions, etc.)
2. The distinction between commitment-creating and merely content-generating mental acts (acceptance vs. mere imagining)
3. The special status of knowledge as not just context-external but *epistemically authoritative*—what constrains rather than what merely informs

Without these qualifications, the objection would succeed. With them, the thesis survives but becomes more complex: the explanation isn't just "context-internal vs. context-external," but "context-internal commitment-creation vs. context-external authoritative epistemic constraint." That's still a commitment-source story, but it's more nuanced than the original formulation suggests.

The thesis lives, but it must acknowledge these refinements or face death by overextension.

KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims that the voluntary/involuntary distinction tracks context-internal versus context-external sources of commitment. But consider this counterexample: mathematical proof within a conversation.

Suppose we're discussing whether the square root of 2 is irrational. I work through the proof during our conversation—constructing the reductio, deriving the contradiction, concluding irrationality. This proof is paradigmatically context-internal: it's created by our discourse moves right here, right now. The commitment to √2's irrationality arises from reasoning I perform within this very conversation, not from something I imported.

Yet this commitment feels completely *involuntary*. Once I see the proof, I cannot help but know that √2 is irrational. I cannot accept it "for conversational purposes" while withholding belief. The proof compels assent in exactly the way the thesis associates with context-external knowledge, not context-internal acceptance.

The weak point is the premise that context-internal commitments feel voluntary while context-external ones feel involuntary. Mathematical proof generated in conversation is context-internal by any reasonable measure (it's created by our discourse moves, not imported from outside), yet it produces knowledge with the full involuntary phenomenology. The source being internal to our conversation doesn't make the resulting commitment feel voluntary or optional.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious problem. The thesis predicts that commitments arising from within-conversation reasoning should feel voluntary, but mathematical proof shows they can feel maximally involuntary. The thesis needs a real answer about why context-internal proof produces involuntary knowledge rather than voluntary acceptance.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The objection misidentifies what makes mathematical proof context-internal. The proof's *presentation* happens in conversation, but the *source of commitment* is not our conversational moves—it's the logical relations themselves, which are context-external constraints we discover, not create.

Three critical points:

First, discovering versus stipulating. When I work through the proof that √2 is irrational, I'm not *making* it the case that the reasoning is valid—I'm *recognizing* validity that holds independently of our conversation. The logical relations (if √2 = p/q in lowest terms, then p² = 2q², then p is even, then q is even, contradiction) aren't created by our discourse moves. They're context-external constraints I'm making manifest. The thesis can distinguish: what's context-internal is my *act of presenting* the proof; what grounds the commitment is the logical necessity itself, which is paradigmatically context-external. The commitment-source is the mathematical facts, not our conversational activity.

Second, the timing fallacy. The objection assumes that because the proof happens temporally within our conversation, its source must be context-internal. But "source of commitment" isn't about when I voice something—it's about what makes it commitment-worthy. I might first learn my friend's name during our conversation, but the source of my commitment to that name isn't our conversation—it's the fact about their identity. Similarly, I might first work through a proof in conversation, but what I'm working through are logical relations that exist independently. The thesis distinguishes temporal occurrence from normative ground.

Third, the proof constrains us both. Here's the key phenomenological test: when I present a valid proof, you cannot reject the conclusion while accepting the premises without conversational fault. The proof's force is *shared constraint*, not my personal commitment. This is exactly what the thesis predicts for context-external sources: they're not "up to us" conversationally because they're imported as binding on all parties. Compare genuine context-internal acceptance: if I say "let's accept for argument's sake that √2 is rational," you can decline without logical fault—that's a conversational proposal, not a discovered constraint. The proof's involuntariness comes from its being a context-external constraint we're jointly recognizing, not a context-internal commitment we're jointly creating.

The objection's force depends on conflating "happens during conversation" with "has its source in conversational moves." Mathematical proof is activity within conversation that makes manifest context-external logical constraints. The commitment-source is those constraints, not our activity. That's why it feels involuntary despite being reasoned through conversationally.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds. The objection treats "context-internal" too coarsely, as if anything that temporally occurs within conversation must have its source in conversational moves. But the thesis is about commitment-*source*, not commitment-*timing*.

Mathematical proof is actually the perfect case for the thesis: it feels involuntary precisely *because* its source is context-external logical necessity, even though we work through it in conversation. The proof doesn't create the logical relations; it reveals them. We're not making √2 irrational by our discourse moves; we're recognizing irrationality that constrains us from outside our conversational agency.

The objection would succeed only if mathematical proof were genuinely creating logical facts through conversational fiat—if the validity of the reasoning depended on our agreeing to count it as valid, the way acceptance depends on our agreeing to treat something as a premise. But that's not how mathematical proof works. The proof's compulsory force comes from its tracking context-external necessity.

This actually strengthens the thesis: it can explain why mathematical knowledge acquired in conversation still feels involuntary (because the source is logical constraint, not conversational stipulation), while conversational acceptance feels voluntary (because its source is our discourse moves themselves). The distinction holds.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims to offer a substantive reframing of the voluntary/involuntary distinction, but it actually just relabels the phenomenon without explaining it. The weak point is that "context-internal source of commitment" and "context-external source of commitment" are merely technical redescriptions of "voluntary" and "involuntary" respectively—the thesis stipulates that we should call voluntary commitments "context-internal" and involuntary ones "context-external," but this is just terminological substitution, not theoretical progress.

Consider what's actually claimed: acceptance feels voluntary and comes from "speech acts within this conversation"; knowledge feels involuntary and comes from "evidence available pre-conversation." But *why* does context-internality produce voluntary phenomenology? *Why* does context-externality produce involuntary phenomenology? The thesis offers no mechanism, no deeper explanation—it simply asserts the correlation and declares victory. This is like saying "the distinction between hot and cold tracks not temperature but molecular kinetic energy" when molecular kinetic energy *just is* what we mean by temperature. Similarly, "what's up to us conversationally" versus "what constrains us from outside" is just a spatial metaphor for voluntary versus involuntary—it's the same distinction wearing different clothes.

The thesis presents as if it's revealed something hidden about Yalcin's framework, but it's actually just offered a synonym. "Context-internal commitment-source" doesn't explain voluntariness; it's just another way of saying "the kind of commitment that feels voluntary." The purported reduction is really just a verbal stipulation dressed as discovery.

STRENGTH: 2/5 — This attack has some force but ultimately fails. While the thesis could be clearer about the explanatory mechanism, it does more than merely relabel. The context-internal/external distinction points to a structural feature of conversational scorekeeping (what's created by discourse moves versus what's imported as constraint) that can ground the voluntary/involuntary phenomenology. The thesis isn't just saying "voluntary = context-internal by definition"; it's claiming that the phenomenology of voluntariness arises from whether commitments are generated by our conversational agency or imposed from outside it. That's a substantive claim about what grounds the phenomenology, not just a verbal substitution. The attack would succeed only if there were literally no explanatory gain from the reframing, but the shift from mental state types to commitment sources does change what we're looking for in an account of these attitudes.

DEFENDER

[DEFENDER] BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses explanatory reduction with mere relabeling by ignoring what the thesis actually explains: not voluntariness itself, but why we *mistakenly thought* we were dealing with different mental state types.

Three decisive points:

First, the explanandum is misidentified. The thesis isn't trying to explain what makes something feel voluntary—it's explaining why acceptance and knowledge *seemed* to be different kinds of mental states when they're actually the same kind of commitment differing only in source. The voluntary/involuntary phenomenology was Yalcin's *evidence* for a mental state type distinction. The thesis says: that evidence is misleading; the phenomenology tracks source, not type. This is genuine theoretical progress—it dissolves a putative ontological distinction (two mental state types) into a functional distinction (one commitment type, two sources). That's not relabeling; that's eliminativism about mental state kinds.

Second, the mechanism is implicit but real. Why does context-internal source produce voluntary phenomenology? Because conversational agency *just is* the capacity to create commitments through discourse moves. When I accept p for conversational purposes, it feels voluntary because I'm exercising my authority as a conversational participant to add p to our scoreboard. When I know p, it feels involuntary because I'm *recognizing* a constraint that binds me regardless of my conversational moves—I cannot make p false by refusing to commit to it. The thesis points to scorekeeping structure as the ground of phenomenology: what we can create feels optional; what we must acknowledge feels compulsory. That's not a verbal stipulation—it's a claim about how conversational structure generates phenomenological character.

Third, the molecular kinetic energy analogy backfires catastrophically. The objection says this is like claiming molecular kinetic energy explains temperature when they're identical. But that's exactly what successful reduction *looks like*! Before kinetic theory, heat seemed like a sui generis phenomenon (maybe a fluid, maybe a primitive property). Kinetic theory revealed: heat isn't a separate thing; it's molecular motion. Similarly, the thesis claims: voluntary acceptance isn't a separate mental state type from involuntary knowledge; both are commitments, differing only in whether they're generated conversationally or imported as constraints. The objection accidentally endorses the thesis's reductive strategy while thinking it's attacking it.

The charge of triviality assumes that unless you explain why context-source *produces* phenomenology from more basic principles, you've done nothing. But that's an unreasonable standard. The thesis explains a philosophical puzzle (why acceptance and knowledge seemed like different mental state types) by showing the apparent difference reduces to commitment-source difference. That's the explanatory work. Demanding a further account of why source affects phenomenology is demanding a different project—one about the metaphysics of consciousness, not about Yalcin's attitude classification.

VERDICT

The defence succeeds completely. The objection fails to recognize what kind of explanation the thesis offers. The thesis isn't explaining the phenomenology of voluntariness from first principles—it's explaining why a particular philosophical distinction (acceptance as voluntary mental state versus knowledge as involuntary mental state) is misconceived.

The explanatory gain is real: instead of two mental state types, we have one commitment type with two sources. Instead of a mysterious difference in voluntariness between acceptance and knowledge, we have a straightforward difference in whether commitments arise from conversational moves or from extra-conversational constraints. This isn't relabeling—it's ontological parsimony plus functional explanation.

The molecular kinetic energy comparison actually reveals the objection's confusion. Yes, reducing temperature to molecular motion seems "trivial" once you accept the reduction—but that's because successful reductions naturalize what seemed mysterious. The thesis does the same: it shows that what seemed like a deep fact about mental state types (some are voluntary, some aren't) is really a surface feature of how commitments relate to conversational context.

The objection dies on its own sword. By comparing the thesis to a successful scientific reduction, it inadvertently confirms that the thesis achieves exactly what good reductions achieve: showing that an apparent ontological distinction is really a functional difference in a more parsimonious framework.

O9. Conversational scorekeeping generates normative statuses that persist even after all participants disavow them, which demonstrates that common ground cannot be constituted by any configuration of participant attitudes.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 4/5 · worst 4/5 · dead
Move · Target
counterexample — Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's shared assumption that common ground supervenes on participant mental states
Sketch

Consider institutional discourse where a motion has been 'deemed accepted' by procedural rules despite every participant voting against it, or contractual negotiation where an offer remains 'on the table' by convention despite both parties wishing to retract it. The key premise is that these normative statuses (what can now be presupposed, what counts as changing the subject, what would constitute inconsistency) are real features of the conversational situation—they govern what moves are available—yet they are not grounded in any participant's acceptance, belief, or knowledge. If common ground is what explains presupposition licensing and accommodation, and these cases exhibit those phenomena without the mental correlates, then common ground must be something other than a state of participants' minds.

Appraiser (blind)
The persistence-despite-disavowal argument is compelling but covers similar ground to earlier institutional cases without adding sufficient new theoretical leverage.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 1/5, answered. The thesis correctly identifies both targets' commitment to mental-state constitution of common ground
  • TRIVIAL — landed 4/5, unanswered. The examples show only verbal disavowal with functional acceptance persisting, which is unremarkable
  • EQUIVOCATION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The thesis slides between thick psychological rejection and thin verbal disagreement without justification
