full exchange (10 turns)

KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)

ATTEMPT. The thesis claims that Stalnaker's mentalist view commits him to "radical holism" where one participant's lack of a mental state causes ALL presuppositions to fail simultaneously. But Stalnaker's account is more nuanced. In "Common Ground" (2002) and related work, Stalnaker defines common ground as what is mutually accepted *for purposes of the conversation*, not as a global all-or-nothing mental state. The common ground is proposition-specific: a proposition p is in the common ground when participants accept p for conversational purposes. If one participant secretly dissents from some proposition q, this means q is not in the common ground—but it doesn't follow that every other proposition fails. Stalnaker explicitly allows that participants can be mistaken about what's in common ground, and that common ground can be partial or incomplete. The view is that *each presupposition* depends on whether its specific content is mutually accepted, not that all presuppositions stand or fall together based on whether participants are globally "mentally engaged." The thesis attacks a crude version of mentalism where mental engagement is binary and global, but Stalnaker's actual view is proposition-by-proposition.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This is a serious misattribution. Stalnaker's account allows common ground to contain some propositions while lacking others, so the "radical holism" described is not actually entailed by his view.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection misunderstands the structural point. The thesis is not about proposition-by-proposition acceptance but about the *participant structure* of mutuality. Grant that Stalnaker's account is proposition-specific: proposition p is common ground when all participants mutually accept p. The radical holism emerges not from treating mental states as global, but from the logic of mutuality itself.

Consider what "mutual acceptance" requires. On Stalnaker's account, p is common ground only if: (i) each participant accepts p, (ii) each knows the others accept p, (iii) each knows that each knows this, and so on. This is a condition on *all participants* for *each proposition*. Now introduce a participant who is globally disengaged—pretending throughout, or fundamentally absent-minded. This participant fails the mutuality condition not for some specific proposition they reject, but for *every* proposition, because they fail to genuinely accept anything for conversational purposes.

The holism is radical because it concerns participant structure, not content structure. When one participant is pretending, the mutuality condition fails for every proposition, even uncontroversial ones like "we are indoors" or "today is Tuesday." It's not that these propositions are themselves controversial—it's that the *mutuality* cannot be achieved when one participant is fundamentally not in the right mental state regarding any content.

Stalnaker's allowance that participants can be "mistaken about what's in common ground" doesn't help. That concerns epistemic access to an existing common ground. The thesis targets something deeper: whether common ground exists at all when mutuality systematically fails. The proposition-by-proposition structure doesn't prevent holistic failure when the failure is at the participant level.

VERDICT

The defence fails, but not decisively. The objection is correct that Stalnaker's account is proposition-specific, and this does block the most literal reading of "every presupposition fails simultaneously." But the defence identifies a real structural problem: if mutuality is participant-relative and one participant is systematically disengaged, then mutuality fails for every proposition, even if for different (participant-structural) reasons than content-based disagreement.

However, this reformulation weakens the thesis considerably. The "radical holism" now depends on a participant being *globally* disengaged—merely pretending throughout or fundamentally absent-minded. This is a much narrower and less interesting case than the thesis suggested. The thesis loses force because Stalnaker can reply: "Yes, if someone is comprehensively pretending about everything, common ground comprehensively fails. That's a feature, not a bug—such a person isn't really conversing."

The objection succeeds in showing the thesis misattributes a crude view to Stalnaker. The defence shows there's a structural issue remaining, but it's not the "radical holism" originally claimed.

KILLER (TRIVIAL)

ATTEMPT. The thesis presents itself as exposing a problematic *commitment* of mentalist views—that they entail "radical holism about presupposition failure." But once we examine what's actually being claimed, it dissolves into a trivial logical point dressed as a substantive discovery.

The core claim is: if common ground requires mutual mental states among all participants, and one participant lacks those mental states, then the mutuality condition fails. But this is simply what "mutual" means. It's analytically true that if something requires mutuality among a group, and one member of the group doesn't participate, mutuality fails. This is not a discovered commitment of mentalism—it's a direct restatement of what mutuality is.

The apparent force comes from calling this "radical holism" and describing it as "absurd." But there's no holism here in any interesting sense. The thesis isn't showing that mentalism treats presuppositions as interconnected in their content, or that rejecting one presupposition forces rejection of others. It's just pointing out that a relation defined over all participants fails when not all participants satisfy it. That's true of any universal quantification.

The "absurdity" likewise evaporates on inspection. When the thesis says "presuppositions about the day of the week still succeed" even when someone is pretending, this just means we *treat* them as if they succeed for practical purposes. But mentalists like Stalnaker can simply accept that technically, if mutuality fails, common ground fails—while noting that this doesn't prevent conversation from proceeding *as if* there were common ground. The thesis hasn't discovered a commitment; it's stipulated that "failure" must mean something stronger than mentalists need it to mean.

STRENGTH: 4/5 — This significantly undermines the thesis. What's presented as a problematic commitment is really just the meaning of "mutual" plus a tendentious description of the consequences.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis merely restates what "mutual" means and manufactures absurdity where none exists. But this misses the dialectical force entirely. The thesis is not discovering that mutuality requires all participants—that is indeed analytic. Rather, it's exposing that *this analytic truth generates unacceptable consequences* that mentalists have not adequately confronted.

Consider the structure of the argument more carefully. Mentalists face a choice between two horns:

First horn: Maintain that when one participant is disengaged, common ground genuinely fails for all propositions (because mutuality fails). But then you must accept that presuppositions like "we are having a conversation," "today is Tuesday," "we are indoors" all fail—even though the conversation manifestly proceeds successfully using these presuppositions. The objector says mentalists can "accept that technically common ground fails while conversation proceeds as if there were common ground." But this is precisely the reductio. If your theory says common ground fails when the conversation demonstrably succeeds by every functional criterion of success, your theory has divorced the technical notion from the phenomenon it was meant to explain.

Second horn: Say that common ground doesn't really require full mutuality—perhaps it's enough that most participants have the mental states, or that participants are sufficiently engaged. But this abandons mentalism. You're no longer constituting common ground by mental states; you're constituting it by something else (perhaps patterns of conversational uptake, functional role, or normative expectations) and treating mental states as merely typical or defeasible indicators.

The "triviality" objection assumes mentalists can happily accept the first horn—that technical failure is fine so long as we can say conversation "proceeds as if" there were common ground. But what does this "as if" come to? Either it's tracking some other phenomenon (in which case that phenomenon, not mutual mental states, is doing the real work), or it's mere pretense (in which case we've lost our grip on what makes presupposition succeed or fail).

The thesis is not claiming to discover a surprising logical consequence. It's arguing that an obvious logical consequence is *philosophically unacceptable*—that it reveals mentalism is explaining the wrong thing. When a theory entails that paradigm cases of success are technically failures, that's not a feature to be accepted with equanimity.

VERDICT

The defence fails.

The objection is right that the thesis trades on ambiguity about what "failure" means and what theoretical work it must do. The defender's two-horn dilemma looks formidable but actually collapses.

The first horn is not genuinely problematic. Stalnaker can coherently say: "When one participant is secretly disengaged, common ground in the technical sense fails, but conversational presupposition accommodation proceeds because participants are *disposed to act as if* there is common ground, and these dispositions—not the mental states themselves—do the proximate explanatory work in that moment." This isn't divorcing the theory from the phenomenon; it's recognizing that mental states and behavioral dispositions come apart in edge cases, and the theory can acknowledge this without crisis.

The second horn is a false dilemma. Accepting that mental states and functional success can come apart in pathological cases doesn't require abandoning the view that mental states *constitute* common ground in normal cases. Mentalists can say: common ground is constituted by mutual mental states, and when those states are absent, there is no common ground—but conversation can proceed via other mechanisms (pretense, accommodation, inertia) that approximate or simulate common ground's functional role.

The deeper problem is that the thesis assumes any divergence between technical definition and folk success-conditions is automatically a reductio. But this is not how theoretical terms work. "Water is H₂O" doesn't fail because XYZ in Twin Earth scenarios would be called "water" by folk standards. Similarly, "common ground is constituted by mutual mental states" doesn't fail because conversation can proceed without them in edge cases.

The thesis has identified a real phenomenon—conversations can succeed when mutuality fails—but has not shown this is *absurd* for mentalism rather than simply a case where conversational practice outruns the technical notion. The objector is correct: this is triviality dressed as discovery.

KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)

ATTEMPT

The thesis equivocates on "presupposition failure" between a technical sense (not meeting the constitutive conditions) and a functional sense (conversational breakdown).

The argument's plausibility depends on reading "failure" in the technical sense: if common ground requires mutual mental states and one participant lacks them, then the constitutive conditions for common ground aren't met—presuppositions "fail" to have their technical grounding. This reading makes the argument valid.

But the argument's apparent interest—its claimed absurdity—depends on reading "failure" in the functional sense: that presuppositions about Tuesday or being indoors somehow stop working, that the conversation cannot proceed using them, that communicative breakdown occurs. The thesis says it's "absurd" that these presuppositions "fail" when "the conversation manifestly proceeds successfully."

The argument needs both readings. On the technical reading alone, there's no absurdity—just the anodyne point that when constitutive conditions aren't met, the thing isn't technically instantiated (water without H₂O isn't technically water). On the functional reading alone, the argument is invalid—mentalists never claimed that lacking mutual mental states causes communicative breakdown; they can allow that conversations proceed through other mechanisms.

The phrase "presuppositions still succeed" in the thesis reveals the equivocation: "succeed" functionally (the conversation uses them) while "failing" technically (they lack their mental-state grounding). The thesis treats this as a contradiction when it's merely a distinction mentalists can straightforwardly accept.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This seriously damages the thesis. The entire force depends on conflating technical and functional failure—making the conclusion seem absurd by switching between what "failure" means.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis equivocates between technical and functional failure, but this misdiagnoses the argument's structure. The thesis is not conflating two senses of "failure"—it's arguing that mentalism cannot coherently *separate* them in the way the objection requires.

Consider what mentalism is supposed to explain. Stalnaker and other mentalists offer their account as a theory of *presupposition*—a phenomenon individuated by its functional role in conversation. Presuppositions are whatever does the work of: being taken for granted, projecting through embeddings, requiring accommodation when absent, causing zeugma when conflicting, etc. The mentalist claim is that mutual mental states *constitute* the thing that plays this functional role.

Now the objection says mentalists can accept that when mutual mental states are absent, presuppositions "fail" technically but "succeed" functionally—the conversation proceeds using them through "other mechanisms." But this response is not available to a *constitutive* theory. If mutual mental states constitute common ground, and common ground constitutes what's presupposed, then when the mental states are absent, there is no presupposition in the primary sense—only something else doing presupposition-like work.

The water-H₂O analogy actually supports the thesis rather than the objection. If we discovered that in many ordinary cases of successful "water" use, H₂O was absent but conversation proceeded fine, this *would* be a problem for "water is H₂O" as a constitutive claim. We'd have to say either: (a) these aren't really cases of water-talk succeeding, or (b) something other than H₂O constitutes water. The mentalist faces the same dilemma.

The objection's escape route—"other mechanisms" can do the work when mental states are absent—concedes the game. If other mechanisms can successfully do presupposition's functional work without the mental states, then either:

1. Those mechanisms, not mental states, are what presuppositions really are (abandoning mentalism), or
2. There are two completely different things both called "presupposition"—one constituted by mental states (technical), one constituted by these other mechanisms (functional)—and they just happen to usually coincide.

Option 2 makes mentalism explanatorily idle. If the functional phenomenon can be fully realized by non-mental mechanisms, then citing mental states explains nothing about why presupposition works as it does. The mentalist account becomes a description of one possible implementation among others, not a theory of what presupposition is.

The thesis is not equivocating. It's arguing that a constitutive theory cannot treat technical and functional failure as casually separable. When your constitutive conditions are absent but the phenomenon proceeds identically, your theory has failed to identify the real constituents.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it exposes important costs for mentalism.

The objection is ultimately correct that the thesis equivocates, but the defence shows the situation is more complex than the objection suggests. The key question is what kind of theory mentalism is, and here the defence makes a significant point: if mentalism is genuinely *constitutive*, then the technical/functional gap is more problematic than the objection acknowledges.

However, the defence's own argument undermines the thesis in a different way. The defence correctly notes that if "other mechanisms" can do presupposition's work without mental states, mentalism faces a serious challenge. But this challenge is not "radical holism about presupposition failure"—it's that mentalism might be explanatorily idle or false. The thesis claimed to expose an absurd *commitment* (that all presuppositions fail together). The defence has now shifted to arguing that mentalism faces a different problem entirely (that it might not identify the real constituents of presupposition).

This shift reveals that "radical holism" was never the real issue. The real issue—which the defence now articulates—is whether mental states are necessary for presupposition or merely one implementation. But that's a different objection, and one that doesn't involve any holism at all.

Moreover, the defence's dilemma is not as sharp as claimed. Mentalists have a third option: mental states constitute common ground in the fundamental sense, but presuppositional *behavior* can be realized by multiple mechanisms, including both genuine common ground and various simulations/approximations. This is not "explanatorily idle"—the mental states still explain the paradigm cases and set the standard that other mechanisms approximate.

The objection succeeds. The thesis does equivocate between technical and functional failure, and the defence's attempt to argue this distinction cannot be maintained actually abandons the "radical holism" claim in favor of a different objection entirely.

KILLER (UNFALSIFIABLE)

ATTEMPT

The thesis is structured to be immune from counterexamples through systematic redefinition of what counts as a "genuine" test case.

When we point to actual conversations where one participant is disengaged but presuppositions manifestly succeed (people use "today is Tuesday" felicitously, accommodation works normally, no communicative breakdown occurs), the thesis has two escape routes that together make it unfalsifiable:

Escape 1: "Those presuppositions only 'succeed' functionally, not technically—they're not real common ground, just simulations/approximations." This redefines away any apparent counterexample by stipulating that what looks like presuppositional success doesn't count.

Escape 2: "If presuppositions are working, the participant wasn't really disengaged in the relevant sense—they must have had the mental states after all." This redefines away the antecedent condition, ensuring we never actually have a case of absent mental states plus successful presupposition.

The thesis claims mentalism faces "absurdity" because presuppositions "still succeed" when mental states are absent. But every case of apparent success gets reclassified as either: not really success (just functional simulation), or not really absent mental states (the person was engaged enough). And every case of apparent failure gets cited as confirming the thesis.

What would falsify this? A case where: (1) mental states are definitely absent, (2) presuppositions definitely succeed, and (3) this is definitely not a problem for mentalism. But the thesis has already ruled out (3) by stipulation—any such case is automatically deemed "absurd" and problematic. The thesis is protected by making "absurdity" the criterion: if it seems unproblematic, we've misdescribed the case.

STRENGTH: 3/5

This is a genuine problem requiring an answer. The thesis does seem structured to deflect counterexamples through redefinition, particularly the move between "technical" and "functional" success. However, the thesis could respond that this isn't unfalsifiability but rather conceptual precision—distinguishing genuine presupposition from mere simulation is necessary theoretical work, not evasion. Still, the pattern of having an escape route for every apparent counterexample is concerning.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection confuses principled theoretical distinctions with ad hoc escape routes. The thesis is not unfalsifiable—it makes a clear empirical prediction that mentalism cannot accommodate, and the alleged "escape routes" are actually the mentalist's own theoretical commitments coming home to roost.

Consider the dialectical structure properly. The thesis claims: *if* common ground is constituted by mutual mental states (mentalism's commitment), *then* when those states are absent, common ground fails (following from what "constituted by" means). The prediction is that mentalists must either accept this consequence or abandon their constitutive claim. This is perfectly falsifiable: show that mentalism can maintain its constitutive claim while denying the consequence, or show that the consequence is not actually problematic.

The objection treats "Escape 1" (distinguishing technical from functional success) as the thesis's move, but it's actually the *mentalist's* move—one the thesis argues is inadequate. When mentalists say presuppositions only "succeed functionally" without mental states, they're the ones introducing the distinction. The thesis responds: if you admit functional success without your proposed constituents, your constitutive claim is undermined. That's not unfalsifiability; that's pressing the dialectical advantage.

Similarly, "Escape 2" (redefining engagement) is not the thesis's fallback but rather the mentalist's last resort. If mentalists must say "whenever presuppositions work, mental states must have been present after all," they've made their theory unfalsifiable, not the thesis. The thesis is precisely *pointing out* this problem with mentalism: the view becomes untestable if it treats any presuppositional success as evidence of mental states.

The objection asks "what would falsify this?" The answer is straightforward: show that conversations where participants are demonstrably disengaged (pretending, lying, fundamentally inattentive—cases we can verify through their own testimony, neural imaging, or behavioral evidence) do NOT exhibit the pattern the thesis predicts. Specifically, show that in such cases, presuppositions fail in a content-specific rather than participant-structural way. If a pretender's secret dissent from "God exists" makes only that presupposition fail while "today is Tuesday" continues to succeed in the full technical sense (not mere functional simulation), the thesis is falsified.

The thesis makes a definite prediction: mentalism cannot distinguish between content-based presupposition failure (rejecting specific propositions) and participant-structural failure (systematic disengagement) without abandoning the constitutive role of mental states. Show this distinction can be maintained while preserving mentalism's constitutive claim, and the thesis fails.

The "absurdity" is not stipulated as a criterion—it's argued for. The thesis claims it's absurd that unrelated presuppositions fail when one participant is disengaged, and supports this by noting that conversations manifestly proceed successfully by every observable measure. Mentalists can reject the absurdity by providing a principled account of why technical failure without functional failure is unproblematic for a constitutive theory. That would be a substantive response, not evidence of unfalsifiability.

VERDICT

The defence fails decisively.

The objection is correct that the thesis has structured itself to be effectively unfalsifiable, and the defence's response actually confirms this rather than refuting it.

Notice what the defence does: it claims the thesis is falsifiable, then describes what would falsify it as: "show that in such cases, presuppositions fail in a content-specific rather than participant-structural way." But this is exactly what mentalists like Stalnaker *already claim*—that presuppositions are proposition-specific, that common ground contains some propositions and not others, that failure is content-specific. The defence has just described the mentalist's actual view as what would falsify the thesis.

The deeper problem is that the defence tries to shift the burden of unfalsifiability to mentalism: "if mentalists must say 'whenever presuppositions work, mental states must have been present,' they've made their theory unfalsifiable." But mentalists don't need to say this. They can say: mental states constitute common ground in paradigm cases; in non-paradigm cases (systematic pretense, disengagement), common ground is absent but conversation proceeds through other means; this is not a problem because constitutive theories need not claim their constituents are present in every case of superficially similar phenomena.

The defence's demand—"show that technical failure without functional failure is unproblematic for a constitutive theory"—has already been met by the water-H₂O analogy (which the defence earlier tried to appropriate). Constitutive theories routinely accept that their technical definitions can come apart from folk or functional criteria in edge cases. The thesis treats this as automatically problematic ("absurd"), but provides no argument for why constitutive theories of presupposition specifically cannot do what constitutive theories generally do.

Most tellingly, the defence says the thesis predicts "presuppositions fail in a participant-structural rather than content-specific way," but then when presented with mentalism's content-specific account, claims this is either "not real success" (Escape 1) or "not real absence of mental states" (Escape 2). The objection is right: these moves together make the thesis unfalsifiable. Any case of content-specific failure (mentalism's prediction) gets redescribed as participant-structural failure (the thesis's prediction), and any apparent counterexample gets dismissed as not really a case of absent mental states or not really presuppositional success.

The objection succeeds. The thesis is structured to deflect counterexamples through systematic redefinition, and the defence's attempt to reverse the charge only highlights how the thesis has insulated itself from refutation.

KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)

ATTEMPT

The thesis presents itself as exposing a problematic commitment of mentalist views of common ground, but this position is not novel—it recapitulates the core of non-mentalist or "scorekeeping" approaches to common ground already articulated by theorists like Robert Brandom and Craige Roberts.

Brandom's scorekeeping model (1994, *Making It Explicit*) explicitly treats common ground as constituted by *normative statuses* tracked through conversational moves, not mental states. His central argument against mentalism is precisely that mental-state accounts make common ground too fragile and all-or-nothing: if mutuality requires actual mental states, then any participant's disengagement threatens the entire conversational structure. Brandom argues this shows common ground must be a matter of *commitments undertaken* and *entitlements attributed* through public conversational moves, which persist regardless of participants' private mental states.

Similarly, Roberts's (1996, 2012) work on Questions Under Discussion treats common ground as a public conversational structure—a "scoreboard" of what questions are under discussion and what propositions are established. Her account is explicitly designed to avoid the problem the thesis identifies: that mental-state accounts cannot distinguish between a participant's rejection of specific content and their wholesale disengagement from conversation.

The thesis's key move—showing that mental-state accounts entail holistic failure when participants are disengaged, and that this is absurd—is the standard argument for preferring public, normative, or functional accounts over mentalist ones. This is the established dialectic in the literature, not a fresh discovery.

STRENGTH: 4/5

This significantly undermines the thesis's originality. The argument that mentalism makes common ground too fragile and fails to distinguish content-specific from participant-structural failure is the standard motivation for non-mentalist alternatives. The thesis has not identified a new problem but restated the core objection that already drove theorists away from mentalism toward scorekeeping approaches.

DEFENDER

BEST DEFENCE

The objection claims the thesis merely restates established non-mentalist arguments from Brandom and Roberts, but this misunderstands both the thesis's specific target and its dialectical contribution.

First, there is a crucial difference between *motivating an alternative* and *exposing a commitment*. Brandom and Roberts argue that scorekeeping models are *preferable* to mentalist ones for various theoretical reasons—they're more tractable, more explanatory, better suited to certain phenomena. But they do not systematically demonstrate that mentalism entails *radical holism* specifically. The thesis makes a sharper claim: that mentalism is committed to the position that presupposition failure is participant-structural rather than content-specific, and that this commitment generates absurdity in a specific way—all presuppositions failing simultaneously when one participant is disengaged.

Brandom's argument about fragility is related but distinct. He argues that mental-state accounts make common ground epistemically inaccessible and practically unwieldy—we can never be certain what others really believe or accept. This is about *epistemic access*, not about the *holistic structure of failure*. The thesis targets something different: the logical structure of how presuppositions fail when constituted by mutual mental states.

Roberts's QUD framework is designed to handle information structure and discourse coherence, not specifically to solve the disengagement problem the thesis identifies. Her scoreboard is motivated by wanting to track what questions are active and how answers relate to them—this is about *conversational dynamics*, not about whether individual presuppositions can fail independently when participants are disengaged.

Second, even if the general concern about mental-state fragility appears in the literature, the thesis articulates a specific *reductio* structure that may not be explicit in Brandom or Roberts:

1. Mentalism makes common ground constitutively dependent on all participants having the relevant mental states
2. This means a single disengaged participant undermines mutuality globally
3. Therefore ALL presuppositions fail, including uncontroversial background ones
4. But this is absurd—conversations demonstrably succeed with such presuppositions
5. Therefore mentalism is false

This is not just "mentalism is less preferable than alternatives" but "mentalism entails an absurd consequence." The reductio structure is a distinctive contribution.

Third, the thesis may be targeting *contemporary* versions of mentalism (like Yalcin's knowledge-based account) that have emerged *after* Brandom and Roberts, potentially claiming to avoid their objections. If Stalnaker, Yalcin, or others have refined mentalism in response to scorekeeping alternatives, the thesis could be arguing that even these refined versions still face the radical holism problem. This would make it a contribution to an ongoing dialectic, not mere repetition.

Finally, even if the core objection appears in the literature, the *specific formulation* as "radical holism about presupposition failure" may crystallize the problem in a way that makes it more forceful or clearer. Sometimes restating an argument in sharper terms is itself a philosophical contribution, especially if it makes the problem harder to evade.

VERDICT

The defence fails, though it identifies some genuine distinctions.

The objection is fundamentally correct that the thesis recapitulates the standard case against mentalism that motivated scorekeeping approaches. The defence's attempts to distinguish the thesis from Brandom and Roberts do not succeed:

On fragility vs. holism: The defence claims Brandom addresses *epistemic access* while the thesis addresses *holistic structure of failure*. But this distinction collapses under examination. Brandom's point about fragility is precisely that mental-state accounts make common ground vulnerable to any participant's mental state failing to match—which is exactly what the thesis calls "holistic failure." The epistemic inaccessibility is a symptom of the same structural problem: if common ground requires all participants' mental states, then it's both unknowable (Brandom's concern) and fragile (the thesis's concern). These are two aspects of the same issue, not distinct problems.

On Roberts and QUD: The defence claims Roberts focuses on conversational dynamics rather than disengagement. But Roberts's scoreboard model is explicitly designed to make common ground independent of participants' actual mental states—to avoid precisely the fragility problem the thesis identifies. Her framework allows presuppositions to remain in play regardless of what individual participants privately think, which is exactly the solution to the problem the thesis raises. The defence is wrong to suggest Roberts's motivation is orthogonal.

On the reductio structure: The defence claims the thesis's five-step reductio is distinctive. But this is exactly the argument structure implicit in non-mentalist critiques: mentalism makes common ground depend on mental states → this creates fragility/holism → this generates absurd consequences in disengagement cases → therefore we need public/normative accounts. The thesis has made it explicit, but the argument was already there.

On contemporary refinements: The defence speculates that the thesis might target post-Brandom versions of mentalism that claim to avoid earlier objections. But the thesis itself gives no indication of this. It targets "Stalnaker's mentalism and Yalcin's knowledge-based account" without arguing that these are refined versions that claim to escape scorekeeping objections. If this were the contribution, it would need to be explicit about what refinements are being targeted and why they still fail.

On crystallization: The defence's final point—that sharper formulation is itself a contribution—is the weakest. "Radical holism about presupposition failure" is not obviously clearer or more forceful than the standard way of putting the objection. If anything, as previous objections showed, the "radical holism" framing introduces confusions (equivocation between technical and functional failure, unfalsifiability through redefinition) that the standard formulation avoids.

The objection succeeds. The thesis has not identified a new problem with mentalism but has restated—in a somewhat less clear way—the standard objection that already motivated non-mentalist alternatives. This is not a fresh discovery but a known position in an established debate.

O18. The appearance that common ground consists of accepted propositions is an artifact of theorizing about simple assertion; in non-assertoric speech acts, common ground is better understood as a shared space of live possibilities that need not be accepted by anyone.

Scores
promise 3/5 · residual 5/5 · worst 5/5 · dead
Move · Target
reframing — Both Stalnaker and Yalcin's assumption that common ground is defined by acceptance
Sketch

The Stalnaker-Yalcin debate assumes common ground is built from accepted propositions because both theorize primarily about assertion and presupposition. But examine imperatives, questions, and conditionals: when we discuss 'what if p?' or command 'see to it that p', we place p in play without anyone accepting it. The argument turns on recognizing that 'in play' is the fundamental notion, and acceptance is just one way propositions enter play (the way characteristic of assertion). In questions, possibilities are in play precisely because unresolved; in commands, because prescribed not accepted; in conditionals, because hypothetical. This reframes the debate: the question is not whether common ground is accepted content (mental) or public commitment, but what it means for content to be conversationally live—a status that sometimes involves acceptance but often does not.

Appraiser (blind)
Reframing around non-assertoric speech acts is worthwhile but 'in play' as fundamental needs more development to be compelling.
Objections
  • MISATTRIBUTION — landed 4/5, unanswered. The objection correctly showed both theorists explicitly address non-assertoric acts within acceptance frameworks; the defence shifted to claiming their treatments fail without proving this.
  • UNFALSIFIABLE — landed 3/5, unanswered. The defence offered examples but never specified what 'conversationally live' means beyond encompassing acceptance, leaving the relabeling suspicion unresolved.
  • ALREADY TAKEN — landed 5/5, unanswered. The defence claimed to offer diagnosis rather than theory, but the objection showed this diagnosis mischaracterizes a debate occurring in full awareness of the alternatives.
  • PROVES TOO MUCH — landed 2/5, answered. The defence successfully distinguished motivated from unmotivated generalization by showing acceptance-based accounts require ad hoc machinery for their own claimed domain.
  • COUNTEREXAMPLE — landed 1/5, answered. The example actually confirmed the thesis by showing acceptance and liveness are distinct statuses, exactly as claimed.
